cia-0000119741: A CIA report sets out the situation in Hungary as of 2 p.m. on October 29, 1956, six days into the revolution, while a ceasefire held. cia-0000132241: Political developments in situation report 558, from January 1991, include Saddam giving an address the heading cuts off at the letters radi, almost surely a radio speech. cia-0000132441:
Cuba under Fidel Castro fills a CIA document dated November 4, 1959. Ten months into the revolution, the new order had a clear name and face. Castro's rule was becoming personal, centered on his own speeches, tours, and decisions.

The document profiles that order as analysts understood it in its first year. It covers how power was gathered and where it seemed to be heading. For readers, the entry is a period portrait rather than a later history. It shows the agency trying to sum up a revolution that was still changing shape. Every month it stayed in power, the shape shifted again.
cia-0000132641: A demand by Guatemala's leader Ydigoras fills a CIA item dated May 3, 1960. He wanted the Organization of American States to probe Cuban charges against his country. The headline breaks off at the word Gu, short for Guatemala. Ydigoras ruled the Guatemala that the 1954 coup backed by the agency had reshaped. The short item reports his demand.
cia-0000132741: Four reaction fronts share a CIA item on Cuba dated March 4, 1961. The item covers Cuba at the United Nations, plus Latin American, bloc, and Western European reactions. Its headline misspells European as Eruopean and breaks off mid-word. The whole world was answering events in Cuba at once that spring. The short item gathers those answers in one place.
cia-0000135941: Dated 5 January 1954, one CIA cable in the open files deals with instructions for the pending arrival of Calligeris, covering the welcome the station had to stage. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136241: Dated 5 May 1954, one CIA cable in the open files deals with Instruction 8 for the Sherwood broadcast, one more script in the long numbered series. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136341: Selection of strategic targets is not a field prerogative, LINCOLN reminds CADICK in this June 1954 cable. He will be informed of chosen targets and their priority as determined above; Matamoros proved an extremely effective target for psychological effect though only lightly damaged. If hostilities resume after the cease-fire, present plans prevail. Success without annihilation of innocent people, the station insists, must be the objective, and spare time should go to training.
cia-0000139041: Gerhart Eisler faced the stiffest test of his party career. Reuters reported it in February 1951. The wire item is preserved in this file. Eisler was propaganda chief of the Russian zone of Germany. He reportedly admitted disloyalty to Stalin. His statement ran in the SED press service bulletin, DPA reported. He admitted attacking Stalin's German policy in public. He admitted backing a compromise group. The file also recounts his 1949 flight from America. A British court refused to extradite him. He later became East German information minister.
un-ga-res-1541:
When does a colony stop being a colony for UN purposes? Resolution 1541, adopted by the General Assembly in 1960, lays down the guiding tests. Under Article 73 of the Charter, states that rule overseas lands must send facts about them to the UN. A team of six had spent a year working out when that duty ends, building on a list of tests from 1953.

The Assembly thanks the team and approves its tests, with a few changes. Those tests weigh whether a land has gained full self-rule, joined a free state as an equal, or linked itself to one by free choice. The list became the yardstick of the great wave of decolonization that swept the 1960s.
un-ga-res-41:
First principles for cutting world armaments were set down in Resolution 41 of the General Assembly, passed on 14 December 1946. Under Article 11 of the Charter, the Assembly claims its part in guarding peace. It states the need for a swift, general ordering and cut of arms and armed forces, across all states at once.

The Security Council is urged to draft the workable steps at speed, in the order of their weight. The plans would go to member states for debate at a special session of the Assembly. Pacts approved there would then go to states for ratification under Article 26. Arms given up by all at once, never by a few alone, is the rule at the heart of the text.
un-ga-res-a-69-41:
Stalled talks on nuclear disarmament are pushed forward in Resolution A/69/41, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the vote of the year before on taking such talks ahead, toward a world free of nuclear arms. Deep concern runs through it at the ruinous toll any use of such arms would bring.

All the peoples of the world, the first disarmament session held in 1978, hold a vital stake in the success of arms talks. All states have the right to sit in them. The roles of the Conference on Disarmament and the Disarmament Commission are restated. The vote is one of a yearly set that keeps the goal of a nuclear-free world on the table.
un-sc-res-341: As number 341 in the Council's series, the resolution is catalogued in this library under 1973. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1441: Preserved as Resolution 1441, this Security Council text carries a 2002 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1741: Security Council Resolution 1741 survives in this collection through a Wikisource transcription of the UN's official record. The text follows the body's standard two-part design, findings before action. Because the Council's authority depends on agreed language, the language itself is the artifact, and this entry preserves it without abridgment or commentary.
cia-0000135741: One of the Spanish papers of Brigade 2506 is dated 1 March 1961. March opened the brigade's last full month before the Bay of Pigs operation. The force had been built by the CIA from Cuban exiles opposed to Castro. The catalog record for this item states no subject. Preserved in Spanish, the document is a dated piece of the brigade's own archive from the operation's final countdown.
cia-0000136741: A Spanish-language paper dated 1 February 1961, from the declassified document cache of Brigade 2506. The brigade, Cuban exiles armed by the CIA, was in final training for the spring landing. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is held in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the brigade's February records, presented as the agency released it.
plos-pone-0000041:
José Malpica, Soledad Sacristán, Aurora Fraile, and co-authors studied germs that do not commit to one host in a 2006 paper. Multi-host pathogens infect several species, moving among them. That flexibility makes them hard to control, since curing one host leaves the others as refuges. The team examined association and host selectivity in such pathogens.

Selectivity asks whether a pathogen uses its hosts evenly or favors some over others, and association asks which hosts it links together. The answers shape how diseases jump between wildlife, livestock, and people. Knowing a pathogen's host preferences helps predict where it will strike next and where control efforts will pay off most.
un-ga-res-41-41: General Assembly Resolution 41/41 survives in the catalog under the doubled form 41 (41), dated to 1987, with no subject named in the record. The numbering ties it to the Assembly's forty-first session, which spanned late 1986 into 1987. Beyond that, the honest account is of form: a formal decision of the whole Assembly, preserved as official record text. Its topic must be taken from the text itself, since neither title nor notes in this record supply one that can be checked.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d41: On October 14, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, in a message that became Document 41 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. That day was a busy one at both ends of the Atlantic, with letters crossing in both directions. The record for this item gives the date and the two leaders' names and no more. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, five days before the Moscow Conference opened.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d141: On November 18, 1943, Churchill wrote to Roosevelt, as the British party also closed on Cairo. His message is Document 141 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Four days remained before the conference opened, and the letters of that week have the feel of men packing for an argument. The record supplies the date and the names. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d241:
Patrick Hurley, the President's personal representative, wrote to Roosevelt from Cairo on 20 November 1943 after inspecting the China theater of operations. He had met Generals Stilwell and Chennault, toured with air commander Stratemeyer, and spent some six hours in talks with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek.

Hurley's conclusions are warm. Chiang trusts Roosevelt fully, favors democracy and liberty, opposes imperialism and communism. He will follow Roosevelt's lead on political questions at the coming conference. He hopes it restates the Atlantic Charter and the Four Freedoms. On strategy he holds one firm line: in the China theater he must remain supreme. He will not take a subordinate place under Lord Mountbatten. Still, he praises Mountbatten and offers full cooperation in Burma.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d341:
Assistant Secretary of War John McCloy sent Harry Hopkins a second memorandum at Cairo on 30 November 1943, separate from the civil affairs agreement of the same day. This one concerns a proposed joint committee for all French questions, an idea from Secretary Hull.

In his talk with Eden, McCloy had raised Hull's suggestion of a new body. It would be modeled somewhat on the combined committees. All dealings with the French would be cleared through it for the time being. Hull hoped it would end the irritation and distrust bred by the two nations' separate French policies. Eden approved promptly, and Hull cabled that the group should sit in London. McCloy pictures it as informal, a military man and a foreign affairs man from each government, drawing on other agencies as needed, and asks whether the President favors pushing it along.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d441: Under the number 441, the Cairo-Tehran volume prints a short editorial note. Department historians added notes like this one throughout the conference record. Their job is to fill gaps, give context, and flag related documents. The surrounding papers come from the Cairo and Tehran meetings of 1943. At those meetings the Allied leaders set the course for the war's next year. Treat the note as the editors speaking directly to the reader.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d541:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on January 7, 1944, in the opening week of the year the Tehran Conference had planned for. Churchill had recovered from the illness that struck him after Cairo. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The Roosevelt-Churchill correspondence never rested for long, and early January found the two governments converting summit decisions into the Normandy invasion plan. A Churchill letter of this date belongs to that conversion: priorities argued, resources counted, and two leaders keeping their partnership warm by constant writing. Readers see the alliance's engine room at the start of its biggest year.
frus-1944-quebec-d41:
Another Churchill message reached Roosevelt on August 31, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. It sits beside the day's other letter.

Two messages on the month's last day fit a pattern. A leader was clearing his desk before a voyage. The Quebec agenda was heavy that September. It covered the final campaigns in Europe. It covered Germany's treatment after defeat. It also covered the terms of American aid. For readers, the message shows Churchill arriving at the conference on paper. His British positions were argued in advance. The conference opened at Quebec City that September.
frus-1944-quebec-d141:
British chiefs of staff representatives answered the American strategy paper on September 2, 1944, in C.C.S. 654/1. They proposed three amendments to the basic undertakings Washington had drafted for the coming staff conference. In all other respects, they said, the American proposals were acceptable, which makes the small wording changes the real subject here.

One amendment added coordinated action with Russian forces to the pledge of aid, noting the armies were converging. Another extended assistance beyond French and Italian forces to other co-belligerents, such as Turkey or satellites changing sides. The third softened the rush to the Pacific: moving forces east should have regard to other inescapable commitments.
frus-1944-quebec-d241:
General Wilson asked the Combined Chiefs for guidance on economic policy for Italy on September 13, 1944. As the battle line moved north, he wrote, the operational phase was ending across large areas, and the approach to civilian supply and rehabilitation had to be re-examined. His directives, built for active operations, no longer fitted the situation he faced as president of the Control Commission.

The armistice promised Italians no material assistance, Wilson noted, yet an expectation of relief had arisen from both governments' known humanitarian policies. Governing only by military necessity risked losing a reasonably prosperous, contented postwar Italy. He cited a winter clothing program: he was now asked to certify it as the bare minimum to prevent disease and unrest, though it had been designed on estimated essential needs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d41: Wilson Brown, the president's naval aide, wrote on 3 January 1945 to Admiral Charles Cooke, chief of staff to the fleet commander. His message is document 41 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta. Naval aides handled the movement of the president himself, so staff papers like this one connect the summit's diplomacy to ships, routes, and sailing schedules.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d141:
Had Roosevelt secretly agreed to the Curzon Line at Tehran? Harriman's memorandum of 16 October 1944 answers a Polish claim that he had. Polish Foreign Minister Romer called at Spaso House in Moscow with a letter from Premier Mikolajczyk. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Romer's letter concerned Molotov's account of the President's Tehran position. Harriman told him the account was wrong. Roosevelt had not agreed to the Curzon Line at Tehran. He had made plain he would take no stand on the boundary, in private or in public. Harriman also explained why he had not challenged Molotov at the meeting itself. He had sat there as an observer, and it was not the place to argue over what the President had said.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d241:
Iran gets a four-part treatment in this briefing paper of 6 January 1945, “Memoranda Concerning Iran.” Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary calls Iran a testing ground for three-power cooperation and for the principles of Dumbarton Oaks.

American policy backs Iranian independence and seeks to strengthen the country from within, so excuses for outside meddling shrink. Along the climb stands the famous master and slave dialectic, where work and recognition remake both parties, an idea Marx and later thinkers seized upon. Hegel finished the manuscript as Napoleon's army approached Jena. The German text is thought's most demanding mountain in this library; readers of the original meet Marx, existentialism, and much modern theory at one of their sources.
tob-13141:
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras compress the whole path of yoga into 196 short sayings. Charles Johnston edited and translated them under the title The Book of the Spiritual Man. The sayings are terse, almost like notes, and each one rewards slow reading.

Johnston's commentary unpacks the eight limbs of yoga, from right conduct and posture through breath control to deep absorption, called samadhi. The goal is to still the movements of the mind so the true self stands clear. Students of yoga still treat the Sutras as their root text, and Johnston's edition remains one of the clearest doors into it.
tob-4214-10741:
Arthur Schopenhauer, the great pessimist, surprised readers with the warm, practical essays of The Wisdom of Life. T. Bailey Saunders translated them into the English most readers still use. Schopenhauer divides human good into what a person is, what a person has, and what others think of him.

Only the first, he argues, truly counts toward happiness. Health, character, and a rich inner life outweigh wealth and fame, which rest on chance and opinion. His advice sounds like Stoic counsel in modern dress. The gloomy thinker turns out to be a shrewd, humane guide to getting through life well.
tob-4141:
Waite restored and enlarged the Hermetic Museum in 1893, and volume one of that fuller edition stands here. The famed tracts include the Golden Tripod, Sendivogius's New Light of Alchemy, and the Sophic Hydrolith, each a classic of the spagyric art. Waite edits and translates with his usual full apparatus.

Instructions for the disciples of the art mix laboratory hints with spiritual counsel, since Waite read alchemy as both at once. Checked from the 1919 printing, the volume improves on the older Latin collection it revives. Students of the old tracts still begin with Waite's Museum when they want the canon in English.
tob-9141:
Part two of Darmesteter's Avesta completes the Zoroastrian scriptures in the Sacred Books of the East form, verified from the 1919 scan. The Yasna liturgy, with its hymns and the Gathas at its heart, leads the volume. The Visperad and the lesser texts, hymns and fragments, follow in order.

Priests still recite the Yasna before the sacred fire, in words few now parse but all revere. Darmesteter's notes trace each rite and being to its roots. With part one, the set gives ancient Persia's worship entire in English. The Avesta's survival, through so many lost centuries, is itself remarkable.
tob-0041:
John Jacob Nutter, a political scientist, published The CIA's Black Ops with Prometheus Books in 2000. The book examines CIA covert action and its effects on foreign policy and democracy. Nutter writes as a critic with a scholar's apparatus.

Case by case, he argues that secret operations bend policy away from public control, prop up clients, and corrode democratic practice at home and abroad. Coups, paramilitary wars, and covert funding all come under his charge sheet. The book belongs to the post-Cold War reckoning with the agency's hidden hand, and it gives readers a sourced, prosecutorial account of covert action's costs.
michelet-proces-des-templiers-vol-1-1841:
Jules Michelet, the great French historian, edited the trial records of the Knights Templar for the Royal Press at Paris in 1841. This first volume covers the case against the order, which France crushed between 1307 and 1314. The text is in French, drawn from the old court papers.

Readers get the questions put to the knights, their sworn answers, and the pope's own documents on the affair. Under torture and fear, many men confessed to charges they later took back. Michelet's edition let readers judge the famous case from the raw record for the first time.
michelet-proces-des-templiers-vol-2-1841:
Jules Michelet's edition of the Templar trials closes with this second volume, printed at Paris in 1841. It picks up where the first volume left off in the court record of 1307 to 1314. The French text prints the rest of the case against the Knights Templar.

More hearings follow, with further sworn statements from knights, servants, and churchmen. The papers show the trial grinding on toward the order's end and the death of its last master. Read with volume one, it gives the fullest old record of the Templars' fall. The two volumes together print the core of the surviving trial record.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol1-1841:
Jules Quicherat opened his great edition of Joan of Arc's trials in 1841 with the record of her condemnation. Procès de Condamnation et de Réhabilitation de Jeanne d'Arc, volume one, prints the Latin trial text of 1431. Joan was nineteen when a church court at Rouen sent her to the fire.

The volume gives the charges, the long questioning, and her answers as the court clerks wrote them down. Readers meet her voice under pressure, session by session. Quicherat's edition became the base for all later study of Joan. The first volume is where that study starts: in the courtroom itself.
robert-boron-saint-graal-michel-1841:
Robert de Boron gave the Grail its Christian root in two romances of the years around 1200. Le Roman du Saint-Graal, in Francisque Michel's 1841 edition of the Old French, holds his Joseph of Arimathea and his Merlin. No earlier texts bind the Grail cup to the Passion.

Joseph tells how the cup that held Christ's blood came west and who kept it. Merlin tells of the prophet's birth, his gifts, and his hand in Arthur's rise. Every later Grail tale, from the great cycles to Malory, descends from these two. Michel's edition prints the founding texts in their first tongue.
hawthorne-grandfathers-chair-1841:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Whole History of Grandfather's Chair in 1841, a history for children. The book tells New England history, from the Puritans to the Revolution, through one old chair. Hawthorne wrote it for young readers in the days before his fame as a romancer grew.

Grandfather, in a Boston parlor, traces his chair's owners through persecutions, wars, and witch trial years. The chair hears of Endicott, King Philip's War, and the Boston Tea Party in its long life. Children Laurence, Clara, and little Alice question, doubt, and dream over the tales by the fireside. Hawthorne makes dry annals into scenes a child can feel, without hiding the era's harsh deeds. It was a pioneer work of American history written for the young at home.
emerson-essays-first-series-1841:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Essays: First Series in 1841, with Self-Reliance and The Over-Soul inside. The book is the founding document of American intellectual independence in prose of rare force and fire. Emerson had honed the essays as lectures, and their voice still sounds spoken and urgent on the page.

Self-Reliance commands trust in one's own thought against conformity, consistency, and the crowd's dull pressure in life. The Over-Soul traces one spirit through all souls, the ground of his calm moral optimism in man. History, Compensation, and Circles round out a set that young America took as a charter of selfhood. Lines like trust thyself entered the language and never left common American speech since that day. The book still serves as the doorway into Emerson for most new readers.
carlyle-heroes-1841:
Thomas Carlyle published On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History in 1841, from a set of lectures. Carlyle argues that great men shape the course of history. He treats the hero in six forms: god, prophet, poet, priest, man of letters, and king. Odin, Muhammad, Dante, Shakespeare, Luther, and Napoleon appear among them.

History, in his famous claim, is the biography of great men. The book stated the great-man theory in its classic form. It shaped Victorian biography and popular history for decades. Modern readers often resist its claims yet enjoy its force. It is a key text for the study of leadership myths.
cooper-deerslayer-1841:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Deerslayer in 1841, the last Leatherstocking tale written and the first in the hero's life. Cooper went back to Natty Bumppo's youth on Lake Otsego, the Glimmerglass of the novel, in the 1740s. The book completes the five-volume arc of America's first epic hero.

Young Natty, called Deerslayer, joins his friend Chingachgook to rescue a kidnapped Delaware maiden from the Hurons. Around a floating ark and a settler's lake castle, scalp hunters and soldiers push Natty toward his first killing. He takes a human life reluctantly and earns a new name, Hawkeye. Cooper builds the moral code of the American hero here: merciful, truthful, and deadly only when forced. It is the genesis volume of the Leatherstocking Tales.
lafontaine-fables-wright-1841:
Jean de La Fontaine published his Fables in France in books that appeared from 1668 onward. Elizur Wright turned them into English verse in 1841, and his version became a classic in its own right. The tales are short poems, most of them about animals who talk and scheme like people.

Foxes, wolves, ants, and grasshoppers act out pride, greed, folly, and wit. Each fable ends with a pointed moral, often sly rather than preachy. La Fontaine drew on Aesop and older sources but made the verse light, shrewd, and musical. French children still learn these poems by heart, and Wright's rhymes carry much of their charm into English.
stanhope-epictetus-simplicius-1741:
Epictetus, a freed slave who taught in Greece under the Roman Empire, left a short handbook of Stoic life called the Enchiridion. George Stanhope turned it into English, and his version first appeared in 1694. The fifth edition of 1741 adds the long commentary of Simplicius, a scholar of the sixth century, plus a life of Epictetus from Boileau.

Simplicius works through the handbook line by line, drawing out its rules on what we can and cannot control. For generations this was the form in which English readers met Stoic ethics. It stays the only pre-modern English version of Simplicius on the handbook.
al-masudi-meadows-of-gold-sprenger-1841:
Al-Masudi was a traveler from Baghdad. He saw India, Africa, and the Caspian lands in the tenth century, and he wrote the Muruj al-Dhahab, the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems. Aloys Sprenger gave the first part of it English form in 1841. Only this first volume of his version ever appeared.

The Meadows is a cabinet of the world. It holds the making of the earth, the kings of Persia and India, the seas, the wonders, and the tales told in ports. Al-Masudi asks questions everywhere he goes and writes down what he hears, gold and dross together. Sprenger's volume lets English readers taste the great Arab Herodotus. The full French version stands in the library beside it.
miller-old-red-sandstone-1841:
Hugh Miller was a Scottish stonemason who taught himself geology in the quarries of Cromarty. His Old Red Sandstone, published in 1841, grew from letters written for a local paper. It made him famous almost at once.

Miller describes the strange fossil fishes locked in red rock layers near his home. He writes of their scales, fins, and armor with a poet's eye. At the time, such finds raised hard questions about the age of the earth. The book became a classic of popular geology for its clear prose and wonder. Stone by stone, he reads a vanished sea full of strange life.
fielding-shamela-1741:
Fielding's Shamela, from 1741, is the sharp little burlesque that started the novel wars. Its full title promises an apology for the life of Mrs Shamela Andrews. Fielding, writing under a comic mask, attacks Richardson's Pamela, the hit novel of the hour.

In letters like Richardson's own, Shamela lets readers see her true game: her virtue is bait to trap her master into marriage. The jokes expose the cant of the original while inventing a livelier rogue. Shamela runs to barely fifty pages, yet it launched Fielding toward Joseph Andrews. Readers still enjoy its wicked speed and its place in literary history.
plos-pone-0003441:
Alain Medawar and co-authors hunted the switch that starts skin formation in this 2008 paper. A protein called p63 guides the growth of layered skin-like tissues. Its exact job, and which form does it, stayed disputed. The team tested p63 in embryonic stem cells as they began to change.

One form, named ΔNp63, proved essential for the first step. Without it, stem cells could not commit to becoming epidermis, the outer skin. With it, the skin program could begin. The finding defines a master switch for growing skin from stem cells.
plos-pone-0003541:
Mauricio H. Pontes and co-authors studied a fly's resident bacterium in this 2008 paper. Sodalis glossinidius lives inside tsetse flies and passes from mother to young. It senses its own density with chemical signals, a system called quorum sensing. Those signals tune its gene expression as numbers grow.

Quorum sensing primed the bacterium's defense against oxidative stress. The cells braced for damage before it arrived. Even a friendly endosymbiont prepares for hostile chemistry. Counting neighbors lets it time that preparation well. Tsetse flies spread sleeping sickness, so their resident microbes draw study.
plos-pone-0003641:
Xiaoxue Fan, Skylar Martin-Brown, Laurence Florens, and colleagues published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Actin filaments give yeast cells their shape and drive their movement. The strands are built and taken apart at a fast rate. The team studied the protein cofilin, which breaks filaments down.

They found that budding yeast cofilin can, on its own, drive turnover of filaments bound by tropomyosin. Tropomyosin coats and guards these strands, so the result was not a given. It shows a core renewal step in the cell's skeleton needs no extra helpers, at least in yeast.
plos-pone-0003741:
Patricia C. Lopes, Élio Sucena, M. Emília Santos, and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Pesticide resistance spreads fast in the wild and offers a clean model of adaptation. How quickly it evolves, and what it costs the organism, were still open questions. The team ran experimental evolution in the worm C. elegans.

Lab populations evolved pesticide resistance rapidly under selection. The resistance came with no apparent fitness costs in their tests. The mating system of the worms also shaped how the process played out, a warning that resistance can arise easily when adapting is cheap.
plos-pone-0003841:
Ya-li Li, Guang-zhi Wu, Gavin S. Dawe, and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The sugars coating a cell's surface shape how it interacts with its neighbors. Two such coatings, sialylation and fucosylation, add sialic acid and fucose sugars to surface molecules. What controls them in nerve cells was the question.

The team found the adhesion molecule L1 regulates both coatings, acting through phospholipase C gamma. The sugar changes cooperate to tune neurite outgrowth, cell survival, and migration. The work links one surface protein to the chemistry that helps young neurons grow and move.
plos-pone-0003941:
Jérôme Beaufays, Benoît Adam, Yves Decrem, and co-authors catalogued proteins from tick saliva in 2008. Ticks feed on blood for long stretches without being rejected. Their saliva carries many proteins that blunt the host's defenses. Lipocalins among them help calm inflammation at the bite site.

Their PLOS ONE article identifies lipocalins from the tick Ixodes ricinus. The team cloned the genes and charted how the proteins relate. They also tested what the proteins do at a chemical level. Tick proteins of this kind are targets for anti-tick vaccines. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004041:
Kentaroh Takagaki, Michael Thomas Lippert, Benjamin Dann, and co-authors improved a brain imaging measure in 2008. Voltage-sensitive dyes let scientists film activity across brain tissue. Signal size is usually scaled by total fluorescence, the delta-F over F method. That scaled signal measures population activity in tissue.

Their PLOS ONE article proposes normalizing dye signals with functional activity measures. Better scaling makes maps from different sessions comparable. It also sharpens estimates of how space is represented. Imaging labs can adopt the fix without new hardware. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see. Each claim in it can be checked in the full text that sits with this record.
plos-pone-0004141:
Craig McClain and colleagues published this deep-sea study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The deep ocean below one kilometre covers most of Earth's surface. Scattered across its plains and slopes stand about 14,000 seamounts, underwater mountains rising at least a kilometre off the seafloor.

Ecologists have long debated what seamounts do for sea life: whether they host unique species found nowhere else, and how their animal communities are built. The team surveyed one seamount in the northeast Pacific, recording which species live there and how the community is structured. Their data test long-standing ideas about seamounts as islands of unique life in the deep sea.
plos-pone-0004241:
Sandra Diaz and colleagues published this detection study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Humans cannot make Neu5Gc, a sialic acid common in other mammals, but we absorb it from food, especially red meat and milk. The absorbed molecules end up in human tumours, fetuses, and some normal tissues, and in biotherapeutic products made in animal cells.

The team present a sensitive and specific method for detecting Neu5Gc in human tissues and products. Reliable detection matters for judging the safety of animal-made medicines and for studying what dietary molecules do inside us. That makes the test useful for checking such medicines before they reach patients.
plos-pone-0004341:
Hilkka Turakainen and colleagues published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Conditional gene targeting, switching genes off in chosen tissues or at chosen times, is progressively used to study gene function. Every such strategy needs a targeting vector, a DNA construct built to order, and any method that streamlines building them would be valued.

The authors present a transposition-based method for the rapid generation of gene-targeting vectors. The resulting vectors can produce Cre and Flp modifiable conditional knock-out mice. Faster vector building removes a notorious bottleneck between a research question and a mouse that answers it.
plos-pone-0004441:
Cows may know each other's faces, a claim tested by Marjorie Coulon, Bertrand Deputte, Yvan Heyman, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Social animals need to read social cues well to keep their groups together. True recognition of individuals by sight had been shown in only a few mammal species.

The team showed cattle flat images of heads from different breeds and watched how the animals responded. They looked for proof that a cow treats one known individual as itself, not just that it can tell two pictures apart. Evidence of face-based recognition would change how farmers think about herd life. It would also place cattle higher on the scale of social smarts than many assume.
plos-pone-0004541:
Natural background radiation in Kerala, India, may have left unique signatures on the male Y chromosome, report Sanjay Premi, Jyoti Srivastava, Sebastian Padinjarel Chandy, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ionizing radiation most often causes chromosome lesions and cancers, though the whole genome may be affected. The Y chromosome is a good place to look for such effects.

Because the Y is passed only from father to son and does not swap parts with a partner chromosome, changes in it accumulate in a clean line. Kerala has areas of unusually high natural radiation. Comparing Y chromosomes there with those from low-radiation areas can reveal long-term, low-dose effects that lab studies cannot. The work speaks to radiation safety for whole populations.
plos-pone-0004641:
The full genome of a pig gut pathogen reveals how it is built for life in the large intestine. Matthew Bellgard, Phatthanaphong Wanchanthuek, Tom La, and co-authors report on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacterium is Brachyspira hyodysenteriae, an anaerobic intestinal spirochete. It colonizes the large intestine of pigs and causes swine dysentery, a disease of significant economic importance.

The team determined the genome sequence of strain WA1, the first representative of its group to be sequenced. Reading the whole genome reveals adaptations to its lifestyle in the porcine gut. Genes for feeding, attaching, and surviving without oxygen can now be listed and studied. That list supports vaccines and tests for a disease that costs pig farmers heavily.
plos-pone-0004741:
Anna Abraham and Yves von Cramon asked if brain response to fiction rests on how relevant it feels, in PLOS ONE in 2009. People slip into made up worlds each time they read a novel or watch a film. Yet little was known about how the brain keeps real and made up apart without effort.

Their study was the first brain scan work on that split. They tracked the brain default network as people judged real versus fiction. Shifts in that network tracked how close or relevant scenes felt. The work links self thought networks to how we enter stories.
fdr-four-freedoms-1941:
Franklin D. Roosevelt gave his Four Freedoms address on January 6, 1941. The State of the Union speech named the aims worth defending. Freedom of speech and of worship lead his famed list.

Freedom from want and freedom from fear complete the four points. Roosevelt spoke as war raged abroad and America still stood apart. His phrases gave the coming struggle a clear moral charter. The speech urged aid to nations fighting Hitler's armed might. Four short phrases still sum up America's best account of itself in wartime. Painters and posters soon carried the freedoms into every American home.
fdr-day-of-infamy-1941:
Roosevelt addressed Congress on December 8, 1941, the day after Pearl Harbor. His Day of Infamy speech runs barely six minutes in full. Few addresses in the nation's history carry such concentrated weight.

A date which will live in infamy, he calls the attack's day. He lists Japan's strikes across the Pacific in a grim roll. Then he asks Congress to declare that war has been thrust upon America. The vote came within the hour, and the nation mobilized at once. Six minutes of calm fury took the United States into world war at last. The speech is still taught as a model of crisis address.
atlantic-charter-1941:
Roosevelt and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter in August 1941. The two leaders met aboard warships off the coast of Newfoundland. Their joint text set aims for the war and the peace.

No land hunger, the charter pledges, and self-rule for all peoples. Free trade, shared labor gains, and seas free to all follow. Victorious nations will disarm the beaten foes and guard the peace. America had not yet entered the war when the words were signed. The promise of a better world became the Allies' moral charter for victory. Its pledges later fed the charter of the United Nations itself.
massachusetts-body-of-liberties-1641:
Massachusetts Bay Colony adopted the Body of Liberties in 1641, its first full code of laws. Minister Nathaniel Ward did much of the drafting, drawing on the Bible and English legal practice. The code lists about one hundred liberties, duties, and rules for colonial life.

Its clauses protect life, property, and fair trials, and they limit cruel punishments. Other parts cover women, children, servants, strangers, and even cruelty toward animals. Some rules feel harsh today, since the colony tied law closely to Scripture. Even so, the code stands as an early American attempt to write rights down.
cia-0000008641:
January 1973 opened with a report of a downed American jet in Nam Ha province, North Vietnam. The heading indicates the pilots' fate formed part of the report, though the title breaks off. Nam Ha sits south of Hanoi, along routes the air war struck for years.

Reports filed this close to the January ceasefire straddle war and postwar accounting. Officials needed to know which losses were confirmed and which men might still be held. A downed jet with named crew could anchor a case file for years. The entry shows the record still growing as the fighting stopped.
cia-0000008941:
Haiphong province is named in an April 1973 report on the death of an American pilot in North Vietnam. The port city region saw intense bombing in 1972, including mining of its harbor. By spring 1973, prisoners were coming home, but the dead still had to be accounted for.

A death report could rest on witnesses, graves, or local records passed through many hands. Analysts graded each source before adding it to a man's file. This entry shows that grading process beginning with a single provincial report. The accounting it fed continued for decades after the war had ended.
cia-0000009441:
Americans remaining in Saigon leads a June 1976 CIA item, followed by a reported capture of two Americans near a place the title cuts off. Saigon had been under communist rule for over a year by then. Reports from inside the city reached Washington slowly and indirectly.

The item gathers what could be learned about Americans who stayed through the takeover. A reported capture added urgency, since postwar detentions had no clear process or end. Analysts logged names and claims in hopes of later confirmation. The file shows the fall of Saigon still generating cases well into 1976.
cia-0000011841:
Revolution was the fear hanging over Latin America in 1968, and a CIA paper that February measures the potential for it across the hemisphere. Cuba's example had inspired guerrilla movements from Guatemala to Bolivia, while military regimes ruled many countries. The paper came in a year of upheaval around the world, from Paris to Mexico City.

Analysts surveyed the guerrillas, the generals, and the grievances that fed revolt in each land. They judged where unrest might turn into real bids for power. The survey reads as Washington's map of a tinderbox, drawn by men counting sparks country by country.
cia-0000012341:
John Maury, a CIA officer, wrote a memo for the record in March 1962 about conversations with men whose names are blanked out. The memo belongs to the Penkovsky file's working layer, below the summit letters. There, officers set down talks as they happened, while tone and detail were still fresh in the mind and could still be checked.

The plain value of writing things down fresh shows in every line of such records. They became the case as it truly happened, before memory could reshape it. For readers, Maury's notes are the handlers' craft at its most basic and most useful.
cia-0000013241:
Viet Cong policy and treatment of prisoners of war are studied in a CIA paper from July 1968. The year was the war's peak, and the doctrine had hardened with it. The paper sets out the southern system's official rules for captives. It then tests those rules against what the camps actually did, as reported by escapees, defectors, and the released.

The study shows policy and practice pulling against each other. Rules written at headquarters met hunger, distance, and local cruelty in the jungle. For readers, the paper is the southern doctrine read whole, at the moment the war burned hottest.
cia-0000013841:
Twelve American prisoners were captured in Kontum province, and a CIA item from March 1967 counts them. Kontum, in the Central Highlands, saw some of the war's hardest fighting. The highlands' war was fought over ridges, trails, and small camps far from the coast. Its captives paid accordingly, marched into a prison system whose highland camps were among the war's most obscure and most feared.

The item fixes the twelve in the record while their trails were warm. Twelve men in one note is the highland war's scale in miniature. For readers, the page is the highlands' chapter of the accounting: the twelve, taken.
cia-0000015441: Minutes of a branch chiefs' meeting held August 11, 1952, survive in a CIA record dated July 1, 1952. Branch chiefs ran the working parts of the young agency, and their minutes note what leaders raised. Flying objects were drawing wide public attention that summer. The catalog title alone does not say what the chiefs decided, so nothing more is claimed here.
cia-0000022241: A United States prisoner of war was sighted in Huu Quan village, in the Haiphong area, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. Haiphong was North Vietnam's great port, ringed by villages. A village sighting placed a captive outside the known prison camps. Each such glimpse was mapped and dated, in hope of fixing where men were truly held.
cia-0000022341: Questions put to Powers about the cause of the crash fill a CIA record dated in 1962. The heading adds the words fair image, clipped from a longer line. Why the U-2 came down, missile, failure, or flameout, was argued for years. Asking the pilot himself was the plainest path, and the questions show officials still seeking his answers after his return.
cia-0000023241: An American prisoner of war was held in Viet Cong Inter-Region 5, a CIA record dated in 1971 reports, with a cover memo attached. Inter-Region 5 was the Viet Cong's zone across the central coast provinces. Knowing which region held a man narrowed the map for rescue and accounting work. The cover memo shows the report moving through channels in the usual way.
cia-0000044041:
Cristiani promised an investigation into the assassinations, in a CIA record dated October 6, 1989 in the catalog. The title ties the promise to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Assassinations, in the plural, was the president's own framing here.

Inside, the pledge of an inquiry is preserved as he made it. Promises made under world pressure are tested by what follows them. In this case the test ran through years of hearings and trials. The file holds the pledge at its bright beginning, when the words were new and the country was still waiting to learn what they were worth.
cia-0000046641: General Dmitri Volkogonov reported progress in tracing American servicemen missing from the Vietnam War, and a CIA item dated November 2, 1992, kept his update. Volkogonov, a Russian historian-general, was opening Soviet-era archives to the joint search. His reports marked a strange new chapter: Moscow's files helping to close America's oldest war cases.
cia-0000049041: Military commanders in El Salvador decided in 1982 to ask the president to reopen a legal case, and a CIA item from that year preserves the request. Generals petitioning a president inverted the usual order, which is what makes the item stand out. The case behind the request sits in the document's pages and in the Truth Commission files around it.
cia-0000049141: A thousand fresh FMLN troops moved toward San Salvador in 1989, and a CIA item tracks the movement and the planned role of Father Ignacio Ellacuria. Ellacuria, the Jesuit university rector, was the country's best-known voice for a negotiated peace. Troop movements and peace feelers in one file: the war's two tracks, running side by side in the same record.
cia-0000049241:
Roberto D'Aubuisson's terrorist activities are the subject of a CIA paper from 1984, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. D'Aubuisson, a former army major, led El Salvador's far right and founded the ARENA party. American officials of the era tied his network, in private and sometimes in public, to the death squads.

A paper with this title, in the agency's own files, marks how directly the charge was stated inside the government. It covers the activities attributed to his circle at the height of the terror, when naming him carried diplomatic cost. The paper remains a key document for anyone tracing the squads to their political home.
cia-0000049341: Increasing violence and terrorism in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049341, dated March 6, 1981. Noted for the Truth Commission, the item tracks a rise in violence as its central concern. The short file preserves that assessment in its heading, offering readers a dated marker of how the agency described conditions in the country then.
cia-0000095041: Analysis of the problems created by the schism in the Gaullist majority, partly deleted, is declassified CIA document 0000095041, dated July 3, 1967. The heading names a split inside the Gaullist majority in France. The brief file is an analysis item on that political problem, preserved with its deletion marker visible in the catalog title.
cia-0000096941: Program Interagency Relationships is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000096941, dated May 4, 1972. The title concerns how programs related across agencies, in bureaucratic wording. The brief file shares its date with the neighboring program objectives record, and together they sketch an internal paperwork pair from the counterintelligence staff's files. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.
cia-0000098441: Take one of two and take two of two, presenting El Salvador FDR's Ungo on kidnapping and dialogue, form declassified CIA document 0000098441, dated September 2, 1985. The heading reads like broadcast takes. Readers find a two-part record of Ungo speaking, preserved in take form rather than as a finished transcript or report.
cia-0000098741: Max Planck Society founds physics institute in eastern Germany, according to declassified CIA document 0000098741, dated October 4, 1991. The heading names the society and the new institute's field. Readers get a short declassified founding notice, a science item preserved among the agency's records from the first years after German reunification. The catalog keeps the record under its original subject heading.

plos-pone-0004841:
Mara Almog and Alon Korngreen marked voltage gated calcium conductances in layer 5 neocortical pyramidal neurons from rats, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neuronal voltage gated calcium channels are involved in electrical signaling and converting signals into cytoplasmic calcium changes. One key function is generating regenerative dendritic calcium spikes. Yet calcium dependent steps in pyramidal dendrites remained incompletely defined despite their role in synaptic integration and plasticity.

Detailed conductance profiles clarify dendritic computations. Layer five neurons are major cortical outputs. Their calcium signals shape learning and perception. Pharmacology can now target specific channels. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0005441:
Manuel Forero and colleagues built a tool to count dying cells in fruit flies for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Cell death shapes growth, cancer, nerve disease, and the effects of drugs. Yet counting dead cells by hand is slow and often rough.

Their program, DeadEasy Caspase, counts cells marked by a key death enzyme in fly tissue images. It does the count on its own, in a fast and even way. A reliable count helps workers compare drugs, genes, and disease states without the bias that creeps into hand counts. Counts from the program can be compared across flies and treatments in minutes rather than hours.
plos-pone-0005541:
Frantz Depaulis, Ludovic Orlando, and Catherine Hänni warned about timing in population genetics in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. New data sets mix DNA from samples of very different ages, thanks to ancient DNA work and fast-evolving microbes. Classic analysis tools assume all samples come from one time.

The authors showed that ignoring the age spread can warp the results. They set out how to handle samples drawn from different times. Their guidance matters for anyone reading the history of species, farms, or germs from DNA of mixed ages. The same caution applies to farm animals and microbes sampled across long spans of time.
plos-pone-0005641:
Ingrid Olsen and co-authors isolated T cells from the gut of Crohn's disease patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Crohn's disease is a long-lasting inflammation of the intestine whose cause is unknown. An overreaction to gut bacteria in people with the wrong genes is the leading idea.

The team fished out T cells from gut samples that react to a bacterium suspected of a role in a similar animal disease. Finding such cells in patients supports the bacterial overreaction idea. It also names a target for tests and treatments. Such reactive cells in the gut wall are hard to reach, which is why isolating them at all is a step forward.
plos-pone-0005741:
Benjamin Myers, Yaron Sigal, and David Julius compared a cold-sensing channel across species in 2009. The channel, TRPM8, opens in the cold and gives the cool feel of mint. Animals that keep a steady body heat and those that drift with the weather both use it.

Yet the channel answers heat very differently in different species, the team found. They traced those gaps to the channel's evolution. How a frog and a mammal sense cold need not match, even with the same part. The study shows evolution tuning one sensor to many climates and ways of life.
plos-pone-0005841:
Pär Comstedt and co-authors mapped the tangled population structure of a Lyme disease bacterium in 2009. Borrelia garinii causes Lyme borreliosis across Europe and Asia. Birds carry it in two great cycles, one marine with seabirds, one land-based with songbirds.

Sampling across subarctic Eurasia, the team found a complex mix of strains tied to those cycles. Migrating birds can move strains vast distances, blurring local patterns. That mixing complicates tracking which strains infect people. The map helps health agencies read Lyme risk in northern regions where the disease is spreading with warming climates.
plos-pone-0006441:
Jiayuan Quan and Jingdong Tian presented a simpler way to clone genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Modern genomics and synthetic biology need fast, cheap ways to assemble genes, gene libraries, and whole pathways. Existing methods can be slow or costly. The authors set out to build a method that avoids those limits.

They describe circular polymerase extension cloning, a technique the title calls extremely simple. It aims to join complex gene sets in a streamlined process. A method like this can speed up building test genes and synthetic pathways. Lower cost and effort also put advanced cloning within reach of more labs.
plos-pone-0006541:
Rachel Kendal, Jeremy Kendal, Will Hoppitt, and colleagues offered a new method to spot social learning in animals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Studies of natural populations reveal widespread evidence for diffusion of novel behavior patterns. They also show variation in behavior within and between populations. But telling social learning from individual discovery is hard.

Their 'option-bias' method offers a statistical way to identify social learning. It asks whether animals disproportionately choose the option their group favors. A reliable method can settle debates about animal culture. It applies to wild populations where experiments are impossible.
plos-pone-0006641:
Julius Halaschek-Wiener and co-authors surveyed genetic variation in the healthy oldest-old in PLOS ONE in 2009. Individuals who live to eighty-five and beyond without developing major age-related diseases are special. They may achieve this, in part, by lacking disease susceptibility factors, or by possessing resistance factors. The team studied genetic variation in such healthy oldest-old people.

What the exceptionally healthy lack can be as informative as what the sick carry. Their genomes are a natural experiment in successful aging. Comparing them with general populations may reveal protective variants. Protective factors are attractive drug leads, since mimicking them should be safe.
plos-pone-0009441:
Diane Brown and colleagues used mice to model a rare immune crisis in PLOS ONE in 2010. The crisis is called HLH. In it, the immune system runs out of control and harms the body. It can follow infections, cancers, or immune diseases. A good animal model of the full syndrome had been lacking.

Mice with a long lasting typhoid like infection grew the full set of HLH signs on their own. No extra trigger was needed. That makes the model close to how the syndrome can arise in people. Researchers can now follow its course in mice and test ways to calm it.
plos-pone-0009541:
James Stevens and co-authors issued a caution about a common lab tool in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in the enzyme SOD1 cause some cases of ALS, a disease that kills motor nerve cells. To study SOD1, many labs attach a glowing tag called GFP to it. The tag lets them watch the protein in living cells. The team asked whether the tag itself changes the protein.

They found that the GFP tag does alter how SOD1 behaves. Its traits in tests shifted when the tag was present. That means some past results may reflect the tag, not the disease protein. The paper urges care in how tagged proteins are used across ALS research.
plos-pone-0009641:
Victoria Wang and co-authors traced a low oxygen response gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. When oxygen runs short, cells switch on hypoxia inducible factors. Two main forms exist, HIF-1 and HIF-2, and they prefer different genes. One gene favored by HIF-2 makes a protein called PTPRZ1, a receptor type phosphatase. The team characterized how HIF-2 alpha turns that gene on.

Detailing the activation shows how the cell tailors its reply to low oxygen. Different HIF forms may ready the cell for different stresses. PTPRZ1 is of interest in brain tumors, which often face low oxygen. The work links a tumor relevant gene to the oxygen sensing system.
plos-pone-0010441:
Minseok Kim and colleagues built a tiny device to diagnose breast cancer from tissue markers in PLOS ONE in 2010. Doctors read cancer markers with a staining method that reveals proteins in tissue slices. Testing several markers at once improves diagnosis and prognosis. The standard method, though, is slow and uses much sample. The team shrank it onto a microfluidic chip, where fluids move through hair-thin channels.

Their platform ran many marker tests in parallel on small samples. Faster, cheaper marker panels could reach more hospitals. They could also guide treatment choices that depend on marker patterns. Breast cancer care already turns on such patterns, like hormone sensitivity. This device aims to deliver those answers with less tissue and time.
plos-pone-0010541:
Anton Formann examined how the Newcomb-Benford law behaves across common statistical distributions in PLOS ONE in 2010. The law notes a strange pattern: in many data sets, numbers starting with 1 occur far more often than other first digits. The pattern is striking and keeps surprising newcomers. Formann asked how the law relates to familiar distributions used in statistics. Some distributions follow it naturally; others do not.

Knowing which is which makes the law a sharper tool. Auditors use first-digit patterns to flag cooked books and faulty data. A tool misapplied, though, accuses the innocent. This analysis sets the law's proper boundaries. It is pure mathematical groundwork with practical uses in fraud detection.
plos-pone-0010641:
Nikodem Poplawski and colleagues simulated growing tumors in three dimensions, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Early tumors have no blood vessels of their own. They live on nutrients that seep in from nearby tissue, which limits their size and shape.

The computer tumors did not stay smooth. Under some settings their edges buckled into rough, invasive fronts. Limited nutrient supply and surface forces drove the buckling. Rough fronts let real tumors invade tissue earlier than smooth growth would. Physicists and doctors together can use such models to predict which tumors will turn aggressive.
plos-pone-0010741:
Neelakanteswar Aluru and colleagues studied a plastics chemical passed from mother trout to eggs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is used to make many plastics and leaks into water widely. Fish absorb it, and it can lodge in their eggs before spawning. The offspring then start life already exposed.

Young rainbow trout from BPA-laden eggs grew more slowly than controls. Their stress responses were also blunted when challenged. Harm arriving through the egg means pollution effects can skip a generation's own exposure. Water standards based only on direct exposure may therefore understate the true cost to fish stocks.
plos-pone-0010841:
Andreas Androutsellis-Theotokis, Stuart Walbridge, Deric Park and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neural stem cells can renew themselves and later form brain cells, so learning what controls their growth matters for repair medicine and for cancer research. The team found that cholera toxin, a bacterial protein, switches on two known stem cell markers.

In rodent brain stem cell cultures, the toxin raised levels of the Tie2 receptor and quickly moved the Hes3 factor into the cell nucleus. After that, the cultured stem cells expanded strongly and kept dividing even without the usual growth signals. Androutsellis-Theotokis and colleagues propose a new control route for stem cell renewal. Such a route could give researchers a cleaner way to grow these cells and a fresh target in stem-like cancers.
plos-pone-0010941:
David Lucas, Lapo Alinari, Derek West and co-authors published this blood cancer drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drugs that block deacetylase enzymes, which control how tightly DNA is packed, show promise against B-cell cancers, but early versions were weak or caused harsh side effects. The team tested a new entrant, AR-42, across several B-cell malignancies.

In lymphoma and leukemia cell lines, low doses of AR-42 halted growth within two days, and it killed patient leukemia cells at similar levels. The drug raised chemical marks on both DNA-packing proteins and structural proteins, and triggered the cell's self-destruct machinery even when protective support cells were present. Lucas and colleagues also report activity in living animals. Their results make AR-42 a candidate worth carrying toward clinical trials.
plos-pone-0011041:
Khyati Kapoor, Mohd Rehan, Andrew Lynn and co-authors published this antifungal study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mdr1p is a pump that Candida albicans, a pathogenic yeast, uses to expel antifungal drugs, and its family of transporters shares a common design. The authors wanted the specific residues, the individual building blocks, that make this pump an antiporter rather than a sugar carrier.

They applied information theory measures comparing the antiporter family against a sugar porter family, flagging the thirty positions where conservation patterns differ most. Nineteen top candidates were then mutated one by one to test their role in drug transport. Kapoor and colleagues blend computation with bench verification to map a resistance pump's working parts. Such maps can guide drugs designed to jam the pump and restore antifungal power.
plos-pone-0011141:
Sambo, Trovoada, Benchimol and colleagues studied sick children in Angola for PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria can turn deadly when it reaches the brain. The team asked whether two genes, one shaping immune signals and one handling iron rich protein breakdown, change a child's risk.

Variants in both genes were tied to higher risk of the brain form of malaria. That genetic pattern could help explain why some children fall gravely ill while others recover. In time, risk knowledge might guide closer watch or early care for the most at risk children. The study centers African children in research where their burden is greatest.
plos-pone-0011241:
Spinella, Rosano, Del Duca and colleagues studied melanoma cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skin cancer cells can turn on a low oxygen program even when oxygen is present, helping them survive. The team traced how a vessel signal called endothelin switches that program on in melanoma.

The signal blocked an enzyme that normally tags the program's master protein for removal. With the tag withheld, the program stayed active. Interrupting that chain could starve tumors of their adaptation to stress. The study names clear steps in the chain as targets for new melanoma drugs.
plos-pone-0011341:
Heath Kelly and colleagues reconstructed the start of the 2009 flu pandemic in Australia in their 2010 paper. By mid-June 2009, the state of Victoria seemed to have the highest reported rate of the new H1N1 flu anywhere in the world. That odd lead raised a question: was Victoria truly hit hardest, or had the virus arrived there earlier than anyone realized?

The team argued that spread within local communities was already well established in Victoria when the virus was first identified in North America. In other words, the pandemic was moving quietly before surveillance caught up. The lesson reaches beyond one state and one year. Early case counts can badly lag real spread, so plans for the next pandemic should assume the virus is already wider than the first reports suggest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1241:
Secretary of War Stimson wrote to the President on 20 July 1945. Stimson's letters to Truman during the summit carried the War Department's counsel in its most direct form. This one dates from the first week's close, with the talks in full swing.

The war secretary's brief touched everything the army owned: the hold on Germany, the Pacific plans, and the secret atomic work he supervised. A letter to the president fixed his advice where the decider would read it. This message is part of the steady counsel that reached Truman at Potsdam, from the cabinet's most seasoned hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1341:
The Soviet delegation at Potsdam put a written proposal before the conference on 23 July 1945. Delegations used such papers to place exact wording on the table for the other leaders to accept, amend, or reject. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Proposals matter because they fix a government's opening position in its own words. Readers can compare what the Soviet side asked for with what the final conference texts later said. Papers like this one turn the summit from a story of talks into a record of drafting. Single phrases could shape the peace in Europe for years.
frus-1945-50-intel-d41: A memorandum for information, dated 2 November 1945, is one of the slimmest papers in the intelligence volume. Papers of this kind passed facts upward without asking for a choice. They kept senior men current. Meanwhile, the shape of the postwar intelligence system was fought over in longer memos. The title gives no author and no reader. So the paper stands on its place in the run, amid the autumn 1945 argument among State, War, the Budget Bureau, and the FBI.
frus-1945-50-intel-d141:
National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 1, dated 8 February 1946, is the new board's first numbered order. It followed the authority's first meeting by three days. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

First directives from a new board turn a charter into rules the whole system must obey. Directive No. 1 set the terms on which the departments' intelligence arms would work under central direction. Readers should end the volume's core run here, with the machinery complete. A president's directive, a board, a director, and an advisory board were all in place. The board's own orders were now flowing down. The argument of 1945 had become the system of 1946, on paper, in order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d241:
Dated 25 September 1947, this memorandum runs from the General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 241 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d341:
The Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) addressed a memorandum to Secretary of State Marshall on 8 March 1948. Readers meet it as document 341 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1861-d41:
George Dallas wrote from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 April 1861. The dispatch is document 41 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Early April found London unsure what the American crisis would become. Dallas reported the talk of ministers and markets as he heard it. His view from the scene helped Seward plan the handover to Adams, who would face the same men within weeks. London's stance, once set, would guide the rest of Europe in its dealings with the war. Every other court in Europe would take its cue from that stance in time.
frus-1861-d141:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 July 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. The dispatch is document 141 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The crossing letters again show the two ends of the Paris link at work. Dayton still lacked the full Bull Run story as he wrote. His page and Seward's, read together, mark the seam between two states of knowledge. Dayton's page and Seward's crossed in the sea mails, as so often that year. The seam between two states of knowledge is where this file's drama lives.
frus-1861-d241:
Washington's orders went out to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands in a dispatch dated 1 July 1861. Congress received it as Document 241 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d41:
Washington's orders went out to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London in a dispatch dated 2 April 1862. Congress received it as Document 41 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d141:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 13 September 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 141 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d241:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to William Stuart on 25 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 241 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The two men exchanged letters the same day, a sign of brisk business.

The emancipation plan announced on 22 September was the talk of every capital that week. Seward had long held that foreign governments should keep hands off the war. His letters after the proclamation worked to make the new policy a reason for Europe to stay out, not step in. This exchange with Stuart is part of that argument's first week.
frus-1862-d341:
Three Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 4 November 1862, and the first is Document 341 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Early November was decision week in London on the French truce proposal, and Washington wrote Paris accordingly. A three-letter mail let Seward cover the question from several sides at once. This first letter of the set belongs to the final round of the autumn campaign to keep Europe out of the war. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d441:
Closing the year's printed exchange with the Spanish minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this note to Gabriel García Tassara on 15 November 1862. It is Document 441 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

November 1862 found the Union army changing commanders and the emancipation order weeks from taking effect. Foreign legations measured the government anew, and Seward's notes carried a firm, even tone to each of them. For Spain, the standing concerns were Cuba, neutral duties, and Mexico. The note ends the volume's Washington-Spain file for the year, a record of friction managed without rupture, which was exactly the result the Union needed.
frus-1862-d541:
Roest van Limburg replied to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 August 1862, two days after Seward's note. His letter is Document 541 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

The quick turn-around in the Dutch file that week suggests a question both sides wanted settled. Van Limburg's government traded widely and ruled colonies near the seat of war. Its minister's duty was to keep Dutch rights clearly on the record. Seward welcomed that clarity in return: a neutral that stated its position in writing was easier to satisfy than one that brooded. The exchange is a small model of correct wartime dealing between a belligerent and a careful neutral.
frus-1862-d641:
Townsend Harris addressed this dispatch from Japan to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1861. It is Document 641 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Three Harris letters in six days close the July cluster of the Japanese file. He wrote in the last week before the armies met at Bull Run, though the fact would not reach him until autumn. His reports describe the daily substance of the Edo mission in its final Harris season. The treaty ports were working and the legation's standing was maintained. The minister himself was counting his remaining strength. The letter is part of a remarkable tail to the volume, where the Civil War's record runs out into the Pacific.
frus-1863p1-d41:
On 17 October 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote to a Monsieur Tabouelle. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state, writing from Richmond in a busy week of letters. The letter is document 41 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, in the group of Confederate papers printed there.

The French address hints at the web of contacts the South kept in Europe, where its envoys sought money, ships, and friends. Benjamin's pen fed that web from the center. This short piece of it survives because the Union printed the other side's mail in its own book. It is a glimpse of the South's quiet work abroad, kept in the foe's record.
frus-1863p1-d141:
London answered Washington's same-day letter with this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 2 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 141 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set just after a Seward letter of the same date.

Adams wrote in the week the British moved on a Southern raider in their hands, a test of the law the Union had long pressed. His reports that spring carried the facts Washington craved most. This dispatch is the London half of a same-date cross in the file. It shows the post at the heart of the season's great question: would Britain hold its own ships back from the South?
frus-1863p1-d241:
An instruction dated 18 July 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 241 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

After emancipation became official policy in January 1863, Seward could argue that aiding the South meant aiding slavery. That argument runs under much of the year's diplomacy. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d341: Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 December 1862. It is document 341 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, among the formal British papers in the Civil War correspondence. Through such notes London lodged protests and guarded its neutral rights against Union measures at sea.
frus-1863p1-d441:
3 April 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers.
