Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d541:
F. W. Seward, the assistant secretary sent an official note to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 28 May 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d641:
A dispatch dated 17 October 1863 went from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020141:
Vanina Guernier, Michael E. Hochberg, and Jean-François Guégan mapped human diseases worldwide in PLOS Biology in 2004. They asked what drives the pattern of where diseases occur. Their answer gives ecology a lead role: climate, hosts, and vectors shape the map more than wealth or health systems alone.

The authors compared disease richness across countries with a wide set of factors. Warm, wet places with rich wildlife tended to hold more kinds of human disease. That pattern warns that changes in climate and land use may shift disease maps in coming years. The paper frames health as part of ecology, a view that has only grown since in the study of emerging infections.
plos-pbio-0020341:
Delphine Fagegaltier and Bruce S. Baker studied gene balance in fruit flies in PLOS Biology in 2004. Male flies have one X chromosome, females two. Dosage compensation boosts the male X so both sexes get equal gene output. A protein complex lands on the male X to do the boosting.

The team found certain sites on the X can call the complex in on their own, even when moved elsewhere. Those sites act as entry points from which the complex spreads. Knowing them explains how a whole chromosome gets singled out for special treatment. The fly system is the clearest case of chromosome-wide gene control, a puzzle with echoes in human X-linked disease.
plos-pone-0000141:
Maki Yoshihama, Hung D. Nguyen, and Naoya Kenmochi published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies introns, the stretches of DNA that are cut out of a gene's message before a protein is made. The focus is the genes for ribosomal proteins, the parts of the cell's protein factories, which are unusually rich in introns.

The authors trace how these introns have been gained, lost, and moved over evolution. Because ribosomal protein genes are ancient and shared across life, their intron history offers a window on how genomes change. The work helps settle how dynamic introns really are across long spans of time.
plos-pone-0000241:
Hong Sjölinder and Ann-Beth Jonsson published this infection imaging paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Meningococcal sepsis is a fast, often fatal blood infection. The authors use imaging to follow disease dynamics, how the infection develops and spreads in the body over time.

Sepsis kills by speed, so a clear picture of its timeline is clinically valuable. The approach turns a disease that unfolds in hidden stages into one that can be watched step by step. Watching the disease unfold in images shows which organs are hit and when. The work supports faster recognition and better-targeted treatment of meningococcal disease, where hours decide outcomes.
plos-pone-0000341:
Masaki Nishida and Matthew P. Walker published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Daytime naps are known to help consolidate motor memory, locking in a practiced skill. The authors connect that benefit to sleep spindles, brief bursts of brain activity during sleep. They show the spindles act in regionally specific parts of the brain.

A nap is not uniform rest; specific rhythms in specific regions do the memory work. The study links spindle activity to the size of the learning gain after waking. The finding refines advice on naps and practice, and informs research on sleep-based rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0000441:
Carlos S. Moreno and colleagues tested a hard question about ovarian cancer treatment, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein p53, when working, can arrest the cell cycle, halting division. Chemotherapy often relies on cells dividing to kill them. The team gathered evidence that p53-mediated arrest can actually inhibit chemotherapeutic treatment of ovarian carcinomas.

The idea is uncomfortable: a protective protein might shelter tumor cells from the drugs meant to kill them, by putting them into a resting state. If so, a tumor's p53 status could predict whether a drug will help or underperform. The study warns that more cell-cycle arrest is not always better in cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0000541:
Kany-Kany Angelique Luabeya and colleagues ran a randomized controlled trial of supplements for South African children, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. The trial tested zinc or multiple micronutrient supplementation to reduce diarrhea and respiratory disease, two leading causes of child illness and death in poor regions.

Randomized trials are the gold standard because they separate the supplement's effect from luck and background differences. Zinc had strong prior evidence for diarrhea, while multi-micronutrient mixes were cheaper to deliver. A head-to-head trial in the children most affected tells programs which investment actually buys health.
plos-pone-0000641:
Shuxian Jiang, Yigong Fu, John Williams and colleagues described the cannabinoid system inside mouse embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. What decides whether a stem cell renews itself or becomes a specialized cell is a core question in biology. The team looked at two receptors, CB1 and CB2, and the cannabinoid signals that bind them.

They report where these receptors are expressed and what they do as stem cells form embryoid bodies and turn toward blood cell lines. Cannabinoids are best known from cannabis and from adult tissues. Finding their machinery at work in early embryos opens a new angle on how cell fate is steered.
plos-pone-0000741:
Mohammed Bakkali studied short bits of DNA that some bacteria go out of their way to take in. Many bacteria can absorb DNA from their surroundings and add it to their own genome. That uptake has real medical and money stakes, since it can spread drug resistance genes. Two bacterial families, Pasteurellaceae and Neisseriaceae, prefer DNA that carries certain short sequences.

Those favored sequences appear far more often in the bacteria's own genomes than chance would explain. Bakkali asks how such short sequences build up, move, and persist over time. One idea is self-recognition: by favoring their own sequence marks, bacteria trade genes mostly with kin. The study maps the pattern and weighs what could keep it in place.
plos-pone-0000841:
John P.A. Ioannidis, Nikolaos A. Patsopoulos and Evangelos Evangelou asked why pooled gene studies so often disagree with each other. A meta-analysis pools the results of many studies into one sum, and checks how much the parts differ. Such pooling was used more and more on genome-wide association studies. There, teams hunt the same gene effects and try to copy each other's finds.

The team's subject is heterogeneity: real gaps between study results. Some gaps are noise. Others are signs that groups, designs, or biases truly differ. Gene hunters who know how much gap to expect will not cheer too soon, or drop a true find too fast. The study is a guide to reading pooled claims with care.
plos-pone-0000941:
Biju Parekkadan, Daan van Poll, Kazuhiro Suganuma and colleagues tested whether molecules from stem cells can rescue a failing liver, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fulminant hepatic failure is sudden, severe liver collapse. Calming the immune system may offer a way out that avoids needing donor liver cells.

Mesenchymal stem cells, taken from bone marrow, are known to temper immune responses. The team asked whether the molecules these cells release, rather than the cells themselves, could reverse the failure. A cell free treatment would be easier to store, dose and approve. The study is an early step toward that idea, tested in a severe disease model.
plos-pone-0001041:
S. Hoyt Peckham, David Maldonado Diaz, Andreas Walli and colleagues documented turtle bycatch in small scale Pacific fisheries, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Industrial fishing bycatch, animals caught by accident, is known to harm seabirds, mammals and turtles. The impact of small scale coastal fisheries had been largely overlooked.

The team show that such fisheries jeopardize endangered Pacific loggerhead turtles. Small boats working close to shore can meet turtles where they feed and breed. Counting that harm changes the conservation ledger: protecting turtles means working with local fishers, not just fleets. The paper pairs the finding with the scale of coastal fishing worldwide.
plos-pone-0001141:
Northeast India is the only land bridge between the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. It may also have been a corridor for early human migrations into East Asia. B. Mohan Reddy and co-authors present genetic evidence on that route in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their focus is the Austro-Asiatic speaking tribes of the region.

The Austro-Asiatic language family is considered among the oldest in this part of Asia. The authors argue that these tribes supply a genetic link between South and Southeast Asia that had been missing. Their data bear on how the first peopling of East Asia unfolded.
plos-pone-0001241:
In some animals, RNA from mitochondria, the cell's power plants, turns up outside them, positioned in the egg at the spot that seeds germ cells. Youichirou Ninomiya and Shizuko Ichinose checked whether mammals do the same, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The phenomenon had been reported in several non-mammal groups but not in mammals.

The authors examined the expression and distribution of mitochondrial ribosomal RNA in the mouse oocyte and zygote. Whether the RNA localizes to a germ cell determinant in mammals bears on how universal that mechanism is. Their study brings the mammal case into an otherwise broader story.
plos-pone-0001341:
Two groups of tiny cyanobacteria, Prochlorococcus and Synechococcus, carry out much of the ocean's photosynthesis. Christophe Six and colleagues studied how they divide the ocean's light environment between them, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Phytoplankton cells are entrained in the water column and so are often exposed to rapid changes in irradiance within the upper mixed layer.

The authors report that light variability illuminates niche-partitioning among marine picocyanobacteria: the groups specialize on different light regimes. Who wins where determines how much carbon the ocean fixes. Their work links a physical variable, flickering light, to global primary production.
plos-pone-0001441:
Farba Karam and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a blood test for hidden TB in people with HIV. Finding and treating hidden TB in this group can cut illness and death. The team tested a home built blood test that reads a key immune signal. They asked if the test stays sound as HIV gets worse.

They report the test kept its power to spot hidden TB in HIV patients. But its readings did shift with how far HIV had gone. That caveat matters for how results are read in clinics. The work supports use of the test, with care, in places where both ills are common.
plos-pone-0001541:
Phillipa Hay and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on eating disorder acts in South Australia. Proof on whether such ills are rising had been mixed. The team used two matched community surveys ten years apart. Both asked the same questions on eating acts in the general public.

They found that eating disorder acts had in fact risen over that span. A matched design makes the trend claim much firmer than loose reports. A real rise urges more funds for early care and school based guards. It also prompts work on what drove the rise in that decade.
plos-pone-0001641:
Arnaud Muller, Elise Glattard, Omar Taleb, and their co-authors measured morphine made by the body itself in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Morphine is best known as the main active drug in opium from poppies. Yet it also turns up in animal tissues and cell types, including the mammalian brain. Its making pathway had already been traced in a human nerve cell line.

The team studied a human cell line called SH-SY5Y and the cerebellum of mice to pin down where this in-house morphine occurs. The full text gives the detection methods and the amounts found. It also covers what the pattern suggests about why nerve cells would make a pain drug of their own. The work adds to the view that morphine-like signals form part of the brain's own chemistry, not just plant medicine.
plos-pone-0001741:
Vikram Paruchuri, Anil Prasad, Kevin McHugh, and their co-authors studied a calcium-binding protein in breast cancer cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. S100A7 is a small protein first noted in psoriatic skin lesions and later in squamous tumors of skin, lung, and breast. Its expression tracks with high-grade HER-positive tumors and a high risk of progression.

The team reports that lowering S100A7 inhibits signaling from epidermal growth factor in breast cancer cells. It also blocks the formation of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. The full text gives the cell experiments and pathway readouts. Bone is where breast cancer often spreads, so a protein linking tumor signals to bone-eating cells is a target worth attention.
plos-pone-0001841:
Jordi Moya-Laraño, Dejan Vinković, Eva De Mas, and their co-authors modeled spider body evolution with pendulum physics in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Animals were thought to gain from pendulum mechanics as they hang and swing, trading height for speed. Convincing evidence was lacking.

The team shows the shape evolution of spiders is predicted by pendulum mechanics. Leg and body proportions match what good swinging needs. The full text gives the model and the species data. A law of physics that predicts anatomy across species is a rare result. It explains why hanging spiders evolved their marked long legged build.
plos-pone-0001941:
Nita Bharti and co-authors modeled how measles spreads along coasts in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Models help map how epidemics move through space and time, and what control steps might do. A leading model for spread between places, the gravity model, weighs both distance and the size of towns.

The team asked whether the mix of land and sea at coasts warps that spread in ways plain models miss. Coastal areas bunch people in lines and ports rather than even spreads. If models ignore that shape, they may misjudge where measles goes next. Better maps of spread help aim vaccines where they count most.
plos-pone-0002041:
Karine Bagramyan and co-authors built a test that spots botulinum toxin at vanishing levels, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Botulinum neurotoxin is among the most potent poisons known, a threat in spoiled food and a feared bioterror agent. A fast, cheap, and highly sensitive test for the active toxin in foods or blood was badly wanted.

As the title states, their method detects toxin type A at attomolar levels. That is a billionth of a billionth of a mole per liter, even in complex samples. Such sensitivity could flag tainted food early and let doctors track the toxin in patients.
plos-pone-0002141:
Amanda Dixon-McIver, Phil East, Charles Mein, and co-authors profiled small RNA molecules in leukemia patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Acute myeloid leukemia is the most common acute leukemia in adults, yet the gene changes behind it are still not fully mapped. The team measured 157 mature microRNAs, tiny RNAs that tune how genes are used.

Their samples came from 100 patients whose chromosome patterns, called karyotypes, covered the known range of the disease. Certain microRNA patterns matched certain karyotypes. Links like these can help sort patients into groups, which is a first step toward care and trials matched to each group's biology.
plos-pone-0002241:
Massimo Giuliani and co-authors grew a new kind of regulatory immune cell from blood stem cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Natural killer cells are known as killers of virus-infected and tumor cells. They can also regulate the immune system, but whether a defined NK subset does the regulating was in doubt.

The team used membrane-bound IL-15, a growth signal fixed to a surface, to guide blood CD34 progenitor cells into a novel regulatory NK subset. A lab source of calming immune cells could one day help control unwanted immune attacks, in transplantation or autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0002341:
Benjamin Elder and Kyriacos Athanasiou combined pressure and growth factors to grow tissues in the lab, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hydrostatic pressure is a real force in many tissues, including cartilage, the knee meniscus, the jaw joint disc, the spine's discs, bone, bladder. Blood vessels. Engineers growing replacement tissues need to know how pressure shapes growth.

The team tested hydrostatic pressure together with growth factors, the chemical signals that urge cells to build tissue. They found the two work together with synergistic and additive effects on tissue formation. Combining physical and chemical cues gives tissue engineers a stronger recipe for growing cartilage and like tissues.
plos-pone-0002441:
Peterson and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names A. Townsend Peterson, Aimee Stewart, Kamal I. Mohamed, among others. Its subject is shifting Global Invasive Potential of European Plants with Climate Change. Global climate change and invasions by nonnative species rank among the top concerns for agents of biological loss in coming decades.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002541:
Li, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Weijiang Li, Hiroyuki Kurata, among others. Its subject is visualizing Global Properties of Large Complex Networks. For complex biological networks, graphical representations are highly desired for understanding some design principles.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002641:
Amol Pawar and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of finite size effects in simulations of protein aggregation. The catalog record names Amol Pawar first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. It is becoming increasingly clear that the soluble protofibrillar species that proceed amyloid fibril formation are associated with a range of neurodegenerative disorders such. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002741:
In 2008, Anton L. Beer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about a motion illusion reveals mechanisms of perceptual stabilization. Authorship is credited in the record to Anton L. Beer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Visual illusions are valuable tools for the scientific examination of the mechanisms underlying perception. A further point appears in the abstract. In the peripheral drift illusion special drift patterns appear to move although they are static. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002841:
In 2008, Maria Öström and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was retinoic acid promotes the generation of pancreatic endocrine progenitor cells and their further differentiation into β-Cells. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Maria Öström, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. The identification of secreted factors that can selectively stimulate the generation of insulin producing β-cells from stem and/or progenitor cells represent a significant step. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002941:
Ursula Mager, Tatjana Degenhardt, Leena Pulkkinen and co-authors checked ghrelin receptor gene variants in people with poor glucose tolerance in 2008. Ghrelin helps control appetite, energy balance, and body weight. Its effects run through the growth hormone secretagogue receptor, the GHSR gene product.

The team typed seven variants in that receptor gene and tested links to obesity and glucose handling. Participants already had impaired glucose tolerance, a step toward diabetes. Published in PLOS ONE, the study adds human data on a hunger hormone pathway often targeted in obesity drug research. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003041:
Zulfeqhar Syed, Torleif Härd, Anne Uv and co-authors surveyed mucin proteins in the fruit fly in 2008. In vertebrates, vital organs are shielded by barriers built largely from mucins. These proteins carry repeated stretches rich in proline and sugar-bearing amino acids, and their sequences are poorly conserved.

Whether fly mucins play comparable roles was the open question. A potential role for Drosophila mucins in development and physiology is the paper's claim, stated cautiously. Published in PLOS ONE, the fly offers a fast genetic model for mucus barrier biology tied to gut and lung health.
plos-pone-0003141:
Gerald Kastberger, Evelyn Schmelzer and Ilse Kranner study a striking defence by giant honeybees in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Apis dorsata nests in the open and has evolved many defence behaviours. Against wasps and hornets the bees show coordinated cascades like Mexican waves across the nest surface, a behaviour called shimmering. It starts at distinct spots on the nest.

The title states what the waves achieve: they repel hornets. Readers watch a colony act as one unit to drive off a predator without each bee having to fight. The study is a vivid case of group defence in social insects.
plos-pone-0003241:
Nicole C. Grieder and co-authors study a cell transport protein in the fruit fly in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. More and more work shows that tweaks to basic cell jobs shape how tissues form and how disease starts. The team made loss-of-function cases to learn what COPI coat transport does as the fly develops.

The title reports that one part, gammaCOP, is needed for protein release at the cell's top surface and for shaping epithelial sheets. Readers see a housekeeping job prove vital for building tissue. Flaws in basic transport can thus lie behind flaws in growth.
plos-pone-0003341:
Sandro Alves, Isabel Nascimento-Ferreira, Gwennaëlle Auregan and colleagues test RNA silencing for a brain disorder in rats in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recent studies showed that RNA interference is a hopeful approach for treating autosomal dominant disorders. But wild-type and mutant transcripts must be told apart. The wild-type copy's expression and function must be preserved. A single nucleotide polymorphism is present in the target gene.

The title reports allele-specific RNA silencing of mutant ataxin-3 brings neuroprotection in a rat model of Machado-Joseph disease. Readers see gene therapy aimed at only the faulty copy. That precision is the key hurdle for dominant inherited brain diseases.
plos-pone-0007441:
Jedrzej Szymanski and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was how the bacterium E. coli reshapes its chemistry when conditions change. Cells respond to stress by adjusting their metabolites, the small molecules of daily metabolism. Some responses are shared across stresses, while others are specific. The team took a broad view of how metabolite levels move together.

They measured the links between metabolites under varied conditions. Some links stayed stable no matter what the cells faced. Others shifted with the stress at hand. That mix shows a metabolism that is part fixed backbone, part flexible response. Knowing which links hold steady helps predict how bacteria adapt. The map is useful for anyone engineering microbes or fighting infections.
plos-pone-0007541:
Soledad Galli and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 proposing a new view of ERK1, a famous signaling protein. ERK1 and ERK2 belong to the MAPK family, which relays outside stimuli into cell responses. Their long-term effects run through gene expression in the nucleus. Fast responses were known to happen elsewhere, but the details stayed vague. The team studied ERK1's interactions in HeLa cells.

They found ERK1 in structural association with mitochondria. That location is a surprise for a signal usually pictured in the cytosol and nucleus. A kinase parked at the cell's power plants could coordinate energy with growth signals. The authors frame it as a new paradigm for MAPK biology. If the pathway has standing business at mitochondria, many old results gain a new reading.
plos-pone-0007641:
Yuanbiao Guo and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the fetal liver's double life. Before birth, the liver both builds blood and matures into a metabolic organ. Blood-making and liver-building coexist there in mid-pregnancy. The switch between the two roles is thought to be a critical moment in development. The team profiled gene and protein activity in the midtrimester fetal liver to characterize that relationship.

The dynamic profiles capture an organ in mid-transition. Hematopoiesis wanes as hepatogenesis takes over, and the molecular data show the handover in motion. Understanding that timing matters for developmental biology and for medicine alike. Liver transplants and cell therapies both dream of replaying fetal programs. A map of the real transition tells engineers what to copy. The study records a rare moment when one organ does two jobs at once.
plos-pone-0007741:
Camille Szmaragd and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It builds a model of bluetongue virus spread among British farms. Bluetongue is a livestock disease carried by biting midges. Recent outbreaks pushed officials to plan for its return.

The framework describes how the virus moves within a single farm. It also tracks spread between farms across the country. Models like this let officials test control options before an outbreak hits. They can compare vaccination, movement bans and other steps on a computer first. That preparation can save animals and money.
plos-pone-0007841:
Steve Crampton and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It connects two major signaling systems inside cells. The Wnt pathway, driven by the protein beta-catenin, guides growth and development. Integrin signaling reports on a cell's grip on its surroundings.

The authors show the two systems are integrated through an adaptor molecule, Grb2. Adaptors physically link one pathway's parts to another's. Through Grb2, matrix and growth signals can tune the Wnt response. Such cross-talk helps explain how cells weigh several cues at once. It also adds detail to pathways often hit in cancer.
plos-pone-0007941:
Nicholas Delihas wrote a solo study of jumping genes in Lyme disease bacteria for PLOS ONE in 2009. The bacteria, Borrelia, carry small DNA rings called plasmids, crowded with copied and fused genes. One jumping element, IS605, leaves short stem-loop marks in the DNA near its landing spots.

Delihas found those marks linked to genes for lipoproteins, proteins that sit on the germ's surface. That link hints at how the germ shuffles the surface it shows to hosts. Shuffling its coat helps it dodge immune attack, so the marks point to a trick behind its staying power.
plos-pone-0008041:
Bernard La Scola and Didier Raoult sped up the naming of germs in blood infections for PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood cultures are the standard test, but they take days while patients wait on broad drugs. A mass spectrometry method can name germs from their protein fingerprint in minutes, once colonies grow.

The team showed the fingerprint method works straight from positive culture bottles, skipping a day of waiting. Faster names mean faster switches to the right drug. In blood poisoning, hours count, so a shortcut of this size can save lives.
plos-pone-0008141:
Zhida Su and colleagues found that a spinal scar calls in repair cells even as it blocks regrowth in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. After cord injury, a glial scar walls off the damage. Olfactory ensheathing cells, which support smell nerves, are transplanted to help repairs, and they migrate toward the scar.

The call turned out to be TNF alpha, a signal shed by the scar's reactive astrocytes. A scar that both blocks and beckons is a mixed blessing. Boosting the call while easing the block could draw more repair cells to the right place after injury.
plos-pone-0008241:
Peter I. Duncan and colleagues revisited sialic acid in newborn rats in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Milk is the only food of newborn mammals. It is thought to have evolved alongside the needs of the suckling young. Sialic acid is a conserved part of milk found on many sugar-coated molecules. The brain and colon are among the tissues where it matters.

The authors reviewed how newborn rats use and make sialic acid. Knowing whether pups rely on milk or their own synthesis guides nutrition research. The work connects milk chemistry to early brain and gut development. It updates an older picture of this nutrient.
plos-pone-0008341:
Dang Thi Minh Ha and colleagues evaluated a tuberculosis test for children in PLOS ONE in 2009. The MODS assay is a liquid culture method for detecting tuberculosis. It had been shown effective and rapid for early diagnosis in adults. Diagnosing tuberculosis in children is notoriously hard. The team evaluated the assay in Viet Nam with consecutive samples.

Samples included sputum and gastric fluid from children under evaluation. A faster diagnosis means treatment starts sooner for sick children. Culture-based proof also confirms which drug regimens will work. The study tests a practical tool where the need is great.
plos-pone-0008441:
Xin Liu and co-authors present a way to predict protein change in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Many diseases stem from proteins that fold the wrong way. The first step is a shift in a region that keeps the normal shape stable. That shift weakens the shape and exposes parts that should stay hidden. The authors call the key region a switch region.

They build a method to find such regions in a protein. Finding them could help predict which shifts cause disease. It could also help design drugs that hold the shape in place. The paper tests the method and shows how it can be used.
plos-pone-0008541:
Slavica Pecioska and co-authors test diabetes genes against fatness in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Type 2 diabetes disturbs carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism. It also involves insulin resistance. Most patients with the disease are obese. Obesity by itself may cause insulin resistance. The team ask if known diabetes loci act through measures of fatness. Loci are the genome positions where diabetes risk variants sit.

They evaluate associations between those loci and body fat measures. Some loci link to fatness, others act independently of it. Splitting the paths helps explain how each variant raises risk. That knowledge can refine prevention aimed at weight versus other mechanisms.
plos-pone-0008641:
Christopher Uhde and co-authors identify a marker RNA in mouse brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Specific markers for regions of the developing nervous system are useful tools. They illuminate development, regulation, and function of those regions. By expression profiling, the team identify a putative non-coding RNA called Rmst. It shows a striking, restricted expression pattern in embryos. It marks the ventral mesencephalic floor plate, where dopamine neurons are born.

Rmst also marks anterior dorsal midline cells of the brain. As a novel marker, it lets researchers isolate and study those populations. The floor plate is central to Parkinson-relevant neuron development. A non-coding RNA marker may itself play a regulatory role.
plos-pone-0008741:
Rick Shin, Junran Cao, Sierra Webb, and colleagues tested how a stimulant sharpens rat interest in cues. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Amphetamine makes animals respond more to signals tied to reward. Many such signals are learned through pairing. The team instead used plain visual signals with no training history. They placed the drug in the ventral striatum, a motivation hub.

Treated rats interacted more with the unconditioned visual signals. The boost happened without any learned reward value. That result widens theories of how stimulants capture attention. It also informs work on addiction and attention disorders.
plos-pone-0008841:
Nicole Cadieu, Stéphane Fruchard, and Jean-Claude Cadieu watched canaries try new foods and teach each other. Their bird study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Feeding innovation means eating something new or learning a new feeding skill. Adult canaries eat many seeds but avoid large ones. A bird that cracks the large-seed problem becomes a demonstrator. Whether flock mates copy the innovator was the question.

Some innovators spread their habit through watching flock mates. Others, though, were poor teachers despite their skill. Being first does not guarantee being influential. Social learning research must weigh personality alongside innovation.
plos-pone-0008941:
Tsufit Gonen-Gross and colleagues examined how a mother's immune cells read a special pregnancy protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, HLA-G, appears where the placenta meets the womb. It helps the mother's immune system tolerate the baby, who is genetically half foreign. Natural killer cells, a front-line immune cell, carry receptors that can bind HLA-G.

The team pinpointed which contact points on the receptor and protein do the binding. They also checked which cells display the protein at the fetal-maternal border. Small changes in the contact surface changed how strongly the cells responded. The work clarifies one way pregnancy keeps the immune system calm.
plos-pone-0009041:
Mahamadou Thera and co-authors gave a malaria vaccine its first test in Malian children, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The vaccine, FMP2.1/AS02A, is built on AMA1, a protein the malaria parasite needs to enter blood cells. Children in Bandiagara, Mali, face seasonal falciparum malaria every year. A phase 1 trial asks first whether a vaccine is safe and stirs immunity.

The trial was randomised, double-blind, and raised the dose step by step. Children's reactions and antibody responses were followed closely. Testing in children who truly face malaria gives the most honest early read. A safe, immune-stirring result would justify larger efficacy trials.
plos-pone-0009141:
Yan Zhao and co-authors traced a stress peptide's nerve cells in the fruit fly brain, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Every animal must answer stress to keep its body in balance. Hormones coordinate the changes in behaviour and body that follow. In flies, a peptide called corazonin is one such stress-linked signal.

Corazonin neurons wired into different circuits in male and female flies. That sex-based wiring shaped how each sex responded to stress. The same hardship thus triggered different behaviour in males and females. A simple fly brain shows how stress circuits get tuned by sex.
plos-pone-0009241:
Johan Lind and Patrik Lindenfors published this chimpanzee study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chimpanzee communities differ in their cultural traits, like tool use and grooming customs. Why some groups keep more traditions than others was poorly understood. In humans, models predict that bigger populations hold more culture.

The authors tested a version of that idea split by sex. They found the number of cultural traits rises with female group size. It does not rise with male group size. That pattern fits females being the main carriers of chimp culture, since young chimps learn most from their mothers and females move between groups.
plos-pone-0009341:
Judith Booij and co-authors published this eye gene study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The retinal pigment epithelium is a cell layer that keeps the eye's light sensors alive. Its failure drives diseases like age-related macular degeneration and retinitis pigmentosa. To study it, researchers need the list of genes this layer uses that others do not.

The team isolated RPE cells, photoreceptors, and choroid cells from fresh human eyes. Comparing the three gave a new strategy for spotting RPE-specific gene activity. They then annotated what those special genes do. The catalogue supports work on diseases that blind millions of older people.
plos-pone-0011441:
Vojtech Adam and co-authors presented in 2010 an electrochemical test sensitive enough to detect vanishingly small amounts of metallothioneins. These small proteins soak up toxic metals in the body, and their levels matter for tracking metal exposure and some diseases. Older methods could not measure them when only trace amounts were present in a sample.

The new method reaches down to the zeptomole scale, far below what routine tests can see. Sensitivity at that level lets labs find the proteins in tiny or dilute samples that once read as blank. That opens studies of early exposure and subtle change that were previously impossible. For environmental and medical testing, the paper supplies a tool whose main virtue is simple: it sees what other methods miss entirely.
plos-pone-0011541:
Mingzhou Li and co-authors catalogued in 2010 the full set of microRNAs at work as pigs develop before and after birth. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that fine-tune gene activity, and their cast changes as an embryo grows into a newborn. Pigs are a key model for human biology and a major farm animal, so a developmental atlas of their microRNAs serves two fields at once.

Their microRNAome spans the pre- and postnatal periods, giving researchers a baseline of which regulators are present at each stage. Deviations from that baseline can then be spotted in disease, poor growth, or breeding lines. For developmental biology, the atlas turns a fast-moving cast into a reference chart. It also supports pig farming directly, since growth and health traits that breeders select on are steered in part by these small regulators.
plos-pone-0011641:
Glen Borchert and co-authors studied how the immune system targets its own antibody genes for change, in PLOS ONE in 2010. To improve antibodies, the enzyme AID deliberately alters DNA in the variable regions of antibody genes. How AID is aimed so precisely at those spots, and spared elsewhere, is not fully understood.

The team found that histones H2A and H2B carry a single ubiquitin tag at the loci AID targets. Histones are the spools DNA wraps around, so their tags may flag where mutation should happen. The finding adds a signpost to the map of how controlled mutation strengthens immunity without wrecking the genome.
plos-pone-0011741:
David McMillan and co-authors charted the family structure of a rising strep germ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus dysgalactiae subspecies equisimilis can live in and infect humans and is gaining notice worldwide. Its strains are sorted by surface markers, which reveal a complex clan.

Their world survey found far-flung clones side by side with much DNA swapping between strains. That open mixing makes tracking and vaccine design harder, since the germ's make-up shifts across borders. The portrait shows a germ with a fluid genome that health teams must keep following over time.
plos-pone-0011841:
Alexander Bloemendaal, Ellen Brouwer, and Ad Fluit reported in 2010 a case where drug resistance moved between bacteria inside one patient. The resistance at stake was to methicillin, carried on a movable chunk of DNA in staphylococci. One species, Staphylococcus epidermidis, commonly lives on skin, while its cousin Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent cause of serious infection.

During the patient's antibiotic treatment, evidence pointed to the resistance element passing from the skin species into S aureus that had previously been treatable. A transfer caught in a real hospital course, rather than a lab flask, shows how treatment itself can set the stage for resistance to spread. It is a warning for how antibiotics are chosen and monitored.
plos-pone-0011941:
Matthias Rinderknecht and co-workers built in 2010 antibody fragments aimed at a vessel growth signal linked to cancer spread. VEGF-C drives the growth of lymphatic vessels, and tumors rich in it show more vessel density, more invasion into those vessels, and more spread to lymph nodes. The signal works through two receptors, VEGFR-2 and VEGFR-3.

Using phage display, the team produced fully human antibody fragments that block VEGF-C from engaging either receptor. Blocking the signal at its source could slow the lymphatic route that many tumors use to spread. Human fragments are attractive drug material because the body is less likely to react against them.
plos-pone-0012041:
Fabio Cafini and co-workers tested in 2010 whether prior immunity makes an antibiotic work better against resistant pneumococcus. People usually carry some antibodies before a Streptococcus pneumoniae infection begins. The team studied the antibiotic cefditoren in a mouse sepsis model, tracking how long drug levels stayed above the amount needed to stop the germ.

In pre-immunized mice, cefditoren showed enhanced activity against penicillin-resistant strains of serotypes 6B, 19F, and 23F. Drug and immune system working together is easy to say and harder to dose. Quantifying the boost helps design regimens that count vaccination and immunity as part of the treatment, not background luck.
plos-pone-0012141:
Yu Luo, Cameron Good, Oscar Diaz-Ruiz, and co-authors studied cocaine's effects on the mouse brain for PLOS ONE in 2010. Repeated cocaine use makes animals ever more reactive to the drug, a change rooted in altered connections in the brain's reward circuit. A receptor for the signal chemical glutamate is thought to drive that rewiring, but which cells need the receptor was unsettled.

The team focused on cells in a key reward hub that do not themselves use dopamine. Those cells' receptors still supported the growing response to cocaine. The result narrows where in the circuit addiction-like change begins, a map that later drug research can use to aim at the right cells.
plos-pone-0012241:
Aurore Gelin, Modesto Redrejo-Rodríguez, Jacques Laval, and co-authors dissected a human DNA repair enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. APE1 is a central repair worker: it cuts DNA at sites where a base is missing, serving one repair pathway, and nicks damaged DNA to start another. Mutant versions missing the second skill let the team ask what that skill is really for.

Their characterization of these mutants separates the enzyme's two repair jobs cleanly. Human cells juggle several overlapping repair systems, and knowing which enzyme covers which damage decides how cells survive radiation and some chemotherapies. Precise mutant tools like these are how such maps get drawn.
plos-pone-0012341:
Danupon Nantajit, Ming Fan, Nadire Duru, and co-authors reported a survival role for p53 in irradiated cancer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The p53 protein is famous for ordering damaged cells to die, guarding against cancer. Yet under DNA damage, p53 also seems to give tumor cells a survival edge, a contradiction that matters directly for radiation therapy, where doctors count on p53 to help kill the tumor.

The team traced the survival effect to p53 sent into the mitochondria and chemically tagged there by a cell-cycle kinase, switching it into an anti-death mode. Knowing how a tumor converts its own guard into a shield suggests blocking that conversion during radiotherapy. The paradox resolved is a treatment idea gained.
plos-pone-0012441:
Dan Close, Stacey Patterson, Steven Ripp and colleagues made mammalian cells glow on their own, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Bacteria can make light with a five-gene set called lux, needing no added chemicals. Until now the full set worked only in bacteria, so animal cell imaging required feeding cells a substrate each time.

The team got the whole lux set running in a mammalian cell line, and the cells produced steady light by themselves. Self-glowing cells can report infection, cancer growth, or drug response over long periods without repeated dosing. That simplifies live imaging in animals and cuts cost and handling in long experiments.
plos-pone-0012541:
Marcelo de Campos-Nebel, Irene Larripa and Marcela González-Cid compared two DNA repair crews across the cell cycle, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme topoisomerase II manages DNA tangles, and cancer drugs that trap it leave broken DNA strands in tumor cells. Cells fix such breaks by two routes: quick end joining or precise homologous recombination, which needs a sister copy.

The team found the choice of repair route depends on where the cell sits in its cycle. That timing matters in chemotherapy, since tumor cells in different phases will fix drug damage differently. Scheduling drug doses to cycle phase is one strategy such findings support.
plos-pone-0012641:
Ye, Li, Chen and co-authors compared how maize straw and a seaweed break down under heat. Seaweed draws interest as a fuel crop because it grows fast in the sea without farmland. Their 2010 study heated both materials without air, at three set rates, and tracked how they fell apart.

Measuring the energy needed at each step lets engineers judge how each feedstock would behave in a reactor. Maize straw is a common farm waste, so the pairing tests a land crop against a sea crop. Such basics must come before any seaweed fuel plant is built.
plos-pone-0012741:
Roosild and Castronovo watched a human enzyme change shape as it works. Uridine phosphorylase helps recycle the building blocks of RNA and DNA. It splits uridine into uracil and a sugar phosphate, and can run the step backwards as well.

Their 2010 study tracked the moving parts of the enzyme's active site during that reaction. An enzyme that shifts shape poses a moving target for drug design, but also reveals grips that still forms hide. Such enzymes matter in cancer care, where they can activate or block drugs.  Both directions of the reaction matter to cell economy.
plos-pone-0012841:
Van der Poorten, Shahidi, Tay and co-authors reported that hepatitis C switches on the cannabinoid receptor in the liver. Turning on this receptor, CB1, in liver tissue is linked to fat build-up and scarring in lab models of liver disease. Yet its level in real patients with chronic hepatitis C had not been measured before their 2010 study.

They measured CB1 in patient livers and found the virus induces it. That induction ties infection directly to the fat and scarring that follow. Blocking CB1 becomes a more concrete idea for hepatitis care.
pmc-2018741:
Peirce introduces PsychoPy, a free software suite for psychology experiments written in Python. Most studies of vision run on computer screens, where precise timing and display control matter. Commercial tools for such tasks were costly and could be hard to adapt.

PsychoPy was built to make building display experiments easier, using current hardware and software advances. It runs across different computer platforms, so labs can share experiment scripts freely. Open tools of this kind lowered the cost of careful perception research and helped labs repeat each other's setups exactly.  Teachers adopted it for perception courses because student scripts could be shared freely.
pmc-3197541:
Wong reviews apoptosis in cancer, from how the disease begins to how it can be treated. Apoptosis is an ordered, orchestrated process by which cells dismantle themselves. It occurs in both normal physiology and disease, and it is among the most studied topics in cell biology.

Understanding its mechanism matters because faulty cell death plays a pivotal role in disease. Cancer cells often evade apoptosis, surviving when they should die. The review explains those escape routes and treatments designed to restore death in tumour cells, a strategy behind several modern cancer drugs.
pmc-3414841:
Nik-Zainal, Alexandrov, Wedge, and co-authors catalogue mutation patterns in twenty-one breast cancers. All cancers carry mutations acquired during life. Their patterns reflect the DNA damage and repair processes that cancer cells and their precursors endured over time.

To explore those mechanisms, the team generated full catalogues of somatic mutation from the twenty-one tumours. Distinct patterns point to distinct causes, from internal chemistry to outside exposures. Reading such signatures later became a way to infer a cancer's history and, sometimes, its likely weaknesses.  Later signature catalogues across many cancer types grew directly from this approach.
pmc-3964941:
Li and co-authors presented starBase version two in 2013, a web database for maps of how RNA pieces interact. Small RNAs called microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, and other RNA types help set cell fate and play roles in disease. Yet the links among them were still poorly charted when this work appeared.

StarBase draws on large sets of CLIP-Seq data, which capture where proteins bind RNA. From those data it builds networks that connect microRNAs with competing RNAs, other non-coding RNAs, and proteins. Researchers can use the maps to form testable ideas about gene control in health and disease.
pmc-4384041:
The UniProt Consortium described UniProt in 2014 as a hub for protein information. UniProt collects protein sequences and adds notes on their function and features. In the past year alone, its holdings had doubled to a huge number of sequences.

That growth forced an expansion of the accession number space so each entry keeps a unique code. A rising share of entries now comes from automated annotation of new genomes. UniProt is the reference that countless tools link to for protein identity. Keeping it current and well organized underpins research from drug design to evolution.
pmc-4817141:
Page, Cummins, Hunt, and their colleagues introduced Roary in 2015. A typical study of a bacterial population can now include hundreds or thousands of isolates. Questioning such datasets can reveal the genetic structure of bacterial genomes in fine detail.

Roary rapidly builds the pan genome of a large set of bacteria, meaning all genes found across the group. It splits genes into the core set shared by all and the accessory set found in some. That split shows how a species adapts and which genes drive outbreaks. Speed is the point: pan genome work that once took weeks became routine.
pmc-4995441:
The Global BMI Mortality Collaboration, led by Di Angelantonio, Bhupathiraju, and others, pooled data in 2016 on body-mass index and mortality. Overweight and obesity are increasing worldwide. The team assessed how body-mass index relates to death from all causes in different populations.

They combined individual-participant data from a very large set of prospective studies across four continents. To limit confounding and reverse causality, they restricted the analysis, for example by excluding early deaths and smokers in key checks. The huge pooled sample gives precise estimates of risk at each weight range. Those figures inform public health guidance on healthy weight.
pmc-5551541:
Pizzino, Irrera, Cucinotta, and their colleagues reviewed oxidative stress in 2017, covering both its harms and benefits for human health. Oxidative stress arises when cells and tissues make and hold more reactive oxygen species than the body can clear. It also reflects how well the body can detoxify these reactive products.

Reactive oxygen species can play several physiological roles, including signaling and defense against germs. In excess, they damage proteins, fats, and DNA and contribute to many diseases. The review weighs both sides rather than treating these molecules as purely harmful. That balance matters for judging antioxidant supplements, which have often disappointed in trials.
pmc-6029841:
Claire McQuin, Allen Goodman, Vasiliy Chernyshev, and coauthors announced CellProfiler 3.0 in 2018. CellProfiler lets biologists build image analysis pipelines without writing code. It has served the field since the mid two thousands.

The new version handles three-dimensional images, both as whole volumes and plane by plane. That matters as microscopes now stack many slices into deep views of tissue. Pipelines can measure shapes and counts across the full volume. The release keeps the modular style users know while extending it to richer data from modern imaging. The release also improves speed, so larger three-dimensional stacks finish in reasonable time.
pmc-7203741:
Dengfeng Guan, Shane McCarthy, Jonathan Wood, and coauthors presented a tool for cleaning genome assemblies in 2020. Long-read methods now produce near-reference genomes quickly. In variable regions, assemblers often emit both parental copies as if they were separate loci.

Those haplotypic duplications inflate gene counts and break later analysis. The purge_dups tool spots duplicated stretches from read depth and self-alignment and removes the extra copies. It runs fast enough for large vertebrate genomes. Assembly projects for biodiversity programs adopted it as a standard cleaning step. The authors validate the tool on assemblies from the Vertebrate Genomes Project.
plos-pone-0359341:
Meltem Ozagir, Sergen Devran, Orkun Akkoc, Bülent Bayraktar, and Ilker Yucesir wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on exercise training. It studies blood flow restriction training, a method that uses a cuff to partly limit blood flow in a limb during light exercise. The authors test arterial blood flow changes at different compression levels.

The work is a cross-sectional experimental study of a practical version of this training method. Knowing how each cuff pressure changes artery flow helps set safe, effective levels for athletes and patients in rehab. Trainers and physiotherapists need exactly this dose information before using restricted-flow training widely.
plos-pone-0358641:
Yusuf Demirtaş and Saime Şahinöz wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about medical education in Türkiye. It studies medical students in their final year in Hatay and Ordu, two provinces marked by disaster in recent years. The topic is disaster preparedness perceptions, how ready the students feel for disasters, and the factors tied to those views.

Doctors are front-line responders after earthquakes and floods, so their felt readiness matters for real response. Comparing two provinces and the factors behind perceptions helps faculties see where training falls short. Medical schools in disaster-prone regions are the audience for evidence about their own students' confidence.
plos-pone-0359641:
Yecai Guo, Meiyu Liang, and Tianyue Jiang published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a speech enhancement method, software that cleans noisy recordings so voices come through clearly. The method integrates a channel attention mechanism of the squeeze-and-excitation kind, which teaches the network which sound channels matter, with an improved CGAN, a generative model.

Cleaner speech helps hearing aids, phone calls, and voice recognition in noisy places. Attention mechanisms let the model focus on speech-like parts of a signal instead of treating all noise alike. Audio engineers and researchers in speech technology are the readers comparing this design against other enhancement methods.
plos-pone-0359441: Choukair and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on teens with long-term illness in Germany. As these teens move from child care to adult medicine, the team measured strain from physical and mental symptoms. They also looked at how well each teen's family functions. The study draws out what this means for support during the handover. A rough transition can leave young patients lost between two systems.
plos-pone-0358241: Vakili and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that stages sleep from brain waves. Their system reads a single channel of EEG, the signal of brain activity. It joins multi-scale time encoding with layered sequence learning in one model that stays aware of context. Accurate staging from one channel could make sleep studies cheaper and easier to run at home.
plos-pone-0358841: Saarela and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on adults in acute hospital care who carry more than one lung infection at once. A multiplex PCR test can name many viruses and bacteria from a single sample. The team used it to find how often such mixed infections occur. Mixed infections can change treatment, since a drug for one germ may miss the other.
plos-pone-0358441: Bohorquez Santiago and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper on adding copper to a bone-like coating. The coating is synthetic hydroxyapatite, the mineral that hardens bone, laid down as a thin film. Their method uses a laser method aided by plasma to add the copper. Copper can fight bacteria, so coated implants might resist infection while bone grows onto them.
plos-pone-0358741:
Courtney Bir and four colleagues analyze American attitudes toward pandemic rules in a 2026 PLOS ONE article, using survey data from January 2021. COVID-19 controls asked people to give up ordinary freedoms for a shared benefit, and resistance was loud. The authors probed how beliefs about society's duties and personal rights lined up with actually following spread reducing behaviors.

Agreement that healthcare is a human right, that society must protect the elderly, and seat belt wearing all went with a higher likelihood of taking part in protective behaviors. Having someone at high risk in the household also raised participation. Belief that gun ownership is a right pulled the other way, lowering participation across behaviors. The pattern maps a values divide that future public health campaigns will still have to cross.
europmc-pmc7291041: Crawford and co-authors published this study protocol in 2020 on protocol and reagents for pseudotyping lentiviral particles with SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (the virus's spike) for neutralization assays. The paper describes the study design in advance, so others can judge it fairly. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8943941: Doctors and scientists took on aimed at extracellular (outside cells) matrix stiffness and mechanotransducers to improve cancer therapy in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
europmc-pmc9117141: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on effectiveness of mRNA-1273 against SARS-CoV-2 omicron and delta variants. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7265941: Doctors and scientists took on herpes simplex (cold-sore virus) virus: global infection prevalence (how common a condition is) and incidence (new cases) counts, 2016 in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
europmc-pmc8913741: Doctors and scientists took on improved forecasting of protein-protein interactions (how parts affect each other) using alphafold2 in this 2022 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Better ways to spot trouble early give doctors a head start on treatment.
europmc-pmc7666141: Doctors and scientists took on scutellarin eases pulmonary (lung) fibrosis (scarring of tissue) through inhibiting nf-κb/nlrp3-driven epithelial transition and inflammation (swelling caused by the immune system) in this 2020 research paper. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7946541: Robertson and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on predictors of COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy (shot reluctance) in the UK household longitudinal study. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc7756241: This 2020 research paper covers measuring of maternal and neonatal SARS-CoV-2 viral load (amount of virus), transplacental antibody (defense protein) transfer, and placental pathology in pregnancies during. Importance biological (from living things) data are lacking with respect to risk of vertical spread and mechanisms (the inner workings). Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc7118541: A fresh look at predicting commercially available virus-fighting drugs that May act on the COVID-19 through a drug-target interaction deep learning (layered computer learning) model arrived with this 2020 research paper. The infection of a COVID-19 found in wuhan of China is rapidly spreading, and the incidence (new cases) rate is. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
gao-gaoreports-b-310741: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Rocketplane Kistler. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
europmc-pmc8594841: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on systematic (thorough) exploration of escherichia coli phage-host interactions (how parts affect each other) with the BASEL phage collection. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc8494641: Liu and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on DNA methylation (chemical tagging of DNA) atlas of the mouse brain at single-cell (one cell at a time) resolution. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8142841: Earle and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on evidence for antibody (defense protein) as a protective correlate. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc7518441: This 2020 research paper covers PD-L1 on dendritic cells (branching immune cells) lessens t cell activation (switching on) and controls reply to immune checkpoint blockade. Immune checkpoint blockade therapies have shown clinical (in patients) promise in a variety of cancers, but how tumor-infiltrating t cells. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
gao-gaoreports-b-310941: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Eisenhower Real Estate Holdings, LLC. plos-pone-0354141:
Alex Junior Aparecido Silvestrini and three colleagues draw the chromosome map of lentils and their wild cousins with glowing DNA probes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The genus Lens holds the cultivated lentil plus six wild relatives, each with shuffled chromosomes that confuse breeding and genome assembly alike. The team designed short DNA probes from gene order comparisons, painted them onto dividing cells in two colors, and read the patterns chromosome by chromosome.

Each chromosome in six species produced a distinct two color signature, turning identification from guesswork into direct observation. The patterns confirmed that the published genome assemblies had assigned their pieces to the right chromosomes, and they verified the rearrangements that gene comparisons had predicted. Close relatives proved highly similar in sequence despite their structural shuffling. A precise karyotype gives lentil breeders a reliable map for moving traits from wild species into the crop.
plos-pone-0347941:
Chi Le Phuong leads a team of eight asking Vietnamese health students whether deliberately infecting volunteers can ever be right, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Human challenge studies infect healthy volunteers on purpose to speed vaccine and treatment science, and they are being proposed for lower income countries. Students at Ho Chi Minh City's medical university answered a survey after engagement sessions, and joined discussion groups and interviews, as part of a project running since 2020.

Familiarity with the idea was moderate, and support was real but cautious. Deliberate infection made these studies less acceptable to students than ordinary trials or observational research. Those open to joining cited altruism, social value, and national benefit, especially against diseases endemic at home. The context presses hard: the country has no rules for such studies and limited intensive care depth. The authors say local voices, not imported enthusiasm, should set the terms.
plos-pone-0358341:
Angela Hibbs and three colleagues studied new postgraduate students at a UK university, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Students starting taught postgraduate courses arrive with expectations formed by marketing, prior study, and hope. When reality differs, satisfaction and success can suffer. The team explored those pre-arrival expectations in depth.

Hibbs's study maps what incoming postgraduates expect from teaching, support, and campus life. Universities can compare that map with what they actually provide, and close the worst gaps. The work looks beyond the undergraduate experience, since postgraduates are often older, working, or returning after years away. Honest recruitment and better induction both start from knowing what students think they signed up for.
plos-pone-0356241:
Filippo Cendron and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE giving the first look at microRNAs in dolphin milk. These tiny RNA molecules fine-tune gene activity, and milk carries them in quantity in land mammals, but no marine mammal's milk had ever been profiled. The team searched the bottlenose dolphin genome for microRNA families, compared dozens of whale and dolphin genomes, and sequenced the small RNAs in pooled milk samples.

They cataloged several hundred high-confidence microRNA precursors across many conserved families, with a few losses along the dolphin lineage, including nine families missing from all cetaceans. In the milk itself, just four families dominated, accounting for over seventy percent of all microRNA reads, and those same families headline land mammals' milk too. The work is framed as an exploratory first map, suggesting evolution kept milk's regulatory recipe stable as mammals returned to the sea.
plos-pone-0356741:
Muhammad Jawad Asghar and a plant breeding team compare several statistical models for picking lentil varieties that yield well in many places, not just one lucky site. Weather swings make variety performance jump between sites and years, and each stability model sees that jumping differently. The team grew a set of lentil lines across four contrasting environments in blocked plots and scored them with four established approaches.

All models agreed that variety-by-place interaction was real and strong. Older regression sorting, mixed-model prediction, and a combined yield-stability index each highlighted somewhat different winners, with the combined index best at naming broadly reliable lines. Asghar and colleagues advise breeders to consult several models together rather than betting a release decision on any single one.
plos-pone-0357041:
Jooyoung Cheon and Eun Young Choi examined how people in South Korea actually feel in their last month of life. They used family exit interviews from a national aging study. The study covered deaths between 2006 and 2020. Their 2026 analysis included 1,731 adults who died in hospital. It tallied eleven symptoms reported by relatives. It then asked which circumstances predicted each symptom.

The average decedent carried nearly five symptoms. Loss of appetite led, followed by severe fatigue and depression. Each affected more than half. Long illness, dependence on others for daily tasks, and pain in the final year predicted almost every symptom. Yet barely one decedent in twenty had received hospice care. In a country where hospital death is the norm, the authors call the palliative gap critical.
plos-pone-0356141:
Marie Beermann and colleagues asked whether surgeons can judge a fibroid treatment's success in the operating room. Could ultrasound do the job instead of waiting for an MRI? Their 2026 prospective study treated seventeen women with microwave ablation, a heat procedure for uterine fibroids. Fibroid volume was measured before treatment with both methods. The burned volume was read by ultrasound right after. MRI checks followed within a week and at six months.

Ultrasound and MRI agreed closely on ablated volume, close enough for live guidance. But the sobering secondary finding was regrowth. Nearly half the treated fibroids showed living, blood-fed tissue again by six months. That was despite technically successful ablation. The study supports ultrasound for immediate steering. It also warns that a clean first result does not guarantee a lasting one.
plos-pone-0355941:
Miaomiao Li and colleagues set out a plan, published in 2026, for comparing non-drug treatments for cannabis use disorder. No medicine is approved for this condition, so counseling-style therapies and brain-based approaches carry the treatment load, yet they have rarely been compared directly with each other. The planned review aims to rank them in a single framework.

Following their protocol, the team will search major medical databases for randomized trials. They will combine the results in a network meta-analysis, which lets treatments be ranked even when they were never tested head-to-head. They will judge success mainly by verified abstinence and days of use, alongside how many patients stay in treatment and what harms appear. Final results are scheduled for late 2026, and the ranking should help clinics choose treatments on evidence rather than habit.
plos-pone-0354341:
Alexandra Guttentag and five colleagues measure how well Americans understand the costs of their own healthcare, in this 2026 nationally representative survey of more than two thousand adults. Patients are asked to shop and plan around prices they often cannot see. The twelve-question survey probed knowledge of drug prices, insurance terms, and strategies for planning or disputing costs.

Knowledge was patchy. Most people knew drug prices vary between pharmacies, and over half knew how to contest a hospital bill, but only a third understood hospital chargemasters, the master price lists behind bills. Terms like deductible were easier to explain than formulary. Knowing an emergency visit's cost in advance was the hardest planning task. Adults with stronger cost literacy tended to be older and more confident managing their care. The authors see room for education targeted at bills and insurance.
plos-pone-0355741:
Longxue Wei and seven others take stock of the visible diversity in old maize varieties in this 2026 study. Landraces, varieties shaped by farmers over generations, hold genetic raw material that modern breeding needs, but their traits are seldom measured in a planned way. The team grew one hundred nineteen landraces and scored nine yield and flower-structure traits, applying diversity indices, clustering, and regression techniques to find the patterns and the most telling measures.

Variation was wide on every trait. The team distilled the nine measures to four main components, and a composite score singled out ten top landraces for breeding attention. The collection sorted into three groups with distinct flower shapes, grain traits, and field performance. Four traits, mostly describing the tassel's branching, proved most telling for choosing. The authors offer the framework as an efficient way to mine landrace collections for elite material.
plos-pone-0352141:
XuYan Liu and colleagues survey in 2026 how nurses who reshape their own jobs may also act in new and inventive ways at work. Their study drew on questionnaires from nurses in large hospitals in southwest China. Statistical modelling tested whether feeling safe in a team and feeling backed by the workplace linked the two.

Reshaping one's job was linked with more inventive behaviour. Both team safety and felt support carried part of that link on their own, and together they formed a chain as well. The authors suggest managers can help by letting nurses adjust their work, building trust inside teams, and making support easier to feel.
plos-pone-0355841:
Theresa Barberi, Rahila Khuroo, and Alan Friedman report in 2026 on a new line of lab mice. The mice were built to help test immune treatments for human cancers. Those treatments target a growth signal protein found on many tumours. Normal mice reject the human form of that protein. So the team made mice that carry a short human version. Their bodies accept it as their own.

The mice stayed tolerant even after the gene was switched off in adults. They also accepted mouse tumours carrying the same marker. Blood cells carried the marker strongly. Levels were lower in the liver, lung, kidney, and brain. A known antibody still binds the short form. The line offers a safer test bed for such treatments.
plos-pone-0354741:
M David Diggs and co-authors run in 2026 a small exploratory study on whether short bursts of hard cycling help teenagers with attention disorder learn new language words. Older teens with no Portuguese took one online lesson, with three half minute sprints placed before the lesson, after it, or not at all. Learning was checked that day and a week later through recall, recognition, and sentence making.

No difference reached statistical strength, yet patterns hinted that exercise before the lesson helped word memory, while exercise after hurt sentence making and recognition. With fewer than thirty participants, the authors stress the pattern is a lead for larger, wider studies, not a firm rule.
plos-pone-0355341:
Michal Ordak, a single author, published this 2026 analysis of how anti-vaccine posts on Facebook misuse numbers. Working with nearly six hundred Polish-language posts, Ordak built a coding scheme of ten kinds of faulty statistical reasoning and checked how often each kind appeared and which kinds traveled together.

Treating correlation as proof of cause was the most common error, followed by ignoring base rates. Certain mistakes paired up in steady patterns, especially skipping denominators alongside gut-feeling reasoning. Ordak argues that health messages should name and correct these specific errors, since vague appeals to trust science do little against a confident but flawed chart.
plos-pone-0355041:
Amanuale Zayede and three colleagues published this 2026 study of cleaners employed by the University of Gondar in northwest Ethiopia. Cleaners work amid dirty waste daily, and they may quietly carry gut bacteria that resist key antibiotics. The team compared stool samples and surveys from hospital janitors and campus janitors who work outside the hospital.

Resistant bacteria turned up often in both groups, with different risk patterns in each. Recent urinary infections mattered for hospital janitors, while older age and buying antibiotics without a prescription mattered for the others. Zayede argues cleaners belong in national resistance monitoring and deserve stronger hygiene training.
plos-pone-0353841:
Andrew D Meyer led a team of eight authors on this 2026 protocol for a pilot trial of bleeding after children's tonsil surgery. Up to one child in twenty returns to emergency care bleeding, and most are taken back to the operating room. Earlier case reports suggest a mist of tranexamic acid, a clot-protecting drug, might calm the bleeding instead.

Children in the pilot will receive three misted doses of the drug or salt water, and the team will measure feasibility, drug levels, and side effects. The pilot prepares a larger trial of the TEAPOT approach.
plos-pone-0354841:
Cemaliye Karadayı Numan, Yalın Kılıç, and Hülya Şenol published this 2026 survey study of teachers in North Cyprus. Just over three hundred secondary teachers rated their own school's values-centered culture, how fairly the school actually treats staff, and their own willingness to go beyond the job description for the school.

Careful statistical path analysis showed fairness carrying part of the culture effect: value-centered cultures strengthened citizenship behavior partly by making teachers feel justly treated. Numan argues school leaders should build values and fairness together, since each feeds teachers' extra effort.
plos-pone-0350741:
Cintia Ronchi Lemos and seven colleagues gather what is known about the downsides of clear orthodontic aligners, in this 2026 PLOS ONE systematic review. Aligners are popular because they are nearly invisible and removable, but their harms are less advertised than their comfort. The team searched seven databases and grey literature, keeping thirty-four studies that reported side effects.

Pain was the most common complaint, peaking within a day and fading within a week. Roots of moved teeth shortened slightly on average. Reports also covered plaque, white spots on enamel, speech changes, bad breath, and jaw symptoms, though the evidence there was patchier. Patients weighing aligners deserve this fuller picture alongside the cosmetic appeal.
plos-pone-0354241:
Sung Pyo Park and four colleagues follow newly diagnosed glaucoma patients in South Korea for ten years, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of national insurance records.
