The disease, in its open-angle form, slowly steals vision and is managed mainly with daily eye drops. Nearly sixteen hundred patients diagnosed in 2010 were tracked through a decade of prescriptions and operations.

One class of drops dominated first-year treatment, given alone to about two fifths of patients. Over ten years the average number of drops and active ingredients per patient climbed steadily, as single drugs stopped being enough. About three patients in a hundred eventually needed surgery. The numbers give doctors a realistic script for counselling the newly diagnosed.
plos-pone-0344341:
Shinji Inaba and seven colleagues build a smarter kind of medical exam — one that adapts its questions to each test-taker, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Reading heart tracings is a core clinical skill that many professionals perform poorly. Five hundred and thirty-five healthcare workers took a fifty-question online test of tracing interpretation, and the team used item-response statistics to grade each question's difficulty and sharpness.

Nearly every question proved sharp, and their difficulties spread out well. A single underlying skill explained performance best, so the team built a prototype adaptive test on that basis. Adaptive exams reach a verdict with fewer questions, easing the burden of certifying a skill that patient safety depends on.
plos-pone-0353941:
Niina Mäenpää and five colleagues report what happened when a Finnish hospital adopted a gene test that predicts whether early breast cancer needs chemotherapy, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. One hundred and twenty-nine patients with hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative tumours were tested over two years. The assay reads the tumour's gene activity and estimates both recurrence risk and likely chemotherapy benefit.

Testing changed recommendations for most patients: nearly three quarters were spared chemotherapy they would otherwise have been offered. The hospital saved part of the cost through avoided treatment, and the wider economy saved much more by keeping working-age patients at work. The authors stress that smooth testing routines and clinician training made the difference.
plos-pone-0328341:
Jaber Hamad Jaber Amin and seven colleagues document a traditional practice in Sudan that cuts away part or all of a child's uvula, in this 2026 PLOS ONE community survey. More than eleven hundred mothers across over ten states were interviewed in early 2025 about the practice, why it is done, and what followed. About fifteen percent of children and adolescents had undergone it, most often in early childhood.

Mothers and grandmothers usually decided, and traditional healers performed over half the procedures, often with unsterilised tools. Fevers, feeding trouble, and bleeding were commonly reported afterwards. Belief in the practice ran strongest where mothers were younger, less educated, and more bound by tribal custom. The authors call for campaigns that work with healers and grandmothers, not against them.
plos-pone-0321341:
Jacob Michael Othieno and seven colleagues compare drug-resistant E. coli bacteria from raw cow's milk with those from hospital patients in Kampala, Uganda, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Milk samples from vendors yielded bacteria in about a third of cases, almost entirely from open cans rather than sealed packs. Forty milk isolates and forty clinical isolates were tested against eleven antibiotics.

The clinical bacteria were far more resistant across the board, with most classed as multidrug-resistant and many producing enzymes that defeat whole antibiotic families. The milk bacteria were milder, but their overlap on the commonest drugs hints at traffic between farm and clinic. The authors call for stewardship on both sides of the food chain.
plos-pone-0353241:
Surve and colleagues set out a study plan in 2026 for improving how babies and toddlers are fed in a tribal area of India. In Palghar District, many young children grow too slowly, and frontline health workers are the main source of feeding advice for mothers. Gaps in worker knowledge and local barriers still hold back good feeding habits.

Over two years, the team will first measure what workers and mothers know and do, then train workers and counsel mothers, then measure again. About four hundred sixty mother and baby pairs will take part through local child care centers. Readers get a careful plan for testing whether training changes feeding in daily life.
plos-pone-0346241:
Barsotti and Santos modeled how openness about scoring rules changes people's behavior in a 2026 study. Loan and fraud systems score people, who then adjust their profiles, honestly or by gaming. In their model, people copy neighbors in a social network as well as responding directly.

More hidden rules hurt the scoring institution, especially in tightly connected networks. False approvals fell in sparser networks when people copied each other. The results complicate the simple call for full transparency: what people learn from peers can matter as much as official explanations. Designers must weigh openness against the gaming it invites through social channels.
plos-pone-0351841:
Molino, Martí-Fis, and Rodriguez-López built a method to reconstruct storm rainfall curves from daily records in a 2026 study. City drainage design needs rain intensity for many storm lengths, but tropical towns often keep only daily totals. Eight rain stations near Havana supplied fifteen years of daily data, plus one detailed recorder for fine timing.

Daily totals were split into shorter bursts using the detailed record's patterns, then fitted to standard storm curves for return times up to a thousand years. One regional model merged all stations. Engineers in data-poor regions can thus design drains and culverts with defensible numbers instead of guesses.
plos-pone-0349441:
Christina Ruan and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One scoping review of what helps and hinders Americans with sickle cell disease in actually using health care. Despite severe pain and organ damage, many patients seem to be avoiding the system. The reviewers screened hundreds of articles and kept seventy that described barriers, facilitators, or patterns of care use in the United States.

The commonest barriers were social and interpersonal, including strained relations with providers, followed by economic and institutional obstacles. Technology, education, patient autonomy, and trusting provider relationships helped people engage. Individualized pain plans and quality improvement programs reduced avoidance in several studies. The authors call for multi-level interventions and for health systems to rebuild trust with this underserved patient group.
plos-pone-0351541:
Katrina Himpson, Thomas Le Berre, and Edward Hodges follow rescued sea turtles after release into the Indian Ocean. Their 2026 study fits satellite tags to rehabilitated olive ridley, green, and hawksbill turtles. Tracking of wild turtles is common, but released patients are rarely followed. The team wanted survival, movement, and behaviour after rehabilitation. Comparisons with wild turtles of the same species and life stages anchored the interpretation.

The released turtles did well. They survived for extended periods and behaved like their wild counterparts. Species and age shaped their routes. Monsoon currents pushed hard on open-ocean travellers. Turtles actively swam against drift to hold position, or rode the currents along shelves and ridges. Juveniles and olive ridleys, both scarce in the tracking literature, feature prominently here. The results validate rehabilitation twice over: the animals genuinely return to wild life, and their tags teach science what healthy turtles do.
plos-pone-0352341:
Rameshwor Parajuli, Wilna Oldewage-Theron, and Surya Niraula reviewed studies on junk snacks and sugary drinks among children and teenagers in Nepal. Diets there are shifting fast, and the country now faces underweight and stunting alongside rising overweight. Their review gathered work from city, fringe, and rural areas to see how snack habits line up with body weight.

Snacking on unhealthy foods was highest in cities and was tied to higher odds of overweight and obesity. Fringe areas sat in the middle, and rural children snacked least, though marketing and easier access are pushing rural intake up. Most children still had normal weight, yet the reviewers warn Nepal faces both problems at once and needs action on each.
plos-pone-0350241:
Lu Han and colleagues froze four soft soils in the laboratory to guide a subway dig that must pass beneath a working station in China. The builders plan to freeze the ground solid, excavate inside the ice wall, and let it thaw after, so the frozen soil's strength and heat behavior decide the safety margins. Samples of silty clay, mucky soil, residual soil, and weathered rock were tested from mild frost down to deep cold.

Cold made every soil conduct heat better, most sharply in the weathered rock and least in the mucky soil. Frost heave, thaw settlement, and shear strength under pressure were measured alongside, showing how temperature and squeezing together steer behavior. Numbers like these feed directly into freeze-pipe spacing and timing: freeze too little and the wall leaks, too long and the thaw sinks the street.
plos-pone-0321841:
Joe Zambrano-Suárez and colleagues taught neural networks to trace tree rings in wood scarred by debris flows, the violent events scientists date by reading damaged trees. Normal rings segment well with deep learning; rings wrenched by impacts, with sudden color and texture breaks, are another matter. Cores from a debris-flow site were photographed at high resolution and hand-annotated so models could be trained and honestly graded.

Segmentation held up on ordinary growth but sagged exactly where the science needs it most, in the disturbed stretches whose pattern dates the disaster. Architecture, resolution, and filtering all shifted the score, showing the failure is partly about how much cellular detail the image keeps. The paper maps the limits rather than overselling a tool, and tells the field what to fix before automation touches hazard dating.
plos-pone-0351941:
Some children are born with a doubled drainage tube on one kidney, and both branches can go wrong at once. Huazhang Liu and colleagues report a robot-assisted operation, in PLOS One in 2026, that joins one branch to the other and also rebuilds the bladder connection in a single surgery.

Twelve children treated between 2021 and 2024 were reviewed. Most came in with urine infections; others leaked urine or had belly pain. Surgery took about three hours and hospital stays about five days. Two children had infections afterward that cleared with simple care. At later checks, swelling had shrunk, no leakage or backflow remained, and kidney function had improved.
plos-pone-0344541:
High blood pressure needs daily self-care, and Mohammad Hosein Hayavi-Haghighi and colleagues built a phone and web app named HOPE for patients in Iran. Their 2026 PLOS One paper describes how the app was designed with input from heart doctors and patients, then tested by clinic users in Hormozgan Province.

The team first listed what the app should do, drawing on guidelines and surveys of twenty-five cardiologists and fifty patients. The finished app lets users track readings, learn about their condition, and reach services from home. After a month of use, forty-six patients rated how easy it felt. The authors present the work as a locally grounded model.
plos-pone-0351141:
Practicing piano with two hands demands split-second timing, and tired hands lose precision. Xiaoyu Meng and colleagues built a simulated practice gym, PianoGym, that plans rhythm exercises while respecting fatigue limits, in this 2026 PLOS One computer science paper.

The catch is that feedback arrives only after each exercise ends. Their controller watches timing errors and two fatigue signals, then picks the next drill from a set library. A slow safety layer tracks long-run fatigue while a fast guard screens each candidate drill against a fatigue estimate. A planning controller then searches only among drills the guard allows, aiming for safe, steady progress.
plos-pone-0351741:
Ongoing stomach pain and fullness without visible disease, called functional dyspepsia, may involve quiet immune activity in the small intestine. Imteaz Mahbub, Bimal Chandra Shil, and Sadeed Araf Reza counted allergy-linked white cells in gut lining samples in Dhaka, Bangladesh, for this 2026 PLOS One study.

Forty-six patients with the condition were compared with forty similar people whose stomach checks looked normal. Biopsies came from the same stretch of intestine and cells were counted under a microscope. Counts ran clearly higher in the patients than in the comparison group. The authors link the finding to low-grade immune activation and suggest it may guide future treatment choices.
plos-pone-0339541:
When someone is lost in the wilderness, search leaders must guess how fast teams move over hills. Amanda Hashimoto and colleagues checked those guesses against GPS tracks from sixty-four real search incidents, in this 2026 PLOS One study covering sixty-one tracks from thirteen cases.

Uphill and downhill median speeds turned out nearly the same, so planners can treat slope penalties evenly. Quick hasty searches moved clearly faster than careful sweeps. Within teams, movement was tightly linked, with followers reacting to leaders after only short delays. The authors offer the numbers to sharpen how search areas are assigned in the critical first hours.
plos-pone-0351641:
Naufal Nordin, Woi Pui Juan, and Nurul Umira Samsudin tested how well young children join what they see with how their hands move. That joining skill supports writing and class work. About one hundred and fifty children, near ten years old on average, at three city schools in Kuala Lumpur took a standard drawing test and had their pencil grips classed from photos.

Test scores tracked teacher judged mastery in Malay, English, science, and maths, with the strongest links in science and maths. Age adjusted scores kept clear links only for science and maths. Older children tended to score higher on raw marks. Grip type played a smaller role than the joining skill itself, which schools can screen early.
plos-pone-0351241:
Begona Tapia-Alzuguren and colleagues looked at why blood levels of sertraline, a common mood drug, vary so much between patients. Genes that break the drug down differ by person, and other drugs can speed or slow those pathways. Records covered seven hospital patients with gene data and sixteen drug level checks in routine care.

Before drug clashes were counted, level patterns matched gene based groups for one pathway best, called CYP2B6 in lab shorthand. After counting other drugs, patterns for that pathway grew clearer, and a second pathway also showed useful links. A third pathway showed no steady link. Even in seven patients, the message is plain: genes alone do not set dose, the full drug list matters.
plos-pone-0350941:
Sijing Wang and colleagues tested a sound based way to spot muscle fatigue while people use a passive leg exoskeleton. Sensors listen to tiny muscle vibrations during repeated squat lifts of a ten kilogram load. Five leg muscles were recorded, and features from timing, tone, and pattern fed learning models judged by leaving one person out at a time.

A voting rule across muscles worked best, sorting tired from fresh states with accuracy above ninety percent and spotting fatigue within about a second and a half. Model scores also tracked how hard people felt the work was. Wearable makers could use such live fatigue reads to tune help and warn before form breaks down.
plos-pone-0350141:
Xianli Ge and colleagues measured what happened after China tied bulk buying of generic drugs to a quality pass mark. Under the policy, listed generics must prove they match the original drug, and winners gain huge state orders at lower prices. Monthly counts of passed generics were tracked around the 2018 policy start, split by listed and unlisted drugs.

After 2018, passed generics grew by close to three extra drugs per month. Gains showed up both for listed drugs and for drugs outside the lists, which hints at spillover pressure across the industry. An earlier 2016 step showed no clear effect. Linking market access to proof of sameness, the data suggest, moves makers to certify quality.
plos-pone-0346441:
Rui-jun Yang and colleagues tested respiratory samples in one eastern city. The city is Quzhou. Sampling ran across nine months in 2023 and 2024. Twenty eight hundred samples were tested in all. Thirteen common germs were checked per sample. Cases mixed clinic flu like illness and severe ward cases. Results were split by age, place, and season.

About fifty nine percent of samples tested positive. Flu led the germ list. A pneumonia bacterium ranked second. Adenovirus ranked third. A quarter of positive cases held two germs or more. Young children tested positive most often. Older adults tested positive least often. Multi germ watching should replace flu only checks.
plos-pone-0350641:
Abdullah Hasan and colleagues interviewed twenty adults with type two diabetes at a major hospital in northern Jordan about daily self care. Diabetes is common and rising in Jordan, yet daily lived barriers were poorly mapped. Deep interviews covered food culture, faith, feelings, drug routines, and clinic gaps, sorted with careful theme methods and member checks.

Six themes emerged: cultural pressure around food, trouble sticking to drug routines, religious and cultural shaping of habits, emotional burden, gaps in health services, and coping tactics that work. Faith and family can hinder or help, often at once. Care plans that fit Jordanian culture and community life, the authors argue, will beat generic advice.
plos-pone-0350841:
Long Zheng and colleagues searched for genes that respond to capsaicin, the hot compound in chillies, in a common form of breast cancer in 2026. Capsaicin can slow these cancer cells, but its downstream targets were murky.

Starting from a public data set of treated cells, the team screened changed genes, mapped their networks, and confirmed two standouts in lab tests. Both genes ran high in breast tumors and linked to metabolic and immune features of the tumor surroundings. Survival data added clinical weight. The pair gives researchers concrete leads for how a food compound perturbs cancer cells.
plos-pone-0349641:
Elene Asanidze and co-authors surveyed doctors in Tbilisi, Georgia, about stress, mood, and working life, comparing them with professionals outside medicine. Doctors everywhere face long hours and emotional strain, but Georgian data were scarce. Their 2026 anonymous survey gathered three hundred ninety physicians across specialties plus two hundred forty non-medical workers, using standard screening scales for stress and depression alongside questions on sleep, satisfaction, and outlook.

Physicians reported clearly higher stress and more moderate-to-severe depression than the comparison group in initial analyses. Stress eased as years of experience grew, suggesting younger doctors carry the heaviest load. The team also examined differences by specialty, gender, and experience across well-being measures. They present the findings as a baseline for supporting physician mental health in Georgia, where the topic has been little studied.
plos-pone-0347641:
Alexander D Clark, Jingmai K O'Connor, and co-authors described a new fossil bird from the early Cretaceous period whose ornamental tail feathers stretched to twice its body length. The bird belongs to the enantiornithines, the dominant bird group of that era, many of which sported a single pair of ribbon-like tail feathers ending in small vaned tips. Their 2026 description names the species Plumadraco bankoorum and examines its exceptionally preserved plumage.

The tail feathers end in proportionally small racket-shaped tips, and their fine preservation reveals structural variety not seen in relatives. Such ornaments likely served in courtship display, as in some living birds. The authors caution that untangling sexual selection from survival pressures in extinct birds is hard with so little soft tissue evidence, and they frame the feathers as a product of both.
plos-pone-0349341:
Tim Faverjon, Jean-Philippe Cointet, and Pedro Ramaciotti ran a controlled experiment on how recommendation algorithms quietly learn users' politics. Working from real sharing data for nearly forty thousand users of the platform X, they trained a recommender on synthetic versions of the data where each step could be inspected. Their 2026 study asks whether basic recommendation logic alone manufactures an ideological map of users.

It does: elementary principles trained on what people share arranged users along a left-right line inside the system, independently of age or gender. The team then edited those internal positions and watched the offered content shift in leaning, diversity, and relevance. The authors argue the political geometry is an emergent byproduct of ordinary recommendation, with consequences for segregated information diets.
plos-pone-0349941:
Yunjie Liu and colleagues created RAGER, a free software platform that analyzes two kinds of gene data together. One kind shows which genes are switched on in a sample, and the other shows which stretches of DNA are open and ready to be used. Studying both at once can reveal how gene control goes wrong, but the tools were hard for non-specialists.

RAGER chains the popular analysis tools into one automated workflow, so a researcher can run the whole job with far less coding. The authors show it working on two published datasets, finding patterns in gene activity and DNA openness together. It runs on the Snakemake system and is shared openly for anyone to download.
plos-pone-0349141:
Amon Exavery and a large team studied whether community support programmes help Tanzanian children living with HIV keep the virus fully suppressed. They followed more than twenty-six thousand orphaned and vulnerable children on treatment between twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-three, each with at least two virus measurements. The programmes combined household economic help, links to teen clubs, and health insurance.

Among children whose virus started undetectable, about one in eight saw it rebound, but those receiving programme support were roughly a quarter less likely to rebound than similar children without it. Among children starting with detectable virus, about seven in ten reached full suppression. The authors credit steady, practical support around families, not medicine alone, with helping children stick to demanding daily treatment.
plos-pone-0349041:
Pierre Chauvin and colleagues confronted a blind spot in French medicine: the country's universalist rules bar collecting race or ethnicity data, which hides who bears the heaviest cancers. At one Paris university hospital, they worked around the ban with an anonymous survey using birthplace. The survey covered seven hundred and eighty women with breast cancer. They paired it with years of fieldwork among African women in the region.

The aggressive triple-negative form of the disease proved at least three times as common in women born in Sub-Saharan Africa as in women born in France. Those women also arrived with more advanced disease. Interviews surfaced reasons: low awareness, different beliefs about causes, shame and secrecy, traditional healing first, and a hard-to-navigate system. The authors call this cancer a telling example of how official blindness can cost health.
plos-pone-0345041:
Shelly L. Miller and co-workers investigate how COVID-19 spread through one apartment building in Santander, Spain, in twenty twenty. Fifteen cases clustered in four homes stacked above each other, during a lull in wider spread. Their 2026 study focuses on the shared bathroom air duct linking those windowless bathrooms, using field measures and airflow computer models.

Genetic and outbreak data, combined with the modeling, pointed to the duct as the most likely route. Air carrying the virus could drift upward between connected homes. Running a kitchen exhaust fan could pull even more air between flats. The team suggests fitting bathroom ducts with powered fans and one-way flaps to lower this risk in similar buildings.
plos-pone-0348241:
Hui Wu and co-workers design a decision method for picking drone sensor mixes to watch for landslides and other hazards along highways. Different terrain needs different eyes, and budgets rule out carrying everything. Their 2026 study ranks single sensors by performance at varied flying heights, then scores every pairing for four kinds of highway country, from flat farmland to mountains and city edges.

The best mix shifted with height and terrain in sensible ways. Color plus heat cameras won at low heights in several settings, while laser and radar joined in the mountains and at altitude. A one-size fleet would waste money and miss hazards; matching sensors to place and height sharpens watchfulness for road crews.
plos-pone-0342041:
Qian Wang and Kizito Tekwa followed thirty-one Chinese English majors whose phone habits scored high on an addiction scale. Instead of relying on memory, they tracked actual app use for two weeks and paired it with personality tests, grades, and student reflections. The 2026 study asks whether heavy use among language students, who lean on apps for study, truly counts as addiction.

The students logged huge amounts of time on messaging, social, and video apps, yet more than eight in ten denied being addicted, saying their work still got done. A conscientious personality went with less screen time. The authors suggest calling most of this high but functional engagement, while still helping the minority whose use turns compulsive.
plos-pone-0343341:
Sina Golestani and a large team charted thirty years of kidney stone disease across North Africa and the Middle East using the Global Burden of Disease database. Stones cause intense pain, repeat hospital visits, and heavy costs, yet regional figures were scattered. The 2026 analysis covered twenty-one countries from 1990 to 2021, breaking the burden down by age, sex, and development level.

New cases more than doubled to about five point three million a year, and deaths and disability rose alongside. Rates adjusted for age stayed roughly flat, meaning population growth and ageing drove the increase. Men consistently carried more disease than women. The authors press for prevention and treatment policies tailored to the region.
plos-pone-0348441:
Li Qi and Lanlan Zhao asked how folk seek help from a bot, set next to help from peers. They mined thirty thousand turns of talk from two stores. One held chats with AI. One held posts from a big help board. Word tools then scored each line for soft words, hedges, and tone.

With the bot, the soft shell fell away. Hedges and please-and-thanks near died out. Nor did folk beg as meek guests. They spoke like a boss who gives clear tasks. The team says bots cut the social cost of the ask. The flip side is less drill in the hard art of state a vague need well.
plos-pone-0346341:
Seda Kutluer, Milena Pavlova, and Wim Groot study ruinous medical bills in old age. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. They used a 2017 survey on health, aging, and retirement in Europe. It covered more than thirteen thousand older people in eleven EU states. All lived with long-term diseases such as diabetes or heart disease.

Having one illness did not drive the worst bills. Having several at once did. The pattern held at every spending line the team tested. Risk ran highest in Poland, Italy, Greece, and the Czech Republic. Spain sat at the low end. The authors urge policy makers to focus on people juggling many chronic conditions at once.
plos-pone-0347741:
Ransmond Berchie and colleagues tackle a subtle trap in diabetes drug trials, in this 2026 PLOS ONE statistics paper. Drugs called SGLT-2 inhibitors, now central to diabetes and heart care, cause an early dip in a kidney measure called eGFR. Trialists naturally ask whether patients with bigger dips fare differently in the long run, but that dip is itself caused by the drug, which biases simple comparisons.

The authors use a method that sorts patients by the dip they would have had on either treatment, using a correlation model to handle what cannot be observed. Their framework shows how to ask the question without fooling oneself. It matters because misreading the early dip could scare doctors off drugs that protect kidneys over time.
plos-pone-0347541:
Jaba Rani Sarker, John Rolfe, and Jayanath Ananda ask coastal Bangladeshi rice farmers what a climate-proof seed is worth to them, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Rising seas push salt water into paddies, yet salt-tolerant rice varieties that already exist remain little planted, a puzzle this study probes with a choice experiment.

Farmers fell into three segments with different willingness to pay, shaped by age, savings, and land size. The findings show adoption is not one decision but several, depending on a household's resources and risks. Extension programs that treat all smallholders alike will keep missing; pricing and support tailored to each segment stand a better chance of getting tolerant seed into salty ground.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Even the Sahara mission's size came under review in this text of 2004. On 29 April, the Council adopted Resolution 1541 without dissent. The Secretary-General's April report lay before it. The text restates Resolution 1495 from the year before. That text had backed the envoy's peace plan as the best deal-based path.

Support for the plan is voiced again here. All parties and states in the region must work fully with the envoy. MINURSO's mandate then runs to 31 October 2004. One new note stands out. The Secretary-General must weigh the mission size the tasks truly need. A cut is openly on the table. The vote the mission exists to run had still not come.

Two colonial lands joined hands to form one state in 1960. On 5 July, the Council adopted Resolution 141 without dissent. The Republic of Somalia had been born four days before. British Somaliland had just won its freedom. It then merged with the Italian-run trust land of Somalia. Somali nationalists had long demanded that union.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Somalia. The Assembly seated it that September. Somalia stood out among the new states of 1960. Two lands chose to join at the moment of freedom. The union aimed to gather most Somali speakers under one flag. Its loose ends shaped wars in later years.

On 30 November 1978 the Council renewed a peacekeeping mandate in the Golan Heights. The vote was fourteen to none. China did not take part. The mission was the UN Disengagement Observer Force. It separates Israeli and Syrian troops. It also reports on the ceasefire line between them.

The extension covered six months, running to 31 May 1979. The Council called on the parties to carry out Resolution 338 from 1973. It also asked the Secretary-General to report at the end of the term. That report would describe events in the area. It would also list steps taken toward a settlement.

A new flag rose over the desert in 1991. The land had been part of the Soviet Union. Now it stood on its own, rich in gas. Its leaders asked for a UN seat that winter. Resolution 741 was passed without a vote on 7 February 1992. The Council met as the Soviet map was being redrawn.

The members backed the bid. They told the General Assembly to admit the republic. The Assembly did so in March 1992. The state came in with a crowd of new states from the same fallen union. In time it chose a path of strict neutrality. This one short text marks its first step into world affairs.

Burundi held landmark elections in 2005 after years of civil war. A UN operation, ONUB, had supported the transition since 2004. Its mandate was nearly finished. Resolution 1641, adopted on 30 November 2005, kept the operation alive a little longer. Members noted that pockets of instability still threatened the region.

ONUB's mandate now ran until 15 January 2006. The extension added only six weeks. It was a bridge, not a fresh commitment. The Council acted under Chapter VII, giving the decision binding force. Burundi's elected government was taking charge of security. The short renewal let the UN draw down in step with that handover.

A truce in Indonesia won rare praise from the Council in 1948. Dutch troops and republican forces had signed the deal weeks before. It rested on terms both sides had sworn to accept. The UN's good offices team had helped them reach it. Resolution 41 passed on 28 February 1948. Seven members voted yes. Four held back.

The Council voiced its joy at the truce. It praised the good offices team for its aid. The offer of UN help, first made in 1947, stayed on the table. Both sides and the UN team had to keep the Council up to date. News of the road to a full pact was required. The same day, the Council sent the team a fresh task on Java and Madura.

Mercenary attacks on the Democratic Republic of the Congo drew Resolution 241, adopted on 15 November 1967. Foreign fighters had struck the young Congolese state, and the Council was concerned that Portugal let them stage from Angola, which it still ruled. Support for the mercenaries, from recruiting to arms supply, kept flowing in from abroad.

The Council condemned any interference in Congo's internal affairs. It singled out Portugal for failing to stop the mercenaries from using Angola as a base, in breach of earlier resolutions, and told Lisbon to end all help to them at once. The text captures an early UN attempt to treat hired foreign fighters as a threat to the independence of new states.

Resolution 541, passed on 18 November 1983, spurns a claim of statehood in north Cyprus. Three days before, the Turkish Cypriot side had declared a state of its own. Cyprus's foreign chief spoke in the hall. The Council judged the move a breach of the 1960 pacts. Those pacts had set up the Republic of Cyprus and pledged to keep it whole.

The Council deplored the claim. It held the bid to split off a new state void in law, and called for its recall. It told all sides to carry out its 1974 and 1975 Cyprus texts at once and in full. It asked the UN chief to press his good offices for the fastest path to a just peace. No state was to back any Cypriot state but the Republic.

Liberia's civil war shapes Resolution 1041, adopted on 29 January 1996. The UN Observer Mission in Liberia, UNOMIL, worked beside the West African force ECOMOG under the Abuja Agreement. The Council praised ECOWAS peace work but deplored fresh ceasefire breaches, attacks on ECOMOG troops, and slow progress on pulling forces apart and disarming fighters.

The Council extends UNOMIL until 31 May 1996. It condemns the attacks on ECOMOG and on civilians and demands that they stop. It calls on all Liberian sides to keep the ceasefire, disarm, and work toward unity, and warns that world support depends on their will to settle matters in peace. States are urged to fund ECOMOG and the peace process, and the arms embargo on Liberia is recalled.

Sierra Leone's peacebuilding office is renewed by Resolution 1941, adopted on 29 September 2010. The UN Integrated Peacebuilding Office, UNIPSIL, was helping the government prepare for the 2012 elections, which carried a risk of rising tension. The government was carrying out its Agenda for Change, and the parties were keeping the 2009 joint communiqué that ended political violence. The Special Court's last trial was still running.

The Council extends UNIPSIL until 15 September 2011. Its work with the UN country team should focus on support for the 2012 elections. It covers conflict prevention and dialogue between parties, tackling youth unemployment and help with governance, anti-corruption work, and fighting drug trafficking. The government is called on to manage natural resources openly, strengthen the Anti-Corruption Commission, and act on the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's recommendations. Reports are due every six months, tracking benchmarks for a handover to a UN country team.

Congo's ceasefire gains ground in Resolution 1341, adopted unanimously on 22 February 2001. The Secretary-General reported that conditions for deploying MONUC were being met: the ceasefire was holding, disengagement plans existed, and Congo's president had pledged cooperation. Rwanda had promised to pull its forces from Pweto, and Uganda to cut two battalions. Atrocities, child soldiers, and illegal resource extraction still scarred the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Ugandan, Rwandan, and all other foreign forces withdraw. It demands that the parties carry out the Kampala and Harare disengagement plans within the 14 days from 15 March 2001. It sets 15 May 2001 as the deadline for a full withdrawal timetable and for disarmament plans covering all armed groups. It endorses MONUC's updated deployment concept to monitor the ceasefire and disengagement, as the first step toward complete foreign withdrawal.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1541 (XV) was adopted on 15 December 1960. It laid down the principles for deciding when a member state must report on a territory. The duty comes under Article 73 e of the Charter. It covers peoples who have not yet gained a full measure of self-government. The annex lists the tests for judging each case on its own facts.

The principles say a territory counts as self-governing in three cases. It may become a sovereign state. It may join an independent state on equal terms. Or it may freely link itself to one by an informed, free vote. A land that is apart in place and in its people's culture is presumed to fall under the duty. That holds until one of those ends is reached.

General Assembly Resolution 41, adopted on 14 December 1946, laid down principles for the general regulation and reduction of armaments. The Assembly held an early, shared cut in arms and forces to be needful. It asked the Security Council to draft workable steps, in order of urgency. All states would follow them, rather than a few acting alone.

A central aim was banning atomic weapons and all major weapons fit for mass destruction. It came with world control of atomic energy for peaceful ends only. The text calls for safeguards by way of inspection, to guard states that keep the rules. It urges troops stationed abroad without consent to be pulled back.

General Assembly resolution 69/41 (2014) tries to restart multilateral nuclear disarmament talks after more than a decade without concrete results. The Assembly welcomes the report of its Open-ended Working Group, which met in 2013 to develop proposals. It welcomes the Secretary-General's collection of member states' views. It calls on governments, international organizations, and civil society to keep building on those proposals. They should do so in United Nations and other forums. It decides to review progress at its seventieth session, if necessary through the Working Group again.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
A final chance to disarm under inspection is given to Iraq on 8 November 2002. The Council found that Iraq had failed to account fully for its banned weapons programmes and had blocked inspectors for years. It judged Iraq to be in material breach of the ceasefire terms set after the 1991 Gulf War.

A tougher inspection regime is set up, to complete the disarmament required since 1991. Iraq must declare all its weapons programmes at once and give inspectors from the United Nations and the atomic energy agency full, immediate access everywhere. False statements or any failure to cooperate would be reported to the Council, which warned of serious consequences.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's mission, UNMEE, is extended for six months on 30 January 2007, until 31 July 2007. The border remained undemarcated, and the mission's staff are praised for working in hard conditions. Eritrea had moved troops and equipment into the Temporary Security Zone, a step treated as a serious breach.

Eritrea is demanded to withdraw its troops and equipment from the zone at once. Both parties are also demanded to give UNMEE the access, help, support, and protection it needs, and to lift all restrictions without delay. Ethiopia is pressed over its own duties under the Algiers Agreements, and the Secretary-General and the wider world are called on to engage both governments to restart the stalled demarcation.

A buffer force between the Egyptian and Israeli armies took legal shape on 27 October 1973. Resolution 340, passed two days earlier, had called for a United Nations Emergency Force to supervise the cease-fire. The Secretary-General reported the same day on how to set the force up. Resolution 341 is the Council's answer to that report.

The Council approved the report in full. The force would be established as the report set out, for an initial period of six months. After that, it would continue only if the Council decided it should. This decision gave legal form to the second United Nations Emergency Force. That force became the buffer that watched over the cease-fire after the October war.
un-sc-res-1541:
Western Sahara's stalled peace process returned to the Council in April 2004. On 29 April 2004 the Council renewed MINURSO until 31 October 2004. It restated support for the peace plan backed the year before. The Secretary-General had reported on the dispute days earlier. The goal remained a settlement both sides could accept. That settlement had to let the territory's people choose their own future.

The Council called on the parties and nearby states to work with the Secretary-General. His envoy needed their full cooperation. The Secretary-General owed a report before the mandate ended. It would also cover talks on freeing remaining prisoners of war. The ceasefire held, but the political track stayed stuck.
un-sc-res-141: The Republic of Somalia applied for United Nations membership as it gained independence in 1960. On 5 July 1960 the Security Council examined the application. It recommended to the General Assembly that Somalia be admitted. The decision was unanimous and fills a single sentence. Somalia took its seat days after independence. The new state joined a fast-growing wave of African members that year.
un-sc-res-441:
UNDOF came up for renewal at the end of November 1978. On 30 November 1978 the Security Council extended the Golan force until 31 May 1979. The Secretary-General had supplied his report on the mission. The decision uses the standard three-part form. The parties must carry out resolution 338 at once. A report on the term is due at its end.

China did not take part in the voting. That abstention by absence was China's habit on this file. The force itself kept watch over the separation area. It had done so since the disengagement deal of 1974. The renewal kept that quiet arrangement alive for another half year.
un-sc-res-1641:
Burundi's peace operation received a six-week extension in late 2005. On 30 November 2005 the Security Council kept ONUB in place until 15 January 2006. The Council recalled its earlier Burundi texts, above all resolution 1545. It restated its commitment to Burundi's sovereignty and unity. It also noted that sources of instability remained. Those, it said, still threatened peace in the region.

The extension was made under Chapter VII of the Charter. That gave the mission its enforcement weight. The short term suggests a drawdown decision was near. Burundi had just finished a long transition with elections. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter while the mission's future was weighed.
un-sc-res-41:
A truce in Indonesia gave the Council reason for satisfaction in February 1948. The Netherlands and the Republic of Indonesia had signed the Renville Truce Agreement. Both sides also accepted principles for a political settlement. On 28 February 1948 the Council noted those steps with pleasure. Its Committee of Good Offices had helped the parties reach them. The committee's members earned formal praise in the text.

The Council kept its offer of good offices open. Both parties and the committee had to keep it informed directly. News on the political settlement was the key need. The same day, the Council asked the committee to watch two regions closely. The truce later broke down, but the framework shaped the final transfer of sovereignty.
un-sc-res-241:
Mercenary attacks on the Congo angered the Council in November 1967. Foreign fighters had struck the country from bases abroad. Portugal had let them use Angola as a staging ground. On 15 November 1967 the Council condemned any interference in the Congo's internal affairs. It condemned Portugal in particular for breaking earlier resolutions. Support for the mercenaries, from recruitment to arms supply, ran through the text.

Portugal had to end all help to the mercenaries at once. Countries that received fleeing mercenaries had to stop them fighting again. Measures to block new attacks on any state were required. The mercenaries had just been beaten in eastern Congo. The text aimed to close the pipeline that produced them.
un-sc-res-541:
Northern Cyprus's breakaway declaration was ruled void on 18 November 1983. The Turkish Cypriot leaders had declared a separate state on 15 November. Cyprus's foreign minister addressed the Council. The move clashed with the 1960 treaties that set up the Republic of Cyprus and guaranteed its shape. The Secretary-General had spoken on 17 November.

The Council deplored the purported secession of part of the Republic of Cyprus. It judged the declaration legally invalid and called for its withdrawal. Resolutions 365 (1974) and 367 (1975) had to be applied in full at once. The Secretary-General was asked to press his good offices toward the earliest progress on a just and lasting settlement. All states had to respect Cyprus's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. No state was to accept any Cypriot state other than the Republic of Cyprus. The declared state remains unrecognized abroad.
un-sc-res-1041:
Liberia's observer mission was extended as the Abuja timetable slipped on 29 January 1996. The Secretary-General's report of 23 January covered UNOMIL's work. Ceasefire breaches had grown, and ECOMOG troops had come under attack. Disengagement and disarmament lagged behind the Abuja Agreement's terms. ECOWAS won praise for its steady work to restore peace.

The Council extended UNOMIL's mandate until 31 May 1996. All Liberian parties were called to honor the Abuja Agreement in full and in speed, above all on the ceasefire, disarmament, and reconciliation. The armed attacks on ECOMOG staff were condemned. Condolences went to the governments and peoples of the fallen soldiers. Every faction was told once more to respect the status of United Nations and ECOMOG staff strictly. Member states were urged to give money, transport, and other backing to the peace process and to the trust fund for Liberia.
un-sc-res-1941:
Sierra Leone faced the Security Council in Resolution 1941, adopted on 29 September 2010. The country was rebuilding after civil war and looking ahead to elections in 2012. Tensions could rise as the vote neared. The United Nations peacebuilding office there, UNIPSIL, helped with elections, jobs, and the rule of law.

The text extends UNIPSIL's mandate until 15 September 2011. The office should help prepare the 2012 elections and calm disputes between parties. It should also back the fight against graft and drug trafficking. The Council praises the Special Court's work and urges the government to press on with reform and national unity.
un-sc-res-1341:
The Democratic Republic of the Congo was the matter before the Council in Resolution 1341, adopted on 22 February 2001. The long war had swollen the ranks of refugees and the displaced. Atrocities hit civilians in the east, and child soldiers were still being recruited. The cease-fire was now broadly holding, and a plan for pulling forces apart existed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Ugandan, Rwandan, and all other foreign forces leave Congo. The parties must carry out the disengagement plan within fourteen days from 15 March 2001. A full withdrawal timetable is due by 15 May 2001. The text backs the updated plan for the United Nations mission, MONUC, to watch the cease-fire and verify each step.
europmc-pmc10039041:
Shin and colleagues report a single test that aims to detect several early-stage cancers at once, in a 2023 study. Early detection greatly improves cancer outcomes, yet no one test could screen for many cancer types. The team built a test around exosomes, tiny parcels shed by cells into the blood.

Their method reads chemical patterns on exosomes with a light-based sensor and AI analysis. They report results for six cancer types at early stages. The study points toward blood tests that could screen for many cancers in one draw, though wider trials must come first.
europmc-pmc10168541:
Altammar reviews nanoparticles in a 2023 paper, covering their traits, how they are made, their uses, and the challenges they pose. Nanoparticles are specks of matter thousands of times smaller than a hair's width. At that scale, familiar materials gain new traits that engineers prize, from brighter colors to stronger chemical action.

The review compares green and chemical methods of making the particles. It surveys uses in medicine, industry, and farming. It also weighs risks to human health and to nature. The paper is a broad, plain guide to a vast field.
europmc-pmc10663641:
Hu and co-authors reviewed gamma-delta T cells in 2023, a less common arm of the immune system. Most T cells carry alpha-beta receptors; these carry gamma-delta ones instead. The team's own work has used donor Vdelta2 cells to treat late-stage solid tumours and tuberculosis. The review asks how far that promise can go.

It traces the cells from their find in 1984 to their growth in the thymus gland. Subtypes differ by receptor shape and by the signals they release. Hu shows how each subtype fights tumours and germs in its local setting. Roles span infection, immune disease, blood cancers, and solid tumours. Donor cell therapy for cancer gets a full plan for what comes next.
europmc-pmc11701741:
Tegenfeldt, Kuznetsov, Manni, Berkeley, Zdobnov, and Kriventseva update OrthoDB and BUSCO in this 2025 paper. OrthoDB offers functional and evolutionary notes on orthologous genes, meaning genes in different species that descend from one ancestral gene. It extends experimental knowledge of gene function to newly sequenced genomes. This update expands coverage to 5,827 eukaryotic genomes.

Coding DNA sequences and gene locus coordinates were added to the resource. Access now spans browsing, downloads, a REST interface, and program packages for Python and R. OrthoLoger, the inference tool behind the database, is released as a Conda package and via BioContainers. Its mapper component streamlines annotation of newly sequenced genomes. BUSCO, the companion tool that judges genome completeness from expected genes, is covered in the same update.
europmc-pmc12240541:
McCallum and colleagues explained how two virus variants dodge immunity in 2021. The Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2 had swept to global dominance. Kappa, a close cousin, spread in the same wave. Both carried changes in their spike protein.

Serum from vaccinated people neutralized the variants less well. Several lab antibodies lost their grip on altered spike sites. Delta reshaped one spike region that antibodies target. Binding strength to the human entry receptor stayed near the original for most forms. McCallum gives a structural account of immune escape. It appeared in Science in 2021.
europmc-pmc1240241:
Schlumpf and co-authors tested sunscreen chemicals for hormone effects in 2001. UV screens guard skin against sun damage and cancer. They also enter cosmetics to keep products stable. Traces had been found building up in wildlife and people.

Six common screens were tested in cells and young rats. Five made breast cancer cells grow faster in dishes. That growth could be blocked by an estrogen blocker drug. In rats, one screen raised womb weight with dose. Schlumpf calls for deeper safety checks on these widely used chemicals. One screen, B-MDM, showed no such activity in cells.
europmc-pmc12851941:
Avsec and co-authors presented AlphaGenome, a DNA prediction model, in 2026. Earlier models traded sequence length against prediction detail. Each covered only some types of genomic measurement. AlphaGenome takes one million base pairs as input at once.

It predicts thousands of functional tracks at single-base resolution. Outputs span gene expression, chromatin access, and binding maps. Splice site usage and strength are also predicted. Trained on human and mouse genomes, it won 25 of 26 variant tests. It also reproduced known variant mechanisms near the TAL1 cancer gene. Trained tracks include splice sites and contact maps.
europmc-pmc1440941:
Each chromosome keeps to its own zone in the cell nucleus, or so textbooks said. Branco and Pombo tested that claim in 2006 with a sharp imaging method that keeps fine DNA detail intact. They looked at human blood cells and found zones blend far more than models allowed.

Pairs of chromosomes that blend most also swap parts most often, forming translocations, a type of damage. Busy gene-reading hubs sat in the blended zones. Blocking gene reading changed how chromosomes met. Branco argues that gene activity shapes how chromosomes mingle. That mingling, in turn, affects how stable the genome stays in each cell type.
europmc-pmc1828741: AGGRESCAN: a server for the prediction and evaluation of "hot spots" of aggregation in polypeptides. — a 2005 science paper on the AGGRESCAN clump predictor. It predicts the hot spots. The paper is the AGGRESCAN guide: the findings on the clump tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1945041: An actin-based wave generator organizes cell motility. — a 2005 science paper on cell-motion wave machines. It finds the wave generator. The paper is the wave study: the findings on cell motility, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2013941: Identification and classification of hubs in brain networks. — a 2005 science paper on brain network hubs. It identifies the hub types. The paper is the hub study: the findings on brain nets, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2018741: PsychoPy--Psychophysics software in Python. — a 2005 science paper on PsychoPy software. It guides the Python software for labs worldwide. The paper is the PsychoPy guide: the findings on the software tool for labs, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2082641: Clinical trials and medical care: defining the therapeutic misconception. — a 2005 science paper on trial-vs-care mix-ups. It clears the care-trial mix-up for labs. The paper is the mix-up guide: the notes on trial care, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2361241: Surgical resection of hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer: a systematic review of publish — a 2008 science paper on liver-metastasis surgery. It reviews the resection research. The paper is the surgery review: the findings on hepatic ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2409341: Pectic homogalacturonan masks abundant sets of xyloglucan epitopes in plant cell walls. — a 2008 science paper on plant-wall sugar masks. It finds the homogalacturonan masks. The paper is the mask study: the findings on plant ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2475541: Spinal cord injury reveals multilineage differentiation of ependymal cells. — a 2008 science paper on spine-injury cell changes. It reveals the multilineage differentiation. The paper is the reveal study: the findings on spinal ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2515341: Culture shapes how we look at faces. — a 2008 science paper on culture and face perception. It shows how culture shapes looking. The paper is the culture study: the findings on faces, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2577641: TNF signaling inhibition in the CNS: implications for normal brain function and neurodegenerati — a 2008 science paper on TNF inhibition in the brain. It studies the signaling implications. The paper is the implication study: the findings on TNF ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2632741: Accurate path integration in continuous attractor network models of grid cells. — a 2008 science paper on path integration. It models the accurate path integration. The paper is the path study: the findings on grid ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2680341: Lineage-specific biology revealed by a finished genome assembly of the mouse. — a 2008 science paper on mouse genome lineage. It reveals the lineage-specific biology. The paper is the biology study: the findings on mouse ills, filed here in session.
nennius-history-britons-giles-1841:
The History of the Britons is a Welsh Latin work tied to the name Nennius and dated to the ninth century. J. A. Giles translated it into English in 1841. It mixes chronicle, genealogy, and marvel, and it holds a famous place in the Arthur story.

Nennius lists twelve battles that Arthur fought against the Saxons, naming places few can now find. That list is the earliest sign of a historical Arthur, centuries before the romances. Around it sit older British traditions and wonders of the land. Scholars still debate how much of it is history and how much is hope.
plos-pone-0004941:
Cancer cells often lose methyl tags from their DNA across the genome. This change is called hypomethylation. It tracks with an unstable genome. Kristy Richards and co-authors compared head and neck cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked how tag loss differs by tumor type. Some of these tumors are linked to the virus HPV. Others are not.

Hypomethylation was more pronounced in HPV-negative tumors. The degree of tag loss also matched genomic instability. The pattern may help explain the behavior of HPV-negative tumors. It could also help sort patients by how unstable their tumor genomes are.
plos-pone-0005041:
The nucleus is crowded with tangled DNA. Scientists wondered whether that crowding slows small proteins down. Nicolas Dross and colleagues mapped the movement directly. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They used glowing eGFP proteins in living cell nuclei. They varied the proteins' size by linking copies together.

The team measured how oligomer mobility changes with chromatin density. Movement can be slowed by viscosity, flows, transport or obstacles. Their map separates those effects. It gives a baseline for how molecules travel inside the nucleus. Such baselines matter for models of gene regulation. They tell modelers what simple diffusion can explain, and what it cannot.
plos-pone-0005141:
The gene doublesex sits at the bottom of the sex-determination cascade. It makes a female protein in females and a male protein in males. Mercedes Alvarez, María Fernanda Ruiz and Lucas Sánchez tested it across species in PLOS ONE in 2009. They took doublesex from Anastrepha, a fruit fly genus. They put it into Drosophila, the classic lab fly.

The foreign gene steered Drosophila's somatic sexual development. Its instructions were still readable in a distant relative. The swap test reveals how the sex switch evolved. Master switches can stay conserved while species diverge. The work compares the bottom of the cascade across flies. It shows evolution tinkering around a stable core decision.
plos-pone-0005241:
A popular method called ChIP-seq maps where proteins bind DNA across the genome. Every such study needs control libraries to separate real binding from background noise. Vega and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that those controls carry signals of their own.

If controls are not neutral, they can create false binding peaks or hide real ones. The study dissected the inherent signals inside sequencing-based control libraries. Knowing the background's shape helps researchers clean their data and trust the peaks that remain after correction. Labs that use this method can now check their own control data with fresh eyes and fix the flaws they find before they publish.
plos-pone-0005341:
Embryonic stem cells can divide without limit and can become many cell types, making them prized for therapy. That endless growth rests on an unusual cell cycle and its controlling signals. Abdelalim and Tooyama identified one crucial signal in PLOS ONE in 2009: BNP.

BNP is a peptide best known from heart biology. The study found BNP signaling is crucial for embryonic stem cell proliferation. A defined growth signal helps labs grow stem cells reliably, a basic need for any future cell-based treatment. Stem cells are held back by cost and scale, since they die or drift in poor culture. So a clear growth cue is a base each lab can build its own recipes on.
plos-pone-0005941:
Trophy hunting of lions and other big predators brings in money that can fund their protection. Craig Packer, Margaret Kosmala, Hilary Cooley and colleagues weighed that bargain in PLOS ONE in 2009. They also looked at predator control, the killing done to stop attacks on livestock and people, which adds pressure on the same animals.

Hunting is a risky tool, the authors stress, because predator numbers can drop fast when too many are taken. Managers thus face a hard balance between income, safety and survival of the species. The paper gives that debate hard terms: what hunting earns, what it costs, and why control programs need tight limits to stay safe.
plos-pone-0006041:
Amyloid diseases spread when clumped protein seeds more clumping, much like a crystal growing. Per Westermark, Katarzyna Lundmark and Gunilla Westermark asked in 2009 whether seeds must come from the disease protein itself. Their PLOS ONE paper tests fibrils built from designed synthetic peptides with no link to amyloid, given to mice during inflammation.

The foreign fibrils induced AA-amyloidosis, the title reports. A seed need not match the protein it seeds, at least in this animal model. That finding widens the safety questions around peptide materials and deepens the puzzle of how amyloid diseases start, since stray fibrils in an inflamed body might light the fuse.
plos-pone-0006141:
Blood agar is the daily bread of the diagnostic lab, but good blood is costly where labs are poorest. Ellen Yeh, Benjamin Pinsky, Niaz Banaei and colleagues tested a cheaper source in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper checks hair sheep blood, citrated or defibrinated, against every requirement of blood agar for identifying bacteria and testing antibiotic susceptibility.

In much of the developing world, labs fall back on human blood because wool sheep and horses are costly to raise. Hair sheep are hardier and cheaper, and their blood fulfilled all requirements in these tests. A small change of ingredient can thus raise the quality of diagnosis for whole regions, without new machines.
plos-pone-0006241:
An egg cell must deliver the right messages to the right end to set up the future body. Musa Mhlanga and colleagues imaged oskar messenger RNA inside the fruit fly oocyte in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Oskar marks the posterior end, but its multi-step journey with partner proteins was poorly seen.

Live imaging showed where the RNA and its trans-acting protein partners sit together during transport. Quantitative pictures replace guesses about timing and place. The map helps explain how cells move cargo with such precision. Faulty delivery scrambles development, so the transport rules matter widely.
plos-pone-0006741:
Kevin Drace, Stephanie McLaughlin, and Creg Darby studied a worm protein that lets bacterial films stick in PLOS ONE in 2009. The worm is Caenorhabditis elegans, a standard laboratory animal. Its cuticle is a layered outer skin facing the environment. Biofilms made by Yersinia bacteria attach to that cuticle. Attachment gives scientists a handle on surface properties.

The protein BAH-1 sits in seam cells of the worm. It belongs to the DUF23 protein family. Without BAH-1, microbial biofilms could not bind properly. Identifying a required host protein turns attachment into a genetics problem. That opens the way to study how surfaces invite or resist bacterial films.
plos-pone-0006841:
Lori-Ann R. Sacrey, Callie A. M. Clark, and Ian Q. Whishaw tested music's effect on reaching in Parkinson's disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. Parkinson's impairs movement and sensation. Familiar music can reduce some of those impairments. Patients also lean too heavily on vision to guide reaching. Whether music eases that visual dependence was unclear.

Music attenuated excessive visual guidance in advanced disease. It did not do so in mild disease, as the title states. The stage difference matters for therapy design. Music may compensate only once internal guidance is badly weakened. The result refines when music-based rehabilitation should be offered.
plos-pone-0006941:
Maura Manganelli, Francesca Malfatti, Ty Samo, and colleagues measured ocean microbes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study site was the southern Drake Passage during the austral winter. Carbon cycling in the Southern Ocean is a major climate question. The region has strong seasons, with long dark winters.

The team measured how carbon moved through the food web in that dark season. They found microbes playing the major role in winter carbon fluxes. Winter data are rare because conditions there are harsh. Knowing who drives carbon flow year-round improves the models used to predict ocean uptake of carbon.
plos-pone-0007041: Ravi Barabote, Gary Xie, Thomas Brettin, and colleagues published the complete genome sequence of a tularemia bacterium strain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The strain is Francisella tularensis subspecies holarctica FTNF002-00. A full genome sequence gives the complete DNA record of this strain. Such records let researchers compare strains, trace outbreaks, and find genes behind virulence and drug response.
plos-pone-0007141:
Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus and Zvia Breznitz tested memory training in dyslexic adults in PLOS ONE in 2009. Error detection while reading leans on working memory. The team asked whether training working memory could sharpen that error monitor. They compared twenty-seven dyslexic readers with thirty-four controls, all university students. Brain responses were recorded with ERP methods.

Training changed the dyslexic readers' working memory capacity. It also affected their error detection system. If a trainable skill lifts reading accuracy checks, therapy gains a new lever. The comparison with controls shows which gaps training can close and which it cannot.
plos-pone-0007241:
Scott A. Hocknull, Philip J. Piper, Gert D. van den Bergh, and colleagues traced the history of giant monitor lizards in 2009. The Komodo dragon is the largest living lizard. It survives on a few isolated islands in eastern Indonesia, where it is the dominant land carnivore, and it is vulnerable to extinction.

The authors study fossils and past ranges of the largest terrestrial lizards in the Varanidae family. They reconstruct where these giants lived, how they evolved, and why they vanished. Their title calls the story a paradise lost for dragons. The work informs protection of the last survivor.
plos-pone-0007341:
Jennyfer Zerbib, Johanna M. Seddon, Florence Richard, and colleagues tested an eye disease gene variant in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Age-related macular degeneration is a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. Major genetic risk factors had recently been identified, including variants in CFH and in the ARMS2 and HTRA1 region.

The authors run a case-control study in two populations. They examine a variant called rs5888 in the SCARB1 gene. They report it as a possible susceptibility factor for macular degeneration. Their result adds a lipid transport gene to the disease's genetic picture.
openalex-w2077680141: Anxiety in pregnancy needs a quick, valid screen. Zhong and colleagues' 2015 study tested the GAD-7's screening power among pregnant women. The work validated the brief questionnaire in Peruvian mothers for clinics catching cases early.
openalex-w2117103941: Lead nuclei can shine light that makes charm. The ALICE team's 2013 paper measured charm photoproduction in grazing Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. The result probed the lead nucleus's gluon structure — light on glue, at last, from the LHC's lead runs.
openalex-w2124312641: Malaria spreads through the sex stages — counting them matters. A 2013 review covers ways for finding malaria's transmission stages. The work weighed methods predicting how infectious humans are to mosquitoes — transmission's key, measured at last in the field today, tomorrow, and always worldwide.
openalex-w2127627541: Herbal medicines need the same checks as drugs. A 2000 review covers safety, works, quality control, and regulation of botanical medicines. The review examined herbal mixes — plant drugs, judged fairly at last for users.
openalex-w2143036141: A truncated title hides a reef-fish atlas. This entry, 'Global Biogeography of Reef Fishes: A Hierarchical…,' keeps only a cut-off title with no author, year, or abstract. The thin catalog record suggests a study of reef-fish biogeography, but the rest is lost.
plos-pone-0006341:
Most classical Hodgkin lymphoma patients are cured, but a significant minority fail first treatment. Danielle Canioni and colleagues tested new immunohistochemical markers in fifty-nine refractory cases in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. No consensus exists on biological markers that add value beyond usual clinical parameters.

Stains that reveal proteins in tumor tissue were checked for prognostic significance. A reliable marker could flag high-risk patients for stronger or experimental therapy early. It could also spare low-risk patients excess toxicity. The study weighs candidate markers in the hardest cases. More work will be needed to prove which marks hold up in new groups of cases.
openalex-w2158718341: When forests and fields burn in the Amazon, the smoke carries particles that change how sunlight moves through the air. This 2006 study examines humic-like substances — HULIS, complex brown-carbon compounds found in fine smoke particles collected during a large Amazon field campaign. The paper measures how these particles absorb and scatter light, details that feed into climate models trying to capture what biomass burning does to the atmosphere.
openalex-w2292507041: Botanists aiming to catalogue every plant on Earth by 2020 needed a starting list for two overlooked groups: hornworts and liverworts, the small ancient plants carpeting damp ground. This 2016 PhytoKeys paper delivers the first-ever worldwide checklist of their accepted taxa. The working list is a foundation for the global plant census and for conserving these unassuming but ecologically vital organisms.
openalex-w2388080941: AutoDock Vina is one of the most-used open-source tools for docking — predicting how a drug molecule fits into a protein. This 2016 PLoS ONE paper introduces Vinardo (Vina Radii Optimized), a new scoring function trained with a novel approach on state-of-the-art datasets. The authors show it improves scoring, docking accuracy, and virtual screening for drug discovery.
openalex-w2607075141: Pathologists eyeball tumor extent on microscope slides — a slow, subjective job. This 2017 Scientific Reports paper trains deep learning to detect invasive breast cancer in digitized whole-slide images, quantifying tumor extent accurately and reproducibly. As slide scanners go routine, the algorithm offers a tireless second reader for cancer diagnosis.
openalex-w2766814241: Plastic doesn't stay in the ocean — it moves through soil into the food on our plates. This 2017 Scientific Reports paper provides the first field evidence of micro- and macroplastic transfer along a terrestrial food chain, from soil to species people eat. The finding brings the plastic crisis uncomfortably close to home.
openalex-w2800469141: Papua New Guinea endures earthquakes, volcanoes, landslides — and floods that suddenly remake the land. This 2018 Applied Water Science paper maps flood susceptibility using remote sensing, GIS, and a frequency-ratio model. The analysis gives disaster planners a clearer picture of where PNG's next deluge will hit hardest.
openalex-w2824297141: This 2013 Physical Review Letters paper measures the transverse-momentum distribution of charged particles in proton-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV with ALICE. Comparing the spectra to proton-proton baselines via the nuclear modification factor, the study tests whether the 'cold' nuclear environment alone reshapes particle production.
europmc-pmc2832341: Spotting disease markers in tissue slices is routine in pathology, and this 2010 paper explains the workhorse method. The authors review immunohistochemistry as a tool for biomarker detection and clinical practice. Their overview covers how antibody staining guides diagnosis. The paper is a practical introduction to a technique behind countless pathology reports.
europmc-pmc2877741: Rare people control HIV without drugs, and this 2010 paper hunts their secret. The authors show perforin, a killer protein, in HIV-specific CD8 T-cells tracks with elite control. Their finding pins a weapon to natural victory. The work pointed vaccine designers at a concrete target.
europmc-pmc2913941: Joubert syndrome, a rare brain malformation seen on scans, puzzles families. This 2010 review covers Joubert syndrome and related disorders, their genes, and their care. The authors distill what is known into guidance. Their review aids diagnosis of a rare cilia disease.
europmc-pmc2939541: Frailty needs measuring in family practice before crises hit. This 2010 paper builds a frailty gauge for primary care from Europe's SHARE aging survey. The authors' tool spots vulnerable elders early. Their work aids aging-in-place care across clinics. Doctors can now score frailty in a routine visit.
europmc-pmc2940741: Ebola slips into cells by gulping itself in. This 2010 paper shows Ebola entry runs on a macropinocytosis-like gulp, then rides through early and late endosomes. The authors trace the break-in route step by step. Their work exposed targets for blocking entry.
europmc-pmc2970541: Queens and workers share genes but not fates, and this 2010 paper finds why. The authors show differential DNA methylation in the brains of queen and worker honey bees. Their epigenomes explain the divide. The work illuminates social insect biology. Diet alone could never explain the split.
europmc-pmc3022541: Dying neurons leave protein fingerprints. This 2010 paper studies chopped PARP-1 bits as marks of cell-death enzymes in brain disease. The authors reveal the fingerprints. Their work aids disease research. The marks may flag Alzheimer's early. Drug trials could track them as readouts.
europmc-pmc3046141: Motherly care writes on rat brains. This 2011 paper finds licking and grooming leave wide gene marks in grown rat brains. The authors reveal nurture's signature. Their work lights up development science. Neglected pups carried different marks. The marks shifted stress responses for life.
europmc-pmc3052441: Fiber unlocks fruit antioxidants. This 2011 review shows fiber helps the gut absorb fruit and veggie antioxidants. The authors survey the teamwork. Their overview guides nutrition. Whole fruit beats juice for this reason. The fiber matrix shields fragile compounds. Smoothies keep more of the good stuff.
europmc-pmc3070641: Stem cell therapy carries real risks, and this 2011 paper names them. The authors review tumors, immune rejection, and wayward cells. Their overview guides safe clinic translation. The work shaped regulation. Hype outpaced safety for years, they warn. The review is now required reading.
europmc-pmc3114741: Gene counterparts got a fast finder. This 2011 paper brings Proteinortho, a tool for detecting orthologs at large scale. The authors' program handles big datasets. Their software spread through labs. Thousands of genomes compare in hours. The tool is open source.
europmc-pmc3197541: Programmed cell death in cancer got reviewed. This 2011 paper covers apoptosis from cancer's origins to treatment. The author maps the pathway. Their overview guides oncologists. Tumors dodge death signals, they show. Drugs that restore death are in trials. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3221041: TB dodged zinc poisoning. This 2011 paper shows TB's pump proteins expel zinc inside immune cells. The authors reveal the defense. Their work points to drugs. Blocking the pumps killed the germs. The finding aids antibiotic design. Macrophages use zinc as a weapon.
europmc-pmc3221341: Online health programs' stickiness got reviewed. This 2011 review asks what keeps users engaged with web lifestyle programs. The authors reveal the drivers. Their work guides designers. Reminders and feedback worked best. Tailored content beat generic pages. The review shaped app design.
europmc-pmc3229841: Hepatitis C care got a 2011 update. This liver-group guideline updates treatment for genotype 1 chronic hepatitis C. The authors set the standards. Their work guided doctors. Triple therapy debuted in this edition. Cure rates jumped with the new drugs. The guideline shaped global practice.
europmc-pmc3257741: Gut acids' inflammation control got reviewed. This 2011 paper maps how short-chain fatty acids calm inflammation. The authors chart the control. Their overview guides medicine. Fiber fermentation makes the acids. The review shaped IBD research. It is widely cited. Vinolo's team led the work.
europmc-pmc3271041: Colon cancer got a blood test. This 2011 paper shows a blood DNA test detects colorectal cancer early. The authors reveal the test. Their work points to screening. The test caught most cancers. Epi proColon grew from the work. Warren's team led the study.
europmc-pmc3312841: Tiny magnets got a medical review. This 2012 paper surveys magnetic nanoparticles for medical uses. The authors map the uses. Their overview guides engineers. Drug delivery led the uses. Akbarzadeh's review is widely cited. It shaped nanomedicine. The review is a classic.
europmc-pmc3334941: Retinal scans got quality rules. This 2012 OSCAR-IB paper sets quality criteria for eye OCT scans. The authors define the standards. Their work guides trials. MS trials adopted the rules. Tewarie's team led the work. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3348041: Teen self-injury got a global count. This 2012 paper pools worldwide rates of teen self-injury. The authors reveal the rates. Their work guides prevention. Girls reported higher rates. Muehlenkamp's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped school programs.
europmc-pmc3364341: Drug-target pairs got predicted. This 2012 paper predicts drug-target pairs from chemical and genomic data. The authors reveal the method. Their work points to repurposing. Yu's team led the work. The method is open source. The paper is widely cited.
