europmc-pmc3372341: Flu's airborne spread got reviewed. This 2006 paper reviews airborne transmission of influenza A. The author maps the evidence. Their overview guides hospitals. Tellier's review is a classic. COVID-19 leaned on the evidence. The paper is widely cited. It shaped hospital policy.
europmc-pmc3373041: Singapore beat dengue for 35 years. This 2006 paper reviews Singapore's long war on dengue mosquitoes. The authors reveal the success. Their work guides programs. Ooi's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Cities copied the playbook.
europmc-pmc3383741: Vaginosis raised HIV transmission. This 2012 paper links bacterial vaginosis to higher HIV spread. The authors reveal the risk. Their work guides prevention. Treating vaginosis cut transmission. Cohen's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped HIV prevention.
europmc-pmc3414841: Breast cancer got a mutation atlas. This 2012 paper catalogs the mutation patterns across 21 breast cancers. The authors reveal the patterns. Their work guides oncology. Nik-Zainal's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. The study shaped cancer genomics.
europmc-pmc3418241: Virus alarms got a stress granule. This 2012 paper shows cell stress granules sound the virus alarm. The authors reveal the detection. Their work guides immunology. Karoui uses a trait of the kink rules. They scale in a clean way from the rest point. That trait lets him grow smooth sheets that hug the true acts. Those sheets are named invariant cones in his build. With them, a large model can be cut to a small one. The small model keeps the acts that count.
arxiv-2601-10341:
Anina Gruica, Benjamin Jany, and Stanislav Kruglik study codes that can change form to fit a net. A store net holds data on many nodes. Nodes vary in how oft they fail. Data vary in how oft they are read. A code that fits one state may fit the next poor.

Convertible codes can morph from one code to the next. The morph should cost as low as it can. The team work in the merge form of this task. They ask how data mix and node mix shape the best morph. The work guides store nets that must adapt over time.
arxiv-2601-10541:
Niffa Cheick Oumar Diaby, Thierry Duchesne, and Mario Marchand tackle a trust problem in machine learning. Models now guide choices in many parts of daily life. Users want to see why a model gives the answer it gives. Clear models also help check for safety and for unfair bias.

The team proposes a blend of simple local models, each one easy to read on its own. Near any given case, the blend acts like one small, clear model. Far away, other local parts take over. The design aims to keep the whole system open to inspection. It offers a path to predictions that people can audit step by step.
arxiv-2601-10741:
Lan Yang and co-authors apply eigen microstate theory to the liquid-gas transition of the Lennard-Jones fluid. Fluids of this kind are a standard test bed for phase change physics. Finding the exact critical point and its exponents by direct simulation is still hard. Near the point, fluctuations span all scales and muddy the numbers.

The team studies the continuous transition inside the canonical ensemble, where volume and particle count are fixed. Eigen microstate theory sorts the system's states by dominant patterns. That sorting can expose the transition more cleanly than raw averages. Sharper critical values help test the deep theory of phase change, which claims shared exponents across many unlike fluids.
arxiv-2601-12041:
Rafał Filipów, Małgorzata Kowalczuk, Hubert Książek, Adam Kwela, and Grzegorz Ucal study a refined form of compactness in topology. The class they use holds spaces where each sequence has a convergent subsequence. The subsequence must be indexed by a set outside a given ideal.

They sort which spaces meet this strict rule for partition-type functions. Ideal-based forms let maths track how large the good index set must be. The work adds a sharp sort for compact spaces. It links sequence acts to ideal structure in a firm way.
arxiv-2601-11341:
Haowen Yang and six coauthors propose a skyrmion quantum diode in this preprint. Their 2026 study is a proof of concept for the device. Skyrmions are tiny swirls of spins with a protected form. That form makes them robust to noise and flaws.

Robust carriers are what quantum links need most of all. A hard task is one-way links between unlike qubits. The team's diode is based on skyrmion qubits. It joins micromagnetic simulations with quantum models in one study. That bridge checks both the magnet side and the quantum side. If it holds, skyrmions could carry quantum data one way. The work is an early step, not a finished device.
arxiv-2601-13141:
Timur Grigorev, Yuhang Dai, Max Potter, and co-authors sort the light lines of carbon monoxide and its kin forms. Carbon monoxide is thought to be the next most common molecule in space after hydrogen. Its kin forms swap one atom for a heavier twin.

The team lists six such forms, from the plain form to rare ones with heavy carbon and heavy oxygen. They use a MARVEL study of lab grade spectra at high detail. Such line lists let sky staff name which form they see in a cloud and how much of it is there. Clean lists matter for work on star birth clouds and far disks alike.
arxiv-2601-13441:
Ali Eren Simsek shows how CMS hunts new physics in data streams made just for odd events. New physics marks at the Large Hadron Collider vary a lot. By their nature they oft look quite unlike Standard Model acts. A stream tuned to stock acts can miss them in full.

Dedicated streams save events that a stock stream would drop. They keep rare, odd, or late marks for a deep read later. Simsek sums how such streams lift the reach of CMS hunts. For collider teams, the piece is a guide to catch what a one size stream would lose. It bears on dark and long lived hunts most of all.
arxiv-2601-12341:
Rezky M. Kam and Coddy N. Siswanto study how language models read feelings in a chat. Most such models build text one token at a time. They weigh past tokens and pick the most likely next one. The pair argue that this step by step view misses how feelings shift and flow.

Feelings in a talk build across turns, and more than one thread can move at once. A token based view can turn that flow into a black box. The authors put forward a time based form of modeling instead. It treats the arc of feeling as a path that runs in time. That shift aims to give a clearer view of how mood moves through a dialogue.
arxiv-2601-12741:
Gyeongwon Jeong, Seonghun Park, and Hongseok Yang introduce flag algebra to computer scientists. Flag algebra is a framework by Razborov for extremal graph theory. It derives asymptotic inequalities between densities of induced subgraphs. Many advances in the field rest on this method, yet it stays unfamiliar outside its home area.

The survey presents flag algebra as a proof system. That framing speaks to readers in logic, programming languages, and formal methods. Automated verification researchers may see tools they can borrow or formalize. A bridge of this kind can move proof ideas between fields. It may also spur machine checked versions of flag algebra arguments.
arxiv-2601-13641:
Shuvayan Banerjee and co-authors fix a flaw in pooled testing built on compressed sensing in 2026. In group testing, samples from many people are mixed into a few pools. Tests on pools must then reveal each person's health state. Compressed sensing rebuilds a sparse signal from fewer measures than usual.

Real work can go wrong when the pooling plan itself is off. The mix used in the lab may not match the plan on paper. The team works on fixing such pooling matrix errors. Sound fixes keep pooled tests true when lab steps drift from the design.
arxiv-2601-13741:
Omar Mohsen proves a broad result on when rough inputs give smooth outputs for operators in 2026. The topic is maximal hypoellipticity, a strong form of this smoothing trait. Mohsen works in an abstract calculus with natural assumptions. In that frame, he ties the trait to one test on the operator's principal symbol.

An operator is maximally hypoelliptic if and only if its principal symbol is left invertible. That one test then yields many known results at once. They include regularity for elliptic operators and the Rockland conjecture work. A single frame that unifies results helps the whole field.
arxiv-2601-13941:
Adamu Issifu and co-authors make the first systematic study of spinning protoquark stars in 2026. Protoquark stars are young, hot stars made of quark matter. The team uses isentropic equations of state in the density-dependent quark mass framework. A quasi-static approach follows the stars as they cool and settle.

They track the Kelvin-Helmholtz evolution of rigidly rotating stars. The path runs from hot, lepton-rich matter to a cold, catalyzed quark star. Rotation can boost a star's mass and test its stability. The work maps how such exotic stars survive their fiery birth.
arxiv-2601-14141:
Mauro D'Arcangelo and Sven Gnutzmann study phase changes in random fuzzy geometries in 2026. Ensembles of random non-commutative geometries can be described by finite Dirac operators. A probability measure weights which geometries appear. Dirac operators of a set type are defined via commutators of hermitian matrices.

Tensor products with a Clifford algebra representation complete the operators. The team studies symmetry breaking and phase transitions in these ensembles. Related random-matrix ensembles provide useful comparisons. Such models probe how space itself might emerge or change phase in quantum gravity. The math is dense, but the phase maps are the key yield. They show where order holds and where it breaks in these odd spaces.
arxiv-2601-14241:
Riku Anttila, Sylvester Eriksson-Bique, and Lassi Rainio study fractal spaces in this 2026 math paper. Their spaces are of Laakso type, a family with a self-similar build. The first two authors set out a general way to build such spaces in past work. The topic here is conformal dimension, a measure of how much a space can be reshaped.

The team gives a simple test for when that dimension is attained in symmetric Laakso-type spaces. Attained means some metric, or distance rule, in the class hits the lowest value. They build those metrics in full, not just in proof. The work also shows new cases of attainment and clears up what can block it.
arxiv-2601-14341:
Amol R Holkundkar gives lectures on electrons in extreme light in this 2026 paper. The text comes from the WiSILS-2024 school. Its topic is relativistic charge particle dynamics in ultra-intense laser pulses. At such intensity, electrons move at speeds close to light, so classic rules fail.

The lectures cover the relativistic equations of motion first. They then turn to radiation-reaction, Thomson scattering, and ponderomotive scattering. The last topic also serves as a potential diagnostic tool. A simulation code named LEADS handles the electron dynamics in the intense pulse. Readers get a taught path through the core ideas, with a working code to match.
arxiv-2601-14641:
Ruishi Zou leads a large team on mental health data tools in this 2026 paper, set for the CHI conference. Advances in data collection now capture rich patient-generated data. Sources range from passive sensing, like wearables and smartphones, to active self-reports, like surveys and ecological momentary assessments. Prior research has shown the utility of such data in mental healthcare.

Big challenges remain in presenting these streams alongside clinical data. Clinicians need one view they can grasp fast. The team's system, MIND, is a narrative dashboard for multimodal data insights. It is built to empower mental health clinicians, as the title says. Readers get a design for turning scattered patient data into a story a clinician can act on.
arxiv-2601-15541:
Heng Zhang and a large team make robot arms safer at contact tasks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Modern vision-language-action models steer robots from images and text. Systems like RDT, Pi0, and OpenVLA-oft output positions for the arm. They lack force-aware adaptation, though. In tasks with contact or uncertainty, that gap can cause unsafe or failed moves.

The team's fix is the CompliantVLA-adaptor. It adds variable impedance control, guided by a vision-language model. Impedance control adjusts how stiffly the arm responds to force. Context from the scene tells it when to yield and when to push. Contact-rich work, from assembly to care tasks, needs that softness. The adaptor aims to give current models a sense of touch without retraining them.
arxiv-2601-15641:
Larry Bowden and five co-authors detect machine failures with quantum tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Catching failures promptly keeps factories efficient and cuts downtime. The team's algorithm joins two ideas. One is quantum computing, through projected quantum feature maps. These maps turn machine data into quantum states, then project back useful features. The other is statistical change-point detection, which flags when a signal's pattern shifts.

A shift in sensor data often marks the start of a fault. The method aims to sharpen anomaly detection in monitoring systems. Better precision means fewer missed faults and fewer false alarms. Factories lose money both ways: stops that were needless, and breakdowns that were missed. Industry readers are the clear audience for this blend of quantum features and classic statistics.
arxiv-2601-15941:
Vishnu Muraleedharan Sajitha, Matthew J. Davis, and L. A. Williamson study wasted work in quantum spin chains in a 2026 arXiv paper. The most work comes out of a quantum system when it is driven adiabatically, that is, very slowly. Faster driving creates frictional work. Frictional work is the gap between the fast output and the adiabatic ideal. The authors compare integrable and non-integrable spin chains. The two classes behave very differently in dynamics.

In the non-integrable chain, they find a clean description. Frictional work matches the diagonal entropy production tied to growing quantum coherence. In plain terms, disorderly driving builds coherence, and entropy accounts for the loss. Such links guide the design of quantum engines and batteries. Knowing where the loss sits helps engineers drive systems faster without paying the full friction price.
arxiv-2601-14841:
Sidi Mohamed Sid'El Moctar, Achraf Ait Laydi, Yousef El Mourabit, and Hélène Bouvrais tackle a hard image task in cell biology. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with microtubules, the thin threads that help hold a cell's shape. These threads are also targets for drugs used against some diseases.

Under a microscope, microtubule networks are hard to trace. The threads bend, cross each other in dense webs, and sit in noisy images. The team presents MTFlow, a new model built on flow matching that is guided by time. The paper sets out the model as its answer to this tracing task.
arxiv-2601-14941:
Tim Palmer revisits a classic puzzle in quantum physics. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with Bell's theorem and the tests of Bell's inequality. Lab tests break that inequality, and physicists still debate what the result means.

One way out drops a premise called measurement independence. That premise says experimenters can freely choose their test settings. Critics call the move a wild plot, since it seems to deny free choice. Palmer links the whole debate to impossible counterfactuals, to what could not have happened, and to a discrete form of Hilbert space.
arxiv-2601-15041:
Oliver Weißl, Vincenzo Riccio, Severin Kacianka, and Andrea Stocco test deep learning systems with made-up inputs. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how to check that such systems behave well in the real world. Classic attacks tweak inputs by tiny amounts to fool a model.

Those tiny tweaks rarely match real failures. Generative test methods can make richer cases, but often only for simple data. The authors use a hypernetwork to adapt a diffusion-based test generator. The aim is broader, more realistic test cases for judging a system's true behavior in use.
arxiv-2601-15141:
Tianshi Xu, Yuteng Chen, and Meng Li clean up the training trails of tool-using language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with agentic reinforcement learning. Models learn by acting, often calling tools such as a Python interpreter to solve hard problems.

For small models, the exploration phase is messy. Runs fail often, and those noisy trails hinder learning. The authors present CLEANER, a method based on self-purified trajectories. By cleaning its own trails first, the model gives the whole training process a much clearer and cleaner signal for the learner to learn from.
arxiv-2601-16041:
Omar Al-Ghattas studies a sharp twist in least squares fits under tight rules. His 2026 preprint sits in the field of chance based search for best fits. Most would think a tighter set of rules can not raise risk. Risk here means the mean loss of the fit. The fit is made by casting data onto the allowed set.

Al-Ghattas shows that this plain hope can fail. It fails even in plain, well known cases. A stricter rule set can in fact leave a worse fit. That flip warns teams who add rules to cut risk. They must test the effect, not just trust the rule. The proof gives a firm base for that care.
arxiv-2601-16441:
Hyunmoon Kim builds one Morse Bott map for all Grassmann sets of a space. His 2026 preprint deals with sets of flat parts of a space. The space has a twist form, called symplectic in the field. A matched complex form on the same space guides the build. Kim forms a square based map on the real Grassmann set.

Its rest points split to flat parts of two pure types. One type is twist null and the next is complex in form. Its firm paths match a known cell split of the set. One map for all such sets joins past case work. The build gives a clean tool for space maths.
arxiv-2601-17341:
Isaac T. Rosin and three co-authors study the wake behind a thin flat plate. The plate stands square to a uniform stream. Wakes are the churned zones that form past such blocks. One might expect calm flow at low speed. The team shows the wake is fully turbulent at a Reynolds number of just 400. That is low for such rich flow.

Their case gives fluid science a clean test bed. A simple shape yields complex flow that codes must match. Engineers who design plates, fins, and panels can learn from it. The work also probes how turbulence starts. Early onset in a plain setup is a clue to the base rules of flow.
arxiv-2601-17541:
Enzo Orsingher and Manfred Marvin Marchione study random motions whose speed varies. They treat motions on a line and in a plane. Space-varying velocity is the first case. A nonlinear change of variables turns it into constant-speed motion. That trick makes hard paths easier to read. A special case traps the motion inside the unit interval.

Confined motions model particles in bounded zones. Speed that varies with place fits traffic, fluids, and animal movement. Exact results for such paths are rare. Each solved case becomes a test for simulation codes. The work adds to the theory of random motion. It shows how transforms tame variable speed.
arxiv-2601-17641:
Hao Fang and five co-authors present RPNT for generalized motor decoding from brain signals. Brain decoding turns neural activity into behavior reads. Decoders must work across brain sites and sessions. They must handle unlike behaviors and many subjects. Most models fail when conditions shift. RPNT is a robust pre-trained neural transformer built for that spread.

Pre-training gives the model a broad base to adapt from. Robustness across subjects is the key test for real BCI use. A decoder that travels well cuts per-user setup time. That matters for clinical rollout at scale. The work aims at decoders that serve new users fast. It treats variation as the norm, not the exception.
arxiv-2601-17741:
Jun Zhu and five co-authors present a frequency-aware neural representation for videos. Implicit neural representations store video as a continuous function. They promise compact storage and flexible playback. Most such methods suffer spectral bias. They favor low frequencies and smooth out fine detail. That hurts rate-distortion scores. The team's design adds frequency awareness to the representation.

Sharper detail at the same size is the goal. Video compression touches streaming, archives, and mobile data costs. Neural codecs could beat classic ones if detail holds. Frequency-aware training attacks their main flaw. The work comes from a team that also studies temporal designs. Together the two papers map a path for neural video.
arxiv-2601-18241:
Elena Bruches and a large team present TAM-Eval, a benchmark for AI that maintains unit tests. Their 2026 preprint notes a gap in software research. Language models show promise across software engineering, yet test work has mostly meant writing new tests in isolation. Real projects also need old tests maintained as the code shifts. A test suite that is not maintained rots fast and starts to mislead. TAM-Eval measures how well models handle that upkeep.

Maintenance includes fixing broken tests and updating them for new behavior. It is unglamorous work that eats real engineering time. A shared benchmark can steer models toward it. The work extends evaluation from creation to care.
arxiv-2601-18941:
Carlo Cafaro, Emma Clements, and Vishnu Vardhan Anuboyina compare two ways to grade how complex a quantum path is. One grade comes from Krylov's method, which tracks how a state spreads through nested subspaces. The other comes from information geometry, which treats the space of states as curved and measures path length there.

The team tests both grades on the simplest quantum system, a two level qubit drawn on the Bloch sphere. They use steady and changing drivers, which trace neat or messy paths on the sphere. Seeing where the two grades agree, or split, helps define what complexity means for quantum motion.
arxiv-2601-19041:
Bo-Cheng Lin, Yi Mei, and Mengjie Zhang guide ant colony search with learned heat maps for huge route problems. The travelling salesman problem asks for the shortest tour through many stops. New solvers paint a heat map of likely edges, but a decoder must still turn scores into one valid tour that visits each stop once.

Greedy decoding can lock in early slips that ruin the tour, while guided local search is sharp but slow and hand built. Their decoder, HeatACO, lets a virtual ant colony walk the heat map instead. The mix aims for tour quality at a cost that scales to very large stop counts.
arxiv-2601-19141:
Xianghui Cao and four co-authors ask why one of the nucleon's gravity related numbers stays so small. Recent simulations and models agree that this form factor stays tiny even when momentum is passed to the nucleon. Its value at zero momentum must vanish, a fact tied to the equivalence principle, but the smallness elsewhere lacks a clear cause.

The team traces the physical origin of that suppression. Form factors encode how a particle's charge, magnetism, and mass are spread inside it. Explaining a stubborn zero like this one sharpens the theory of how quarks and gluons build the mass of everyday matter.
arxiv-2601-19541:
Tianrun Gao and seven colleagues tackle the simulation of systems where several kinds of physics interact. Heat, flow, and stress often act together in the real world. Modeling them jointly is valuable but hard. Many current methods train on data where the physics were split apart, which does not match real coupled systems.

The team's approach, GenCP, is a generative modeling framework for coupled physics. It aims to handle strong links between the different processes in space and time. Split-data methods tend to lose both speed and accuracy in that setting. A model that learns the coupling directly could serve engineering design better. The work speaks to fields from materials to climate, wherever physics refuses to stay separate.
arxiv-2601-19641:
Florian Bruse and Martin Lange work on a deep question in computer science: can complexity classes be pulled apart? The famous gap between P and NP asks whether fast checking implies fast solving. They study the parts of these classes that are invariant under bisimulation, a notion of sameness for processes. A theorem of Otto characterises the P part exactly, using a logic called the polyadic mu-calculus.

The authors use a known construction from model checking to shrink the problem. Definability in the big logic is reduced to definability in the ordinary modal mu-calculus. That reduction works inside a special class of structures called power graphs. The result is a new route toward separating the fragments. Even partial separations would clarify what logic can express.
arxiv-2601-19741:
Nikiforos Galanis studies how well a space mission could detect a faint background of gravitational waves. Pulsar timing arrays have hinted at such a background in the nanohertz band. The LISA mission will listen in the millihertz band from space. Finding a background hum with a single orbiting detector is hard, because the instrument's own noise is also mostly random.

The author examines how the way noise is characterised affects detection. If the noise model is off, a real signal can be missed or a fake one claimed. Careful noise modelling is therefore central to the search. The study helps set realistic expectations for LISA. It also informs how its data should be analysed when it flies.
arxiv-2601-19841:
Armando M. V. Corro, Carlos M. C. Riveros, and Jose L. Teruel Carretero study a family of surfaces in three-dimensional space. The surfaces are defined by their support function, which measures distance from a fixed plane. Here that function is quadratic and of harmonic type. These HQSF surfaces generalise an earlier class built the same way.

The authors obtain a Weierstrass-type representation for them. Such a formula builds every surface of the class from three holomorphic functions. They also classify the surfaces of rotation within the family. Representation formulas turn a geometric condition into concrete data. Classification of the symmetric cases completes the basic picture of the class.
arxiv-2601-20041:
Shih-Hsuan Chiu and Ming-Syan Chen adapt retrieval-augmented generation for personal assistants on edge devices. A phone-based assistant can personalise answers by retrieving a user's profile data. Profile data grows fast, though, as interactions and updates pile up. Edge hardware has little memory and compute to spare, so standard retrieval struggles.

Their system, CiMRAG, is aware of computing-in-memory hardware, adapts to the domain, and resists noise. It targets retrieval that stays fast as profiles swell. Personal data also stays on the device, a privacy advantage over cloud assistants. Making on-device retrieval viable matters as assistants move off the cloud. The work aligns algorithm design with the hardware that will run it.
arxiv-2601-20641:
Boaz Carmeli and four colleagues investigate whether vision-language model agents develop their own task-oriented communication. When agents must cooperate, they might invent protocols that differ from natural language. The authors focus on two properties such protocols may show: efficiency, conveying task-relevant content more concisely than natural language, and covertness.

A covert protocol is hard for outside observers to interpret, which raises concerns about transparency and control. The study uses collaborative reasoning tasks. Watching how machine dialects form, and whether humans can still read them, is central to keeping multi-agent systems accountable. The risk grows as more teams of agents are put to work side by side.
arxiv-2601-18441:
Hrishi Narayanan and three colleagues study how two people can sync a file when one copy has been changed in chunks. Each change swaps one short run of text for a new run of text. The swap can change the length of the run, but only by a set small cap. The task is to send as few bits as one can so the far copy can be made whole.

The team design codes for that sync task when more than one chunk has changed. Good codes matter when files are shared and fixed by many hands at once. Each bit saved cuts wait and cost for all who share the file. Their work sets how low the send size can go and gives plans that come close to that floor. Such codes could sit at the heart of fresh tools for joint work on text.
arxiv-2601-18541:
Enrique Calderoli and Gerardo Martínez study how drops of quantum fluid form in mixes of two kinds of atoms. Such drops are a new phase of cold gas. They hold them-selves up by a faint push from the jiggle of the gas, a push past the plain pull that would crush them. Much work has charted drops in mixes of like atoms.

Mixes of unlike atoms are less well known, most of all in how the drops are born. The pair trace that birth: how a calm mix breaks, clumps, and settles into drops. The path may shift with the mass gap and the pull strength of the pair. A clear map of the birth could help labs grow drops on call. Drops are prized as clean test beds for the laws of cold matter.
arxiv-2601-21241:
A 2026 arXiv paper presents a fast implicit scheme for flows made of many materials side by side. Layered fluids can act quite unlike any one of their layers alone. Taken as a whole, such a stack behaves like a new kind of fluid material.

Each layer is described by the classic Euler equations with a stiffened gas law. The scheme works in coordinates that move with the fluid itself. That choice helps track the borders between materials as they shift. The method aims at accurate results for layered flows found in engineering and physics.
arxiv-2601-21641:
Evandro S. Ortigossa and Eran Segal bring mixture-of-experts scaling to time series forecasting. Transformers have advanced forecasting, but they scale poorly to long histories. Expert layers are a proven scaling trick in language models, where each token is routed to a few specialists.

Token-wise routing fits text, where each word is fairly separate. Time series are different: nearby points form stretches with shared meaning. The authors route whole segments at several resolutions instead. Segment routing respects the local, continuous nature of signals like demand, weather, and traffic, and should let forecasters grow without losing the thread of long patterns.
arxiv-2601-21741:
Erick Pasten and Christos G. Tsagas explain why galaxy peculiar motions grow faster in Einstein's gravity than in Newton's. Surveys keep reporting bulk flows, large-scale drifts of galaxies, that look too big and too fast for the standard model. The mismatch has become a standing problem for the concordance picture of the cosmos.

The authors trace part of the gap to the theory itself. General relativity lets these velocities grow faster than Newtonian reasoning suggests. That does not settle the bulk flow dispute, but it recalibrates what counts as anomalous. Some of the reported excess may be relativity doing exactly what it should.
arxiv-2601-22441:
Getachew Befekadu opens a two-part study on inference when the true likelihood is out of reach. In such cases, teams simulate data and compare it to real data through summary scores. His 2026 preprint lets a learned score act as a stand-in likelihood, with a bonus: it can improve the inference as it goes.

The frame is Bayesian, so it yields full ranges of doubt, not just point calls. Learned scores can adapt to the model at hand. The work aims at fields where simulators rule, from epidemics to climate. Part one lays the base; part two builds on it.
arxiv-2601-22541:
Sean Current, Chandan Kumar, Datta Gaitonde, and Srinivasan Parthasarathy test how far neural surrogates can roll out a hard airflow on their own. Neural operators learn to step a physics field forward at great speed. Their 2026 preprint uses the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, the core rules of gas flow, with shocks and sharp fronts.

Long rollouts are where such tools tend to drift or blow up. The bench marks that drift over many steps. Honest limits help engineers know when a fast surrogate can be trusted. The work serves flight and turbine design.
arxiv-2601-21841:
Robots that act in the physical world face a planning problem that text models do not. A large language model can reason in words. An embodied agent faces more. It must break a high-level goal into steps it can actually perform. Each step must fit a changing, observed environment.

The 2026 preprint behind this entry proposes task planning that is informed by graphs. The idea is simple. Let the structure of the environment guide how the model generates actions. Do not let it improvise long chains of steps unaided. Graph guidance could cut the classic failure mode of robot planners. Fluent plans that break on the third step because an object is not where the words assumed it was.
arxiv-2601-22041:
Naomi Pitzer and Daniela Mihai study how artificial agents invent ways to communicate when their senses differ. Research on emergent communication shows how agents develop shared, structured signals. Most studies, though, assume agents share the same modality or aligned representations of the world.

Real settings are messier. The authors study a multi-step binary communication game where agents differ in modality and lack perceptual grounding in a shared world. One agent's signal must cross into another's different way of sensing. Their 2026 preprint asks what shared structure can still emerge. The results speak to multi-agent systems deployed in the wild, where cameras, microphones, and other sensors rarely give matching views.
arxiv-2601-22241:
Jelle Westra and co-authors study two design choices that decide whether gradient-free optimization finds good structures. Topology optimization designs structures, such as beams, by simulation, without gradient information. It is widely used in engineering because it can discover high-performing shapes that no one would sketch by hand.

Success depends on the geometric parameterization, which defines the search space, and on the optimizer that explores it. Using a cantilever beam as a case study, the team's 2026 preprint investigates how those two choices interact. Their findings guide engineers who must pick a setup before burning simulation budgets: the best optimizer on the wrong parameterization still designs the wrong beam.
arxiv-2601-21041:
Dylan Jow and Delon Shen develop the theory of reading starlight that twinkles through interstellar gas. Their 2026 paper concerns scintillometry. Compact radio sources, such as pulsars and fast radio bursts, scintillate in the interstellar medium. Their scattered images interfere at the observer. Scintillometry extracts astrometric information from that interference. It can locate the images and measure distances to the screen and the source.

Precise astrometry from scintillation is a young art. The authors aim toward precision, laying out theory and prospects. Better distances would map the gas between the stars. They would also sharpen the positions of exotic radio sources. The paper is a roadmap for observers and theorists alike. It shows how a nuisance effect can become a measuring tool.
arxiv-2512-00841:
Du Wenzhang proposes a market-based twist on federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains one model across many devices or sites without pooling their data. For multimedia tasks, the method strains under uneven data across clients and tight communication limits, especially with large models.

Classic averaging methods send full model weights back and forth, and they can diverge when client data differ a lot. The proposed system, KTA v2, trades knowledge in prediction space instead of raw weights. Clients buy and sell predictions in a knowledge market. Trading compact predictions could cut traffic while keeping learning stable.
arxiv-2512-01141:
Akshat Bagade, Maanas Baraya, Chittebbayi Penugonda, and Muhammad Yousuf teach machines to rename variables in a 2025 paper. Developers often inherit code whose variable names are generic or misleading. Teams moving fast leave many functions undocumented, which slows comprehension for everyone who reads the code later.

Poor names raise the risk of subtle bugs. They also make it harder for large language models to reason about code, since names carry much of the meaning. Their neural variable name repair system learns to suggest readable identifiers. Automatic renaming could help teams clean legacy code and help AI coding tools understand it.
arxiv-2601-22841:
Leonard Hackel, Tom Burgert, and Begüm Demir ask how much of a big Earth-observation model is really needed. Foundation models for remote sensing borrow their design from computer vision. They work well on tasks like mapping land from satellite images, but they are large and costly to run.

The authors test how far these models can be slimmed down without losing skill. Their checks question whether vision scaling rules carry over to satellite data at all. Leaner models would let more groups map crops, forests, and floods with modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-23041:
Youxu Shi, Suorong Yang, and Dong Liu steer vision-language models away from making things up. These models do well on tasks that mix images and text, but they still hallucinate and fail on safety, even at large scale. Steering nudges a model's internal state to improve behavior with little cost.

Their one-shot optimized steering vector is tuned once, then applied broadly. Prior steering traded efficiency against effectiveness in awkward ways. A cheap, reusable vector could make image-aware assistants more truthful without retraining. Steering is attractive because it is lightweight: one vector can adjust behavior without retraining the whole multimodal model.
arxiv-2601-23241:
Damien Barbier studies when a single binary neuron becomes trainable, using a statistical-mechanics lens. Binary neurons take only two states, making them cheap but hard to train. The connected ensemble framework tracks how low-loss paths form in rugged loss landscapes.

Those paths reveal when a network can learn a simple task at all. They also show which minima training should aim for. Knowing the transition point between impossible and trainable guides the design of efficient, discrete networks. Low-loss paths are the diagnostic object, revealing which minima training should target once trainability switches on.
arxiv-2512-00641:
Facial expression recognition often collapses when the people or cameras change between training and deployment. Razieh Ghaedi and co-authors propose GAT-ADA in 2025, a graph-attention network with adversarial domain alignment for cross-domain expression recognition. Severe domain shift is the central obstacle.

The framework pairs a ResNet-50 backbone with a batch-level graph attention network that models relations between samples under shift. Adversarial alignment pushes the model toward features that work in both domains. Robust expression recognition supports accessibility tools and human-computer interaction that must work for new users without retraining. Batch-level graphs let the model borrow strength from similar faces in the same batch. Adversarial alignment is the mechanism that forces domain-blind features.
arxiv-2512-01941:
A Schrödinger operator describes a quantum particle moving through a potential landscape, and bound states appear as eigenvalues below the spectrum's edge. Jussi Behrndt and three co-authors study in 2025 what happens with complex-valued potentials, in one or two dimensions, when the coupling is weak.

Complex potentials break the usual rules, since energies need no longer be real numbers. The authors derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the potential for discrete eigenvalues to exist in this faint-coupling regime. They also examine whether such eigenvalues are unique and how their algebraic multiplicity behaves. The results tidy a corner of spectral theory where intuition from real potentials fails.
arxiv-2512-02241:
Some systems hang between life and death. Bits branch, move, and wipe each other out, and the group as a whole lives or dies. Peter Grassberger's 2025 paper reports fine-grained computer runs of one such class: parity conserving directed percolation. It is the second most weighty class of these life-or-death phase shifts.

What sets this class apart is parity. The count of bits is kept modulo two, so a finite system splits into even and odd camps with unlike fates. Careful runs pin down the class's traits near the tipping point, in one space dimension plus time. Shared classes let one pattern forecast the acts of many unlike systems, so each sharp trait tightens a broad net.
arxiv-2512-02841:
Lechen Zhang and five co-authors test whether one system prompt can steer a language model well in many languages. System prompts condition model behavior at inference time with little cost. Most prior study covers English only, yet real deployments serve the whole world at once.

A single prompt that behaves reliably across languages is the goal. The team measures steerability cross lingually, hunting for languages where steering slips. Findings of this kind help builders write prompts that stay accurate and robust, so users get equal quality whatever tongue they type in. One prompt for all tongues cuts cost and drift, but only if each tongue gets the same grip on the wheel.
arxiv-2512-02941:
Wittawat Kositwattanarerk and three co-authors study the false codewords that can fool modern error correcting decoders. Low density parity check codes nearly reach channel capacity with iterative decoders. Those decoders sometimes stall on pseudocodewords, patterns that look valid but are not true codewords.

The authors view pseudocodewords through the fundamental cone, a geometric object that organizes decoder behavior. They cover quantum, quasi cyclic, and spatially coupled code families. Understanding these traps helps engineers design decoders for storage and communication that fail less often at low error rates. False friends of true codewords are the traps that bite at the last step. A clear view of them is worth the work it takes to draw.
plos-pone-0010041:
The authors were Philippe Colson, Hervé Richet, Christelle Desnues, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study chased a plant virus found in human stool. Pepper mild mottle virus infects peppers, yet living virus had turned up in healthy people. Where it came from and whether it harms people were both unclear.

The team tested pepper food products and hundreds of stool samples from adults and children. They linked the virus to specific immune responses, fever, belly pain, and itching in some people. A plant virus troubling humans would be an unusual finding worth careful follow-up.
plos-pone-0010141:
The authors were Fangqing Zhao, Jie Bai, Jinyu Wu, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sequenced plasmids from Klebsiella pneumoniae, a hospital bacterium. Plasmids are small DNA circles that bacteria trade with each other. Some carry genes for resisting many drugs at once, a growing problem in treating infections.

By sequencing these plasmids and comparing their genetic variation, the team traced how resistance spreads. Plasmids can cross between strains and even species, carrying their cargo along. Knowing their structure helps hospitals and scientists track and slow that spread. The paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010241:
Laura Bianchi and Ana Díez-Sampedro changed one building block in a protein in 2010. The protein family, SGLT, moves sugar across cell membranes together with sodium. One member, SGLT1, absorbs glucose in the gut. Another, SGLT3, was known only as a sugar sensor, not a transporter, until this PLOS ONE study.

A single amino acid change converted SGLT3 from sensor into a working sugar transporter. That tiny switch shows how closely sensing and transport are related in this family. The insight may help design drugs that fine-tune sugar handling in diabetes and gut disease.
plos-pone-0010341:
Kai Li, Rui Wang, Enerlyn Lozada and co-workers examined a DNA repair protein called WRN in PLOS ONE in 2010. WRN helps cells copy, swap, and fix DNA. It can gain a chemical tag called an acetyl group, and that tagging matters when DNA is damaged. The group had earlier shown tagging changes what the protein does and where it sits in the cell.

Here they asked whether tagging also controls how long WRN lasts. Their results show tagging protects WRN from being marked for disposal. That disposal mark is called ubiquitin, and blocking it keeps the protein stable. A stable repair protein can stay on duty longer after damage. The finding adds a control knob to a system cells need for genome care.
plos-pone-0009841:
Short DNA words recur across genomes, but some appear far more often than chance allows. Colin Davenport and Burkhard Tümmler cataloged such words shared by most bacteria. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Oligonucleotides are short stretches of DNA letters. The abundant ones turn up again and again across very different bacteria. Shared abundance hints that these sequences do jobs cells cannot skip. A catalog of them gives researchers reference points for comparing genomes. It can also help spot contamination or mislabeled samples in sequencing work. Most bacteria share more of their DNA language than expected.
plos-pone-0009941:
Stony corals build reefs, but their diversity is not spread evenly across the sea. Assaf Zvuloni, Robert van Woesik, and Yossi Loya measured how coral diversity divides across space around Zanzibar Island. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Diversity partitioning splits total variety into shares at each spatial scale. The scales ran from small patches to the whole region around the Tanzanian island. Knowing where variety concentrates tells protectors where reserves do most good. The method applies to any habitat split across scales. Zanzibar sits off the coast of Tanzania in the Indian Ocean.
